'Incredible' Red Bull upgrade enlivens F1 in Malaysia

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 12:25:57 GMT

Verstappen took his first pole position of 2026 at Sepang

Even Lewis Hamilton, starting from his equal best grid position of the year in second place, fears Max Verstappen will be tough to beat in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Verstappen has dominated the weekend so far on Formula 1's return to the Sepang track for the first time since 2017.

Hamilton joins him on the front row to revive memories of their no-holds-barred title battle five years ago.

But at nearly 0.3 seconds slower in qualifying, and with the pace Verstappen has shown all weekend, Hamilton's mindset on Saturday was to "just try my best to hold on to him tomorrow".

This was Verstappen's first pole position of the year - a remarkable statistic for someone who came within two points of winning a fifth world title last year after one of the all-time great fightbacks.

Red Bull started the year off the pace - the car was on average more than 0.5secs a lap slower than Mercedes in the first half of the year - and for a time there were questions as to whether Verstappen would stick around for 2027.

But after being courted by McLaren, Verstappen signed a two-year contract extension over the summer break, saying he believed in the Red Bull project and didn't mind putting in the work to turn things around.

Verstappen arrived in Malaysia after a run of three consecutive podium finishes, and with Red Bull hoping to prove out an upgrade that had seen them finish less than 0.2secs off victory in Baku last Sunday.

In the tropical heat of Malaysia, around the demanding long corners of this track with perhaps the roughest surface of the season, the upgrade - centred on a new floor - has more than proved its worth.

"It's been an incredible result for us," Verstappen said. "Looking at the season, how it started for us and the progression that we have made. At some tracks we were kind of close, but now I think this weekend it was very positive for us.

"We have been adding bits to the car and they have worked. It's simple as that. When they work, you gain lap time, you have a better overall balance in the car.

"So with tyres that are very sensitive to balance, that gives you also more lap time.

"And then on a track probably where it's all very hot and you want a, let's say, stable balance or connected balance, then that's very important. And that's what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends."

This video can not be played

'It's a proud moment'

Team-mate Isack Hadjar, who missed the first three races after the summer break with a wrist broken while boxing as part of his training programme, says the car felt transformed when he returned in Baku last weekend.

"I jumped in a car that's way better than when I left it in Budapest," said the Frenchman, who qualified third, but will start eighth after a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts.

"Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference. And the last two weekends have been surprising."

A good car balance should put Verstappen in a good place for a race that will be dominated by tyre degradation in the stifling heat, whether the threatened rain holds off or not.

This video can not be played

'I'm so, so, so happy'

Hamilton, for one, but also Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who under-performed slightly in qualifying because of a combination between an unusual tyre strategy and an error on an early run.

The world championship leader's fourth place becomes third on the grid with Hadjar's penalty, and he can usually be relied upon to be a factor in the race.

Antonelli's main focus will be his advantage over team-mate George Russell, who trails the Italian by 66 points and starts four places behind, his momentum from his Baku win stalled, and somewhat perplexed as to his and his team's lack of pace.

At Mercedes, the bigger question is over the aerodynamic upgrade they brought to the car this weekend.

Mercedes are lagging behind their rivals when it comes to developing their car this season, apparently at least in part because they front-loaded their spend early in the season.

But this first big update since the Canadian Grand Prix in June has not yet proved the step they had expected.

The question is whether that is to do with the parts themselves or the very specific conditions of this weekend, in the heat and on the rough track surface, which is putting the tyres through the mill, and massively limiting the useful laps teams can do in terms of set-up work.

Antonelli said: "With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different. So, we're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best, in the high-speed corner and low-speed corners.

"Our high-speed performance has been very strong this weekend. We were very quick in the high-speed, but in the low-speed we lacked. So, we need to understand why and try to move on and improve."

As for the race, Antonelli said: "Track position is going to be very important. Strategy is going to be really important.

"It's a race where we will attack. Because undercut (stopping first and gaining time on a rival on fresh tyres) is incredibly powerful.

"So whenever there's an opportunity, we should go for maybe an undercut and try to maximise our opportunity.

"Tomorrow might be two stops, three stops. We don't know. But the only thing we know is that it's going to be roasting hot out there."

Traitors claim their first victim as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 11:07:52 GMT

A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors.

As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player.

Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment.

"It's gutting to be the first out," Rajan said afterwards, noting that perhaps it was because he had been "a bit bullish with Richard" earlier in the day.

"But you know what, games are games, and just as there are winners, so there have to be losers."

The episode drew in a peak audience of 8.6 million viewers, just short of the debut episode with an average of 8.9 million viewers.

The morning following Rajan's banishment, presenter Claudia Winkleman confirmed the University Challenge host's murder to the other players, joking: "That's what I call a starter for 10."

Acaster, meanwhile, reflected: "I'm gutted to not be a faithful anymore, I don't like lying. But if I don't join them, they'll kill me." You can't fault his logic.

The decision meant that Grant, an Oscar-nominated actor with a Razzie-worthy traitor strategy, did at least manage to commit one successful murder despite his shambolic first day.

The 69-year-old spent much of Friday's episode trying to repair the damage from his earlier exchange in the bar, where he blurted out that he was a traitor to Joe Lycett, Rob Beckett and several others.

Obviously a man who made such an excellent Spice Girls manager in the 1997 masterpiece Spice World: The Movie is hard for anyone to picture as a traitor, so many other players assumed Grant was attempting some elaborate double bluff.

Jama is off to a much stronger start. "I am quite shocked at my ability to just lie to everyone," the Love Island host said in the castle's diary room. "I'm an all-or-nothing kind of honey."

As the players gathered for breakfast, other theories began to surface. Mathematician Hannah Fry said she had spotted Leigh-Anne Pinnock putting on make-up late in the evening, perhaps heading to the turret.

"I think it's James," declared Jerry Hall, suddenly giving viewers hope that the new cast will be better traitor hunters than last year's. Until she clarified that she was talking about James Blunt, not Acaster.

As the players prepared to head out for the mission, conversations turned to far more important matters. "Do you have more teeth than a normal person?" Grant asked Beckett.

The players made their way to the mission, which had the usual slightly convoluted rules that took Winkleman quite a while to explain.

In a nutshell, the celebrities were to be buried alive in pairs, with only one duo left above ground.

Ross Kemp was pre-selected by the traitors to be protected from burial along with his grave partner Romesh Ranganathan, who did a delightful dance when he found out he wouldn't be going underground.

Kemp and Ranganathan then had the opportunity to dig up some gold graves which would add to the prize pot, or alternatively dig up and free their fellow players.

They opted for the latter, which resulted in some other players struggling to get the soil off their faces. In the end, all the celebrities were released, with the exception of Fry and Hall.

The pair were freed early after Hall shouted the emergency word "Haggis!" – effectively a Scottish version of "I'm a celebrity get me out of here!" - because she was visibly uncomfortable being buried alive.

It might have led to an early release, but it ultimately guaranteed that either she or Fry will be murdered next, unless the traitors recruit again.

"Just you and me up for murder," Fry told Hall afterwards. "You'd better not be a traitor or I'm really screwed!"

In a flashback shown to viewers, Acaster explained the decision to protect Kemp from burial, telling his fellow traitors: "I think if we give it to Ross, he'll overthink it, and behave in a way that would draw suspicion."

Very clever. "You're a wonderful traitor," observed Grant. (Certainly better than him.)

Finally, it was time for the first banishment of the series, with Grant still in damage control mode.

"I have a slight pinprick of advantage," he told himself in the castle's diary room. "Nobody would possibly believe that anybody would be so stupid as to come forward and say 'I am a traitor'. I'm hoping that I do get away with it."

His fellow traitors clearly wanted to be supportive, but things were getting dicey.

Acaster described him as a "loose cannon", while Jama said: "I want to save him, even though he's dug himself the biggest hole imaginable."

Back in the castle, Ranganathan pointed out: "If somebody else had behaved like Richard, we wouldn't even be having a debate about this, you would just go 'you've got to vote for him'."

But others had a slightly different take. "Richard feels a little too easy," reflected actress Myha'la, "and then anybody pushing him feels suspicious to me."

Comedian Joanne McNally agreed some players were "using him as a fall guy and a decoy," although she did admit later that he's "made such a shambles of it now".

As discussions got going, it took a surprisingly long time for Grant's name to come up, as the other players debated other suspects such as Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The actress aroused suspicion because she was the first celebrity this year to receive a shield. The group seemed to have overlooked she only got that - in the opening minutes of the first show - after the other contestants voted her the most trustworthy.

But as discussion turned to Grant, Hesmondhalgh put forward one of the most convincing cases of the night.

"You came into the bar, and said you were a traitor," she told him. "It was a bold move. It was chaotic and we love you for your chaos.

"I think we are at risk of being the most idiotic group of faithfuls in the world, if we go for someone else tonight based on nothing at all, when somebody has come into the room and said 'I am a traitor'. There's no reason to say it unless you are."

Miranda Hart agreed that "the joy when he took off his blindfold" when Winkleman first selected the traitors made Grant look suspicious.

Viewers will have to wait until the next episode to see how the round table goes, as the episode finished before voting had even started.

(It's worth saying that, as cliffhangers go, this was far less irritating than ending an episode in the middle of voting, as producers often do.)

"You've given us all a problem," Ranganathan told Grant as the episode drew to a close and the players prepared to vote. "By doing that, it was a big mistake by you, I feel like you forced our hand."

Admittedly, it's not looking good - the round table is shaping up to be a landslide vote against Grant. But we still wouldn't bet against him.

"I do not go down without a fight," he concluded. "I couldn't have survived showbusiness for four decades without a fight."

UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:58:51 GMT

A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.

Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.

Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.

Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."

Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.

"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:27:57 GMT

The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again.

So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up.

Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands."

But Conservative MPs are aware that the party itself still has a much bigger issue - in the words of one shadow cabinet member: "The problem we still have is trust of the party and the brand". The shadow of the years of chaos still looms. And while Badenoch has made good progress since she took the job, most of that was up against an unpopular prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, on whom she landed plenty of political punches. She has to show "what being Conservative is now", says another senior Tory, taking on a different, more popular, rival in Andy Burnham.

The Tories' warm-up to conference has been so far, so traditional. A proposed dramatic expansion of prison places kicks off Badenoch's second big party get-together. With it, a message that echoes the well-known mantra of the early 1990s Tories, issued by former leader Michael Howard at party conference: "Prison works". They are not just talking about adding on a few cells here and there, but spelling out a monumental increase in the numbers of people that the country locks up.

That follows the announcement of a new "tough love" approach for young people trying to claim benefits. Don't expect the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whateley, to produce a moment as controversial as when the then-welfare secretary, Peter Lilley, proclaimed from the stage that he had "a little list" of benefit claimants he wanted to root out. But the Conservatives are determined to keep concentrating on the size of the welfare bill – believing it's right to do so for financial and moral reasons.

You can expect to hear more in the week about fundamental conservative principles: people keeping more of their own money, government only stepping in when really required to, pointed concern about the level of the country's debt and public spending. And again, of course, that means Kemi Badenoch disavowing much of what the Conservatives did in office between 2010 and 2024, when the civil service grew, the tax burden grew, a law was passed to try to combat climate change, the list goes on.

She'll set out at some length in the coming days what she sees as classic conservative first principles: the core beliefs the party was founded on and drifted from, she reckons, in the years gone by. If anything, Badenoch told interviewers this week the party was "finally saying what we believe" and "should be more aggressive" in displaying the party's core.

She believes the arrival of Andy Burnham makes that easier. There's a clearer contrast between the two. A senior ally of Badenoch says Burnham has "opened the door to it quite well, as he has harked back to the '70s in a way that I'm astonished by". Suggesting the pleasing atmospherics of Burnham's Labour are just that, atmospherics, the ally adds: "It's like a fairy story where he has come to the rescue of Britain and he has a wand in his hand and nothing else".

As we talked about a couple of weeks ago, the contrasts between Labour and the Conservatives are sharper now Burnham is in post, and the conference season is only serving to exaggerate that. They are both only too happy to emphasise it with their messages, retro or not, designed to show the true souls of their tribes.

But while Badenoch might find it easier to argue clearly with Burnham, rather than tangle with Starmer over process, it is harder to face an opponent who, at least for now, is proving more appealing to the public. And while plenty of Conservatives are hopeful in private that Reform might have peaked, they can't be sure that's true, or that the swathes of voters who abandoned the Tories for Farage's party will return.

Badenoch has always seemed allergic to the idea of doing any kind of deal with Reform, who she dismisses as a party of protest. And her allies hope, and some believe, that Reform's appeal will fade, making the Conservatives again the obvious alternative government. But fundamental arithmetic displays that, for as long as millions of voters on the right are tempted by Farage, it's harder for the Tories to triumph. One shadow minister admits "we've still got a whole battle on the right" even though "Kemi's boldness" is beginning to break through.

So, in the coming next days, prepare for a "classic showing of Tory wares": an attempt by the party's leader to set out their fundamental beliefs about the country and how it should be governed.

There are pockets of nerves that Kemi Badenoch risks rewinding to an previous era. One when another newly confident leader, David Cameron, ushered in the modern Tory party on the conference stage in front of digitally produced green foliage and sunlight. One former cabinet minister warns that it's "the big risk – so easy to slip into an alienating divisive manner – nasty party stuff".

When it comes to policy, and striking the right tone, they warn that Badenoch must "be mindful that she has to win Cheltenham and Maidenhead as well as Clacton".

But Kemi Badenoch is visibly more confident and is aware of the chance in front of her – seemingly unworried about the possible downsides of making an increasingly direct argument to you, eager to stride that mercifully bigger Birmingham stage.

EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 02:36:19 GMT

Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.

Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.

It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.

Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.

So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?

Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.

It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.

"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.

But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.

Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".

"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.

When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs.

Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.

She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.

On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.

Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.

Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.

But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.

Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.

Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.

Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.

Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the motor starts acting as a generator. This creates resistance that slows the car down and also produces electricity that can be stored in the battery. The accelerator needs to be released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration.

"It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.

This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".

Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.

Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.

She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself.

Some features of electric cars may feel unfamiliar to drivers at first, adds Mike Hawes, head of the Society of Motor Manufacturers.

He says EVs can offer a different driving experience. "However, drivers typically adjust quickly to these characteristics, and many models also allow regenerative braking to be tailored to individual preferences."

Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, according to Hac, and experts say women and children are more susceptible.

Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.

As their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show.

At the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030.

Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy.

The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific".

Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness.

Experts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says.

There are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration.

In some EVs, regenerative braking can also often be turned off.

Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly".

But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.

Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises?

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 02:26:42 GMT

Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.

You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view.

When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.

But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.

Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.

Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months.

While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise.

Aurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul".

It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise".

The 20-year-old criminology student is a huge One Direction fan and says she just about managed to avoid spoilers for Styles' Together, Together tour over summer.

But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted".

"When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says.

"I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get."

Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them.

"I'm the type of person that loves to be prepared," the 22-year-old says.

"I love to know what the stage is looking like, what the set list consists of and where to stand."

McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing.

"Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds.

Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected.

Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run.

But the Guardian's deputy music editor Laura Snapes says it's not just fans who can benefit from these twists.

"One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."

Figures shared by TikTok with Newsbeat show posts using #CharliXCX have increased by more than 40% since the singer launched her Music, Fashion, Film tour last month.

If you want to avoid spoilers, there's only one thing you can do, according to Snapes: "You have to not look at TikTok.

"If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."

Phoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether.

Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out.

McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans.

But Collins says she's "not totally against it".

What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want.

But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds.

"I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script.

"You're always going to be surprised."

Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'

BBC News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 01:43:20 GMT

Hayden Kuhn and Savannah Aanderud had never set foot in Scotland before they decided it was the perfect place to get married last May.

The couple, from Pennsylvania in the US, wanted a destination wedding that would take their family and friends on an adventure with them.

They considered locations across Europe, before deciding on Scotland after Savannah saw photographs of a castle wedding online.

"I think it was on Pinterest," she said. "Somebody got married in a castle and I was like 'Oh, I have to do that'."

The pair are far from alone in seeing Scotland as the ultimate romantic destination.

Nearly a quarter of all marriages registered in Scotland last year involved couples who did not live in the country.

Figures from National Records of Scotland show that 6,596 of the 27,191 weddings recorded in 2025 involved neither partner being a Scottish resident.

But what is it about the country that persuades these couples to travel hundreds and sometimes thousands of miles to get married here?

Nowhere attracts more visiting couples than Gretna Green.

Of the 6,596 marriages involving non-Scottish residents last year, 3,492 took place in the Dumfries and Galloway town, meaning it alone accounted for more than half of Scotland's destination weddings.

The town's association with romance dates back to 1754, when changes to marriage laws in England prompted young runaway couples to cross the border into Scotland, where they could marry without needing parental consent.

More than 250 years later, it remains one of the world's best-known wedding destinations.

It was this reputation that appealed to Patryk and Angelika Klimorowski, both 27, who travelled from north-west England to tie the knot there.

The couple said Scotland had long been woven into their relationship.

They first met when they were 15, when Patryk's parents moved to England from Poland, and one of the first things they bonded over was the 1996 movie Loch Ness.

Years later, that shared childhood favourite took on new significance when Patryk proposed on its shores.

Their connection to Scotland first started on a road trip in 2021, and they have regularly returned to explore the Highlands and celebrate their anniversaries in Edinburgh.

This year alone, they have travelled north of the border every two months.

So Scotland felt like the natural place to say "I do", they said.

Both Angelika and Patryk are history lovers and said they were drawn to the centuries-old tradition of a Gretna wedding.

"It meant something to us being part of that heritage." Angelika said.

Patryk said that his favourite memory was watching his bride walk down the aisle to the sound of Flower of Scotland played on the bagpipes.

"That sort of music just creates such a whimsical and romantic atmosphere that really can't be recreated in many countries outside of Scotland," Angelika said.

Those moments left a lasting impression on their families who had travelled from Poland.

"They hadn't really experienced anything like that before," she said.

The appeal was not just Gretna's history, Angelika said.

Less than an hour‘s drive from where they got married, the couple found themselves surrounded by dramatic scenery for their wedding photographs.

"There's not a lot of places in the world where you can do that," she said.

Although neither bride nor groom is Scottish, both say they feel a deep connection to the country.

"It's not home, but it feels like a home away from home," Angelika said.

Chihon Ley Polanco, from Chile, and Ana-Maria Bucatari, from Moldova, came to Scotland to study, but the country quickly became the backdrop to their love story.

The couple first met in 2018 through a dance society at the University of Edinburgh, when Ana-Maria was on an Erasmus exchange and Chihon was completing his postgraduate studies.

They they spent years as friends, and it was not until Ana-Maria returned to Edinburgh in 2024 that their relationship became something more.

And their romance blossomed in the same place their friendship had years earlier.

"Everything happened again on the dance floor," Ana-Maria said.

Just four months after getting engaged, the pair walked down the aisle on the Isle of Arran.

The couple said they "fell in love" with the island at first sight, due to it having the "complete scenery of Scotland".

"You feel that you're in a magical place", said Chihon. "It's very unique."

The couple said Scotland felt like the natural choice.

"We're from two different continents," Chihon said. "Scotland is where we met and where we built our life together."

Their wedding brought together family and friends from across the world, with parts of the ceremony translated live into Spanish and Russian for relatives travelling from Chile and Moldova.

Chihon said friends from all over the world joined the couple for their celebrations.

The highlights of the night included a traditional ceilidh and a final group karaoke singalong of Sunshine on Leith, led by their Scottish wedding guests.

While some of their international guests were unfamiliar with Scottish wedding traditions, that did little to dampen their enthusiasm.

"We had people saying, 'We have no idea what's going on, but we're going to join in'," Chihon said.

He said Scotland would always hold a special place in their lives.

"Like Robbie Burns said, 'my heart's in the Highlands wherever I go'," he said.

"I think Scotland will be with us forever. I couldn't be more grateful. It was already special to me before, but now that I'm married to the woman of my dreams, it's like I owe everything to Scotland."

The same experience was echoed by Hayden and Savannah.

Despite arriving in Scotland just two days before their wedding, the couple said the country's wedding industry made planning from abroad remarkably straightforward.

They chose a castle near Edinburgh, and were drawn not only by the scenery but also by the sense of history they felt was harder to find back home.

"Scotland has this combination of this lovely countryside beauty and history," Savannah said.

"You don't get a lot of the historical venues like you do here, in the United States."

The couple also wove Scottish traditions into their ceremony, taking part in a Celtic handfasting ritual, using pieces of fabric provided by both of their grandmothers.

They said an important part of their decision was the chance to share the experience with loved ones.

"We wanted to go somewhere that would take our whole family on an adventure with us," Hayden said.

Many of their guests turned the wedding into a longer holiday, extending their stays to explore Scotland and even joining the couple on their honeymoon in the Highlands afterwards.

Looking back, the newlyweds say Scotland exceeded every expectation.

Savannah said: "Scotland is like nothing we've ever seen before. We were just blown away by how beautiful everything was."

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 08:21:54 GMT

If buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the money to get there is a marathon.

The "Your First Home" scheme, announced on Saturday, aims to help first-time buyers in England get on the housing ladder with a small deposit.

Currently a 5% deposit on the average UK house price of £272,000 plus moving costs and legal fees - will set you back about £16,850, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

That's daunting, but here are four ways that experts say you can at least make a start on saving for a deposit.

Depositing an amount you can afford into a regular savers account the day after you are paid is a good way to start, suggests Anna Bowes, savings expert at financial advisers The Private Office.

"It becomes like another bill, but one that you can benefit from in the future," she says.

The type of account that's suitable depends on your circumstances.

Some of the ones that pay the highest interest are only accessible if you hold a current account with the provider, she says.

Other considerations are whether you can lock the money away for longer, to receive a better savings rate.

If you don't have a buffer of other savings, then experts say an easy access account gives you the chance to dip into the money to pay an unexpected bill.

You can save up to £4,000 a year in a Lifetime Individual Savings Account (LISA) and the government guarantees a 25% bonus. So, if you put the full amount in then the government will add £1,000 a year.

But there is a catch, that has left some people out of pocket.

Money saved in a LISA can only be used to buy a first home up to the value of £450,000 - a threshold that has not changed since 2017.

The only other time you can withdraw the money is after the age of 60 or in the exceptional case that you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live.

Withdrawal under any other circumstances means you get hit with a penalty - so you could get back less than you put in.

Ministers are planning to replace the LISA with a new First Time Buyer ISA, but there are no clear details yet about how it will work.

The earlier you start saving the more you can build up thanks to the magic of compound interest. In short, interest is added on a larger and larger pot as time goes by.

Bowes says that saving £50 a month from the age of 20 would give you about £41,000 in 30 years' time when you hit 50, assuming interest of 5% is paid a year.

Start 10 years later, and you'd need to save more than double - £101 a month - to have the same amount at the age of 50.

Investing in stocks and shares is another option, but the value of investments can go down as well as up.

An increasing number of lenders are offering mortgage deals with little or no deposit required.

David Hollingworth, from L&C, points to mortgages that have deposits starting from £5,000 and allow people to borrow up to 98% or 99% of the property purchase price.

They might not always be the best option, and not everyone will be eligible.

And, of course, some first-time buyers turn to their parents for help.

Again that's not available to all, but a survey by the Nationwide Building Society suggests that more than half of parents who charge their adult children rent are putting some or all of the money towards helping their child save to buy their own home.

Earth’s geographic poles wander more than we had thought

New Scientist October 01, 2026

The Earth’s geographic poles – the points where the imaginary axis of the planet’s rotation is located – may be far less immutable than previously known, with a new study finding that ancient sea-level changes provide a clue to their movement.

Earth has two main pairs of poles: its magnetic poles, resulting from its magnetic field, and its geographic poles based on its rotation. The magnetic poles are constantly in movement and are often hundreds of kilometres away from the geographic north and south poles. They can even flip altogether.

The geographic poles are much more stable. But they can move a little, through a phenomenon called true polar wander. This is driven by the way plate tectonics and mantle convection slowly redistribute mass in Earth’s mantle and affect the planet’s spin.

Advertisement

Huge hot blobs inside Earth may have made its magnetic field wonky

When the spin of the planet is thrown out of whack, the solid outer layers of the globe begin to move in order to help Earth find a new stable spin equilibrium. This has the effect of moving the geographic poles.

“The crust and the mantle effectively slip over the core during a true polar-wander event,” says Mathew Domeier at the University of Oslo in Norway.

However, until now much of the evidence for true polar-wandering events has come from ancient magnetic data locked inside rocks that formed millions of years ago, and this evidence has yielded confusing and conflicting results about the frequency and scale of the events.

So, Domeier and his team took a different approach. They analysed the geological record of sea-level change looking for distinctive signals that might be expected during a true polar-wander event.

Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026

Because of the way ocean water can more quickly adjust to the centrifugal potential changes than the rocky sea floor, true polar-wander events are expected to leave a telltale pattern. Sea level will rise in one half of the northern hemisphere and fall in the other half, and it will also rise in one half of the southern hemisphere and fall in the other half.

The northern and southern hemisphere signals are reversed, however, so if it is the western side of the northern hemisphere that experiences sea-level rise, it will be the eastern side of the southern hemisphere that does so, too, creating a beach ball-like global pattern.

“This is a very strange pattern that is not caused by other Earth processes,” he says.

On the time scales we experience, the events would be unnoticeable. But over longer periods of geological time, a wandering pole changes the distribution of land and sea.

Why geologists can’t agree on when the Anthropocene Epoch began

For instance, from their analysis of ancient sea-level patterns, Domeier and his colleagues discovered that the geographic poles moved dramatically, over periods of around 10 million years, four times in the geological past: at 20, 90, 140 and 190 million years ago.

“By the timescales of human experience, the movement may not seem fast,” says Domeier. “We cannot estimate the exact speed, but we can recognise events where the rate of polar motion exceeded about 0.6 degrees per million years.”

He says this is faster than the rate at which most tectonic plates move – fast enough to potentially have an effect on climate systems.

What’s more, we know that true polar wandering continues today, although maybe not at the rate seen during the four fast bursts in the geological past.

Rock weathering has helped keep Earth’s climate relatively stable for millions of years, but the process isn’t fast enough to keep up with human carbon emissions

“[It] is measurable by satellites at a rate of about 10 cm per year, but most people are unaware of this. So these events are totally unrecognisable according to our everyday experience,” says Domeier.

Sabin Zahirovic at the University of Sydney says very few people are aware that Earth’s 2800-km-thick outer shell of the crust and mantle are in motion with respect to Earth’s spin axis.

The study demonstrates that clues in the coastline change provide an independent fingerprint of true polar wander.

“This is a very exciting development that helps us link very deep Earth processes to changes in long-term climate and sea level on the planet,” says Zahirovic.

New Scientist October 01, 2026

A new type of barrier developed in Ukraine defends against fibre-guided attack drones by literally cutting their communications.

Radio-frequency jamming stops most small drones. In response, drone designers have begun using fibre-optic cable instead of radio to communicate with the crafts. The fibre-optic cable unspools as the drone flies.

Russia produced very few of these drones in 2024, and each could only reach a few kilometres. But 20-kilometre-range versions are now common, with 50-km ones also appearing. The drones have become far more abundant, too, with some 60 per cent of Russian FPV attack drones now fibre guided. In places the landscape is draped with discarded fibre cables.

Advertisement

Jet-powered drones pose a new threat to Ukraine – can they be stopped?

The Ukrainian forces have been experimenting with technology to cut the strong fibre-optic cables. One video shared by a Ukrainian government-led platform has shown civilians how to break a line by hand by looping it and snapping the brittle fibre. But other methods for breaking the cables are needed.

“The most reliable defences against fibre-optic FPVs have been passive barrier systems such as the net tunnels installed over key roads,” says Roy Gardiner, Intel Director at the group Defense Tech for Ukraine. Hundreds of kilometres of roads in Ukraine are now covered with these tunnels, which are physical barriers that catch drones or cause them to explode prematurely.

The Chaharnyk (“Shrubbery”), developed by Logika Design Bureau in Kyiv, offers an alternative. An acoustic sensor picks up the sound of a drone passing overhead and activates the barrier. This is a motorised wire fence in which the wire moves like a conveyor belt with hooks to trap any fibre-optic cable laid over it. The hooks carry the fibre to a cutting block where it is severed.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Chaharnyk is supplied as two 50-metre sections, which two people can set up in less than an hour. It is battery-powered and weatherproof, and can be turned on or off remotely as needed – for example, while friendly drones are passing over.

Barriers can be placed across known lines of approach used by drones, or as a perimeter to protect a fighting position or a facility.

“Vulnerable installations in the rear, such as electrical substations that are too extensive to cover with netting, could be given significant protection against long-range fibre FPVs by the Chaharnyk system,” says Gardiner.

Breaking the fibre cable generally disables a fibre drone, and the makers claim that Chaharnyk has a 95 per cent success rate in cutting the cable of any drone flying over. But it only works if it detects the drone.

“The reliability of the acoustic detection system to distinguish threats in the cacophony of the battlefield needs to be proven,” says Gardiner.

Logika Design Bureau didn’t respond to a request for an interview about the Chaharnyk system.

Elephants imitate each other when they produce deep rumbling sounds

New Scientist October 01, 2026

Elephants appear to harmonise their vocal rumbles when they join together to form choruses, tuning their voices to sound more alike as the chorus unfolds.

The findings come from a machine learning study, which also reveals that this convergence is particularly likely to occur during specific kinds of choruses – such as when elephants reconnect with one another or organise group activities – and that the calls themselves may contain information about what the animals are doing.

The findings could offer new insights into how elephants communicate and navigate life within their complex societies, says Sara Keen at Earth Species Project, a US non-profit organisation that uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to attempt to decode non-human animal communication.

Advertisement

IUCN report finds more African forest elephants than we thought

“It’s sort of like what humans do in conversation, where you almost start to adopt the speaking patterns or accents of whoever you’re interacting with,” says Keen.

Elephants communicate using a rich repertoire of body language, but also a wide range of sounds. These include their iconic trumpet call, and also throatier roars. The most common call is the rumble – so low-pitched it is often undetectable by humans – which can travel up to 10 kilometres, transmitting long-distance information that can potentially include the identity of the caller and what’s happening at the time.

Joyce Poole at Elephant Voices, a non-profit organisation based in Washington DC, that promotes the study and protection of elephants, says scientists have long been intrigued by the way elephants will rumble together in choruses. Studying those complex sounds, however, has proved extremely difficult because it is hard to pick out any given rumbling elephant in the chorus – what researchers call “the cocktail party problem”.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

With significant developments in machine learning, however, Poole, Keen and their colleagues have found that computers are up to the task. They used a collection of 902 recordings of rumbles collected across four decades, emitted by wild female African savannah elephants (Loxodonta africana) from dozens of family groups in Kenya’s Amboseli National Park. The calls were grouped according to six distinct social situations: staying in contact while separated; preparing to move; coordinating what to do next; comforting or reassuring calves; greeting close family members; and participating in large family reunions.

Machine analyses revealed that elephant choruses carry multiple layers of information at once, and vary in a way that suggests they encode information about what a family is doing together and what happens next, says Keen. Tracking rumbles of individual elephants in the same chorus, the data showed that in some cases, the calls became more acoustically alike as the chorus progressed. Specifically, this convergence occurred when elephants were staying in contact while separated, coordinating what to do next, and greeting after a separation. This suggests that vocal convergence may play a role in helping elephant families build a plan of action, says Keen.

Earlier research that Poole and her colleagues published in 2005 showed that elephants can learn to imitate each other’s voices when they are calling more generally: the new work shows that this imitation involves the rumbles, too.

A weatherproof box and motion-trigger camera help photographer Will Burrard-Lucas capture images of rarely seen African elephants

Combined with other communication tools, including body language, the rumbling calls seem to help facilitate complex social interactions. “They appear able to negotiate, agree and disagree – and make a plan of action,” says Poole.

The findings not only shed light on elephant communication and cognition, but they could also eventually aid conservation by helping researchers track their behaviour and movements remotely, the team says.

Because rumbles allow for long-distance communication, elephants’ ability to unite through their voices is an exciting reflection of their advanced cognition and evolution in their environment, says Andrew McLean, a member of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature’s Asian Elephant Specialist Group. “Evolving and elaborating this for social cohesion, group survival and foraging efficiency is very adaptive,” he says. “This is a fascinating finding – although it’s not really surprising, given how intensely social elephants are.”

Fossil mammal with reptile-like teeth changes picture of our evolution

New Scientist October 02, 2026

A newly discovered, semi-aquatic mammal – which would have lived alongside the dinosaurs – had the streamlined appearance of a water rodent, feet almost identical to a platypus and teeth that grew like a reptile’s.

The researchers who studied the near-complete, 120-million-year-old fossil, named Dongoconodon platycauda, say its disparate anatomy offers a window into early mammal evolution.

D. platycauda was found in 2018 in Liaoning, China. Shundong Bi at Yunnan University, China, and his colleagues studied the fossil after the collector who found it took it to the Mongolia Museum of Natural History. When it was alive, the mammal would have weighed up to 190 grams and measured about 40 centimetres long.

Advertisement

Spectacular feathered dinosaur fossil shows bird-like adaptations

In its overall appearance, it may have looked somewhat like a small nutria, also known as the coypu (Myocastor coypus), say the researchers. Like this modern aquatic mammal, D. platycauda had a streamlined body and a flattened tail adapted for swimming.

D. platycauda also had broad hands and feet “remarkably like” those of the modern platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus), says Bi. Also, several of its finger and toe bones preserve specialised flanges, indicating that the digits supported extensive webbing.

It would have been a strong swimmer, says Bi.

“The broad, webbed forefeet generated much of the propulsive force, while its flattened, tapered tail functioned primarily as a rudder for steering and stability,” he says.

See Alice Roberts at New Scientist Live 2026

But what makes the ancient mammal most interesting is its teeth. For more than a century, he says, biology textbooks have identified that mammals replace some or all of their teeth just once during a lifetime – a condition called diphyodonty.

“Dongoconodon challenges this long-standing view,” says Bi.

The fossil preserves evidence that incisors, canines, premolar-like teeth and even molar-like teeth were replaced multiple times during the animal’s life – a condition called polyphyodonty.

“It is the only known mammal to exhibit polyphyodonty across all four tooth classes, a pattern previously associated with reptiles rather than mammals,” he says.

The specimen also has what the researchers say is one of the most complete preserved middle-ear regions known from an Early Cretaceous mammal. This includes its Meckel’s cartilage, a transient embryonic structure that temporarily connects the developing middle ear to the lower jaw in all mammals.

D. platycauda preserves an intermediate stage in which Meckel’s cartilage maintained only slight contact with the jaw while remaining connected to the tiny ear bones.

“The discovery changes our picture of early mammalian evolution,” says Bi.

Rather than changes to the teeth and ear bones evolving together as a tightly linked suite of characteristics, he says, these important mammalian features evolved independently, producing a remarkable diversity of evolutionary experiments during the age of dinosaurs.

A stunningly intact marine reptile named Austronaga minuta that lived around 245 million years ago may have looked like a miniature version of more famous later ocean predators, like plesiosaurs

“Our discovery shows that early mammalian evolution was considerably more flexible than the traditional textbook picture suggests,” he says.

Mike Benton at the University of Bristol in the UK says the team makes a good case for at least three sets of teeth and an intermediate ear anatomy.

“This is an interesting, quite late-occurring mammal that for some reason has retained hints of the reptilian ancestry more so than many other Mesozoic mammals that had apparently made those two transitions by the end of the Triassic [about 201 million years ago],” says Benton.

Nature Communications DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77339-w

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

New Scientist October 02, 2026

AI has made staggering progress in mathematics in recent months, unearthing solutions to thorny puzzles that evaded humans for decades. Key to technology companies being able to announce these complex new findings, confident in their correctness, is a niche field called formalisation.

But recently, the developers behind formalisation tools have realised that the AI models have the potential to cheat their way to success. Now, the battle is on to tighten up the tools and prevent that from happening.

Formalising mathematical theorems essentially turns them into code that allows computers to grapple with them directly, methodically working through the logic and exposing any flaws. The process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

Advertisement

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

The leading software to do this, Lean, has risen to prominence in the AI world as a convenient way for technology giants to quickly and decisively prove the output of their models. It’s by using Lean that the companies can make bold announcements about solving complex puzzles. Without it, they would only be able to claim they had found a possible solution to the puzzles and then invite human mathematicians to assess the solutions – work that might take weeks or months.

Leonardo de Moura created Lean in the 2010s while working at Microsoft Research. He says that the software was initially a niche tool used only by human mathematicians, and that there were never any attempts at trickery or manipulation.

That all changed in July this year when software engineer Ramana Kumar announced he had disproved the Collatz conjecture – one of the most famous open problems in all of mathematics – and published a Lean formalisation to back up his claim.

See Jim Al-Khalili at New Scientist Live 2026

De Moura was surprised by the breakthrough, but it seemed legitimate. Not least of the reasons for believing so was that the code had been approved by both the standard Lean kernel – the tiny bit of code at the heart of Lean that actually checks the mathematics – and also a separately developed one designed for Lean, called Nanoda. Lean allows for, and actively encourages, the creation of different kernels because variety equals safety; a specific bug that makes something true look false, or vice versa, in one kernel is vanishingly unlikely to appear in another. Formalised code checked by two kernels was as water-tight as things got.

But then it turned out that Kumar’s disproof wasn’t what it seemed. He had used AI to discover and exploit two separate bugs in two separate kernels, within the Lean code.

“[The AI] managed to do something that we thought was impossible,” says de Moura. “It found different bugs and managed to craft a problem that exploited both of them. After that we were really worried. It was clear we had to improve.”

Can mathematicians still refuse to use AI at this point?

Kumar told New Scientist that he thought the stunt would be “useful to throw some cold water on the hype” of formalisation. He didn’t respond to follow-up questions on why he didn’t then disclose the bugs he had found so that they could be fixed. In any case, a fix was published an hour after the bug was officially logged.

Regardless of Kumar’s motivations, it certainly concerned de Moura, the 20 or so full-time developers working on Lean and mathematicians. They feared that malicious actors could use AI to pull such stunts, as Kumar had done.

But they also worried that AI might perform something similar unprompted. When faced with a serious challenge like formalising a fiendishly difficult and complex piece of mathematics, AI might actually find it easier to simply hack Lean and give the appearance of success. This so-called “reward hacking” can occur when AI is given vague instructions, and researchers have already seen evidence of models trying to exploit Lean bugs rather than actually doing their homework.

The first thing Lean’s developers did was to formalise their own kernel, using Lean to check the code at the heart of Lean – an oddly self-referential safety check – and verify that there were no bugs that could be exploited. They then used AI to convert that kernel into a different programming language, and verified that second one as well. A third kernel written from scratch was also verified. This gave developers a greater sense of security, but it didn’t necessarily mean that Lean was infallible.

Fermat’s last theorem formalised by AI agents in just 11 days

Floris van Doorn at the University of Bonn in Germany says there was a vanishingly small chance that Lean had a very unusual bug that caused it to report itself as error-free even when it wasn’t. If such a bug existed, the boot-strapping safety measures would have been meaningless. “That is completely possible, but in practice this would be very weird,” says van Doorn.

To get around this issue, the Lean developers made a lot more kernels, as diverse as possible, built on all types of software and hardware, to increasingly lower the chances of finding a bug that worked universally. These kernels are tested head-to-head in a battle arena website where league tables record how well they’ve done on known true and false proofs, and unusual problems that have been shown to trip up kernels in the past.

The researchers are now also taking steps to push these kernels into wider use – they only help if they’re deployed. Lean, which is open source, currently ships with just one, and it’s on the user to check their code with others if they want more security. But because of the surprising complexity of AI attacks, the next version will ship with four different kernels as standard.

Mathematician discovers rare eight-faced shape

Developers now believe that Kumar’s approach would no longer succeed. “We want to get much closer to this idea of being bulletproof,” says de Moura. “I can tell you that we’re sleeping much better now. We don’t believe the existing AI will be able to break all these layers of defence.”

Even now, though, there are risks. The diversity of kernels makes the chance of a universal bug that works on them all smaller, but not zero – and future AI models may become so capable that they can continue to find convoluted exploits that somehow work across the board on all kernels.

For instance, when working with engineers from OpenAI, the Lean team found a bug in the runtime of their program – the compiled code that is actually executed by a computer, constructed from the source code using a tool called a compiler. Exploiting this bug, they managed to incorrectly prove a conjecture that is false. The error cropped up because the compiler wasn’t perfect, not because Lean’s code had an error.

Dice discovered that solve decade-long mathematical problem

So the ultimate aim is to show that one particular computer setup, with hardware and software of specified standards, is formalised, verified and guaranteed error-free. This would give Lean users the reassurance not only that the kernel is free of mistakes, but also that the compiler, operating system and hardware are error-free, too. Totally trustable from top to bottom. “That’s the dream,” says de Moura. But it will take a vast effort.

There are other problems. Lean code is a programming language, so it can be crafted to do anything the user wants – including malicious trickery, says van Doorn. This could involve simply writing in the output file created by Lean that a theorem was correct, even if it was false, or changing the actual source code that makes up Lean itself to manipulate results, or report that every proof tried from them on was correct.

“You can redefine addition. And then you can prove Fermat’s last theorem, which mentions addition, and you can say you’ve done it,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London. “But then when people actually look at what you’ve really done, you haven’t done it.”

Mathematicians now have a formidable tool for breaking open challenging problems, but working out how best to use it isn’t going to be easy

These loopholes are also now being closed in Lean. Another effort involves Google DeepMind, which maintains a list of open mathematics problems that have been explicitly defined in Lean and then checked carefully by mathematicians. Anyone claiming to have solved one of these problems can take the appropriate definition off the shelf and use it in an unmodified form to test their proposed proof in Lean. Doing so would demonstrate that they are not trying to cheat by subtly altering the definition of the problem to make it far easier to solve.

When OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes puzzle earlier this month, for example, we knew it was on stable ground because the statement provided to Lean was taken directly from the Formal Conjectures list.

But for some, none of these efforts will ever be enough.

“Computer scientists are, in general, very paranoid people, and probably with good reason because they’ve seen all sorts of things,” says Buzzard. “You can find people that will never believe anything. You say ‘I’ve checked it a million times’ and they say ‘well, what about gamma rays [flipping bits in memory], did you check for them?’ There are some people that you can never convince.”

First week of life seems crucial for future allergy and eczema risk

New Scientist October 02, 2026

Babies who have a strong immune reaction in the first week of life seem to have triple the risk of developing an allergy or eczema by age 1, compared with those who don’t. But the long-term impact of this early immune response, now defined for the first time, seems to be modulated by the microbiome and how babies are fed.

“If you ask 100 immunologists, they would say that immune development begins at birth and continuously develops over time, without discrete phases,” says Petter Brodin at Imperial College London.

But at a talk at an immune conference in London earlier this month, Brodin challenged this idea. He revealed that he and his colleagues have found that if a baby has a strong immune response in the first week of life, this seems to have an oversized impact on how the infant’s immune system subsequently develops. “That’s a novel concept,” he said during the talk.

Advertisement

How older siblings may shape sexual orientation via mother’s immune system

In ongoing research, Brodin and his colleagues have been studying nearly 600 infants in Sweden, collecting and analysing blood and stool samples from the infants throughout their first year of life. The analysis revealed that about half the babies had what the researchers termed a strong “seeding” immune reaction during the first week of life, marked by high levels of inflammatory molecules such as interferon gamma, which activates immune cells. The remaining infants had lower levels of these inflammatory molecules during the first week, which the team called a weak seeding reaction.

Further analysis revealed that babies with a strong seeding reaction had substantially more Bacteroides bacteria in their gut than those who had a weak reaction. “A high abundance of Bacteroides bacteria seems to drive seeding reactions to be very strong,” says Brodin – although it is also possible that the variation in levels of the bacteria actually resulted from differences in the severity of the seeding reaction. Babies can pick up these bacteria via interactions with their mother and family members, he says.

The researchers think the effects of the seeding reaction last for only about a week at the beginning of life because that is when the gut is especially leaky, enabling bacteria like Bacteroides to enter the bloodstream and activate immune cells. “Healthy infants are born with a leaky gut that closes up after about a week,” says Brodin.

See Chris and Xand van Tulleken at New Scientist Live 2026

But the seeding reaction may have lasting effects: by sifting through the infants’ medical records, the researchers found that 39 per cent of those with a strong seeding reaction developed either eczema or a food allergy by age 1. In contrast, just 12 per cent of infants with a weak seeding reaction developed at least one of these conditions, which are caused by excessive inflammation. “What we ideally want is a weak seeding reaction,” says Brodin.

Further analysis revealed that the infants with a strong reaction then followed one of three immune trajectories linked to two main factors: whether they were primarily fed breast or formula milk, and the abundance of bifidobacteria in their gut.

For instance, 50 per cent of babies who had a strong seeding reaction and were breastfed – but had low levels of bifidobacteria – developed eczema or food allergies. Breastfed infants who had a strong seeding reaction and had high bifidobacteria levels were less likely to develop eczema or food allergies, with 25 per cent of them doing so.

Babies are born with the neural foundations for maths

The researchers also found that 33 per cent of infants who had a strong seeding reaction and were fed formula milk developed eczema or an allergy by age 1. In the work presented at the conference, the team didn’t give details of bifidobacteria levels in the guts of these formula-fed babies.

Brodin says the bifidobacteria may be important because they break down certain sugars in breast milk, known as human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), to produce anti-inflammatory molecules called short-chain fatty acids. In turn, these can prevent the immune system from overreacting, he says. The researchers plan to explore why exactly the other links may have emerged in future research, says Brodin.

“This is a really important piece of work. Only a few studies have looked at immune development during the first week after birth,” says Lucy Crouch at the University of Birmingham in the UK. The research could reveal ways to develop personalised medicine for infants, she says.

A revolutionary cancer treatment is now being applied to a wide range of autoimmune disorders. Columnist Michael Le Page finds it is proving to be even more effective than expected

For instance, you could imagine measuring whether a baby has a strong or weak seeding reaction, then, depending on whether they are breastfed or not and their levels of bifidobacteria, you could give them a probiotic that boosts these microbes to cut their allergy or eczema risk, she says.

But further research is needed to establish whether the seeding reaction has effects beyond the first year, says Crouch. Studies should also explore whether the links made in the study really are causal, she says, which could be done by tracking how immune cells within gut organoids – clumps of lab-grown cells that are used to mimic the intestines – react to bacteria in the presence or absence of HMOs.

“The reported differences in allergy and eczema risk are striking, but they show associations rather than demonstrating that particular microbes or immune responses directly cause the later outcomes,” says Lindsay Hall, also at the University of Birmingham.

For now, parents shouldn’t alter how they feed or interact with their infants based on the results. “It is much too early to suggest that the findings should change advice to parents,” says Hall.
