Brain area discovered that may be critical for viable pregnancies

New Scientist October 02, 2026

A tiny set of neurons deep inside the brain is fundamental to viable pregnancies in mice. These neurons are also present in human female brains and could provide clues about unexplained recurrent miscarriages and IVF difficulties.

Nirao Shah at Stanford University, California, and his colleagues discovered the neurons while looking for gene expression changes in different parts of the female mouse brain during pregnancy. They observed a small population of neurons that completely transformed.

The levels of gene expression in these neurons changed over 30-fold when mice became pregnant for the first time, converting them to a new class of neurons that functioned in a completely different way by mid-gestation. “This cell type is exclusive to pregnancy,” the researchers write.

Advertisement

The previously unknown set of neurons is in an area deep in the centre of the brain called the preoptic hypothalamus, which is also involved in sexual and parental behaviours. The neurons have receptors for pregnancy-related hormones like progesterone, which may be responsible for switching the neurons on after the initial fertilisation of an egg.

Paracetamol use in early pregnancy linked to smaller ovaries and testes

Once activated, these neurons appear to coordinate the implantation of the embryo in the uterus and maintain the ongoing pregnancy. When Shah’s team created female mice without this special type of neuron, the mice were able to mate and become pregnant, but their pregnancies all ended at an early stage. This was because their embryos couldn’t implant in the lining of the uterus.

“Certainly, the fact that when you get rid of these neurons, you lose these pregnancies, is really suggestive,” says Jennifer O’Chan at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York.

These neurons comprise fewer than 0.001 per cent of all brain cells, making it remarkable that their selective elimination completely blocks the ability to establish viable pregnancies, write Shah and his colleagues.

However, further research will be required to investigate how these neurons actually do this, says O’Chan. “They’ve shown that these neurons change robustly during pregnancy, but then how are they actually communicating with the uterus? Is it hormonal? Are they secreting some kind of factor? If they could identify that, I would be very convinced.”

It would also be interesting to study whether these neurons are permanently changed by pregnancy or eventually return to their original state, says O’Chan, since her own research has found that pregnancy induces long-lasting changes in the brain.

Free newsletter

Shah’s team also analysed an existing atlas of gene expression in the human brain and found that women have the same special set of neurons in their preoptic hypothalamus, hinting these neurons may play a similar role in human pregnancies. “You can’t do these types of experiments in humans, so we have to extrapolate here, but mouse and human brains do tend to be fairly well-conserved,” says O’Chan.

Just over half of miscarriages are known to be caused by genetic errors in the embryo, but the rest can’t be explained. For example, some people undergoing IVF have multiple embryos that appear genetically healthy, but none seem to implant once they are inserted in the uterus, for reasons that are unclear. Some who conceive naturally also have recurrent early pregnancy losses for no detectable reason.

According to Shah and his colleagues, these fertility challenges may relate to the neurons they discovered, potentially paving the way for new treatments. “We speculate that a subset of such events reflects failure of particular neural circuits to recognize, monitor, or adapt to gestation,” they write.

“If, for example, you found that these neurons were releasing a fundamental signalling molecule that was important for implantation, you might be able to turn that into a therapeutic for people with fertility issues,” says O’Chan.

Read an extract from Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel

New Scientist October 02, 2026

In the first spring after the collapse of the United States, the blossoming of the jacaranda trees felt to Ari like grace. The trees bloomed in the same week that international peacekeeping troops withdrew from Los Angeles, and the convergence of flowers with the absence of foreign soldiers brought a delirious kind of hope. Everyone in the spring of 2031 knew the city was one terrorist attack away from disaster, but that peril made the season more vivid, not less.

It was Ari’s first spring outside of prison in nearly two decades, and she spent hours at a time walking the streets. Prison is a wasteland of sensory deprivation, and now the city was overwhelming. She kept expecting that the details of the world would cease to be extraordinary, but that kept not happening. No one around her seemed to notice the jacarandas, because in Los Angeles there are flowers every month of the year, but she walked streets where the trees were lit up by purple blue blossoms and thought, My god. This place. She was forty-eight years old but felt younger, because so much of the world was new.

Free newsletter

The United States had come undone following a coup d’état. Several states had seceded within a week of the coup, either alone or in alliances with neighbours, and war had broken out within the month. Now the fighting had subsided, for the most part, and Ari had been released into an uneasy aftermath.

Advertisement

“When I think of what the city was a year ago,” Gloria said. Gloria was Ari’s roommate in a very small apartment in Echo Park. She was about a decade younger than Ari, a refugee who’d fled fighting between rival militias in Tennessee. Gloria slept in the bedroom. Ari slept in the living room, with an old sheet stapled to the door frame as a makeshift door, and they met one another in the tiny kitchen. Gloria seemed to spend most of her time reading the news online, her eyes wide and blank in the blue light of her laptop. What the city had been like a year ago was Gloria’s favourite topic of conversation.

“I know,” Ari said gently, although she didn’t. Their experiences were not the same. A year ago, Ari had been imprisoned in what was now a different country and Gloria had been holed up in this apartment with a different roommate.

But tonight the curfew had lifted, and when Ari had gone for a walk earlier, her impression from passing conversations was that everyone in Los Angeles was going out tonight. Gloria was going to her friend Kareem’s party, one neighbourhood over, and had invited Ari to come. But now, with dusk approaching, she’d settled into her familiar position with her laptop at the kitchen table, and showed no signs of getting ready.

“What time shall we leave for that party?” Ari asked.

I am a top drone pilot in the Ukrainian Army – this is what it is really like

New Scientist October 02, 2026

I joined the army on the day of the Russian invasion. I’d studied computer science and only recently landed a great internship at a game company. But I saw the news and knew my options were to sit and wait for them to come and kill me or go running into the fight.

Comparing the early days of the war to now, it’s like two different worlds. Back then there were drones, but most of the damage was still done by artillery. Now, drones are everywhere, from the front line all the way back 30 kilometres. It’s terrifying because you used to be able to come a little way back from the fighting for rest and feel completely safe. Now, danger is always looming over you, wherever you are.

Jet-powered drones pose a new threat to Ukraine – can they be stopped?

I occasionally have the chance to get back to Kyiv and then I feel like I’m not losing my mind quite as fast as usual. It’s a partial respite because on the front line we work 24 hours a day and the non-stop fighting is hugely draining, but you’re still aware of the risk of drone strikes even in Kyiv. You just can’t escape it.

Advertisement

On the front line, we spend 90 per cent of our time underground in bunkers because of the threat of enemy drones. Every time you go outside, you risk being spotted and killed. The conditions are like camping, but it obviously has a very different vibe.

I’ve done a lot of different jobs as a drone pilot, but at the end of the day, the mission was always to protect our ground troops. I spent time as a reconnaissance drone pilot, then flying bomber drones and now I’m doing anti-drone missions in a regiment called Aquila under the control of the 3rd Army Corps.

We specialise in shooting down everything from small first-person view (FPV) drones to the long-range kamikaze models heading for Ukraine’s cities. We’ve got short-range anti-aircraft guns, shoulder-launched rockets and drones. But I’m in a small unit that does drone-to-drone warfare in the skies above the front line.

I’m proud to say that I’m a top performer not just in my regiment but in the wider army. I think it’s because I’ve been doing it for a long time, but I’ve taken out 932 enemy drones. Right now I focus on finding smaller FPV drones that are doing reconnaissance or hunting our troops with explosives, and take them out before they can do any damage.

Robots clash in first naval engagement between uncrewed sea drones

Russians often find our positions on the front line and target them with drones and artillery. We get information from our guys that they’re being hunted and we try to take out Russian drones before they can do any damage. Most of the time we find them.

I remember one time we were retaking a village that the Russians had occupied. In a single day, we erased all the progress they’d made in a year, and we drone pilots were helping cover the guys that were advancing on the ground. There was a soldier wounded, and the Russians were trying to bomb him with a drone. At the last minute, we found it, we hit it and the guy is alive because of that. It’s an amazing feeling.

Spotting those tiny drones among miles of open land is as much an art as a science. You need to be able to put yourself in the shoes of the enemy pilot who’s out hunting for your comrades, imagine what interests them, where they’ll be looking. You need to hunt him.

We have a few distinct jobs in my team. Some assemble and arm drones, others pilot them and there are also navigators who direct us to the enemy and keep meticulous logs of what hardware we get through and which targets we take out. Even though we have specialities, we make sure we can all step into any role in case someone is injured.

On my most recent trip to the front line, we hit 180 targets in 20 days. But there are also missions where you don’t spot a target, run low on battery and have to return, so it can be up to 30 flights per day.

Stealth drone spins so fast that it disappears

We’ve all seen the advanced interceptors and various other drones that Ukraine produces, and they are used for all sorts of missions, but most of the drones that I fly, and also that I shoot down, are commercially available models. They’re cheap and they’re available – they’re good enough for war. Both we and the Russians buy the same Chinese models – that’s the world that we live in. I’ve shot down so many of them and they still keep coming.

We work in what used to be beautiful countryside, beautiful cities, that real people lived in. That people had made their own. Now it’s all destroyed. But you can still see so much potential for this land to bring so much happiness and fulfilment to people. It’s disheartening, and heartbreaking, to be perfectly honest.

The war is horrible, it’s horrid, it’s everything that you imagine it being, but it’s also a very unique experience. It’s the sort of experience that foreigners usually only see in movies. The stakes are so high that everything you do matters. Everything you do has a weight to it. It changes your perspective, and you see so many people die and get injured that you begin to realise that every moment that you’re alive, every person that you meet, everything that you do, is important. You could die at any moment. Every moment that you live is important. We don’t get to choose what happens to us, we just get to choose what we do with that.

I used to be much more angry with the Russians, I think. I used to be much more emotional about it. I’m getting to a point now where I’m trying to find my inner peace.

Killing the enemy, from some points of view, it’s horrible. But if you don’t take care of them, if you don’t kill them, they advance towards our troops and then they have to deal with them, and that’s not fair.

I’m not sure what I’m going to do after the war. It’s a very demanding job, both physically and psychologically, and it takes much from you. When the war ends, yes, you’ll get this freedom, but what to do with this freedom is not a question you get to ponder while you’re still serving. I’ll find some way to keep myself busy.

As told to Matthew Sparkes

Will the backlash against AI data centres hit quantum computing too?

New Scientist October 02, 2026

People aren’t happy about data centres. As interest in AI and its use has dramatically increased in the past couple of years, communities across the world have begun protesting against the massive infrastructure needed to support this technology.

We may finally have a way to rate a quantum computer’s usefulness

In the US, data centres are popping up in residential areas, their construction has been proposed on protected natural lands and, in places where they have been built, they have caused havoc. These enormous buildings produce a lot of noise and use huge amounts of electricity and water. In some places, utility bills are rising and water taps are running dry. Community after community has risen up to fight data centres in their neighbourhoods. It made me wonder whether that battle will stay limited to AI, or if the scrutiny will come for quantum computing too.

Consider the south side of Chicago. The Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP), a 128-acre research and development campus that will house facilities of several leading quantum computing firms, is being built there – and it’s not entirely welcomed by its neighbours.

Advertisement

The project broke ground in September 2025 with enthusiastic support from the governor of Illinois, JB Pritzker, and Mayor of Chicago Brandon Johnson. The most notable tenant of the park will be PsiQuantum, which is aiming to build the US’s first utility-scale, error-corrected quantum computer there by the end of the decade, and as early as 2028. Other companies, such as Pasqal, Infleqtion, IBM and Diraq, will also have facilities at the park.

So far, more than $1 billion in public and private funding has been invested in this campus, which is situated at a steel mill that was a great source of economic activity for the south side of Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s, but has stood abandoned for decades. In the long run, the IQMP is expected to bring $9 billion in investment. In other words, it would be impossible for residents of the nearby neighbourhoods not to notice that quantum is moving in, and at an ambitious scale.

And some Chicagoans certainly did notice. On 15 August, at an event titled “Community Over Quantum”, Johnson faced jeers and antagonistic chants from the audience. The meeting was organised by community advocacy group Southside Together, which has been consistently protesting the development for the past year. Southside Together didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

Other community and environmental groups have been engaged in the matter as well, such as Science for the People Chicago; Environment, Transportation, Health and Open Space; and the Alliance of the Southeast, according to the Hyde Park Herald, a local newspaper. Block Club Chicago reported that, at the event in August, the demands put to Johnson were simple: “Reverse the permits. Shut it down. Mayor Johnson, do it now.”

“This is genuinely exciting technology, and it’s easy to assume everyone will see it that way. But it’s human nature to be uneasy about change, especially change this size,” says Pranav Gokhale at Infleqtion.

“Any project of this scale will draw questions, and we embrace that,” says Rebecca Carroll, a spokesperson for the IQMP. The situation is complicated by the history and context of the IQMP’s location. For one, concerns about environmental damage and toxins in the ground have persisted ever since the steel mill closed in 1992, though there have been remediation efforts through the years. At the end of 2025, the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency approved a new clean-up of the property, and at the event in August, Johnson reaffirmed that these efforts will take place.

Several previous attempts to revive the site failed, letting down the local community, many of whom were excited about the prospect of new investment in their neighbourhoods, says Carroll. But she adds that the project’s developer, Related Midwest, has been meeting with community environmental groups since the IQMP broke ground.

These aren’t the only environmental worries raised by the IQMP’s neighbours, however. Concerns about the water and electricity usage of the new facilities abound, in part spurred by the destructive effects that AI data centres have had on other communities. “Opponents of the quantum campus likened the project to the xAI data center in Memphis,” reported Block Club Chicago.

Josh Sodicoff at the University of Chicago co-chairs the local chapter of Science for the People. They say community members feel that this project has popped up in their backyard at an alarming speed, and worry about its impact on their energy and water prices, as well as access to the jobs that the IQMP promises to bring. “The vast majority of people who now know about this [development] were not informed by the developers. They were not informed by the city. They were informed by people in Southside Together, who have been focused explicitly on just canvassing people in the area to let them know what’s going on. That lack of autonomy, especially when the thing that is being decided on is so substantial [and] does use our taxes, seems to have disgruntled a lot of people,” says Sodicoff.

Many local people who have been speaking out against the development want it to end, and for the federal and state dollars behind it to be put into things that they feel would benefit the community, like grocery stores and pharmacies, says Hanna He, who also co-chairs the Science for the People chapter.

I wondered whether another development at the same scale would face the same pushback if it weren’t related to quantum computing. “When we talk to residents, they don’t know much about the quantum aspect. All they know is that this giant industrial complex is being built in their backyard, and it’s not doing anything for them,” says He.

It is, then, tempting to dismiss the situation in Chicago as a problem of local politics, rather than a quantum one. Yet the opacity of the word “quantum” cannot be extricated from many of the issues at play. As Sodicoff told me, it isn’t well-understood by the public, so all sorts of narratives can stick to it easily. Having reported on the quantum computing industry for almost half a decade, I am keenly aware of this. Whether you want to argue that quantum technology will save or destroy the world, “quantum” lends the claim a type of enabling mystique. In Chicago, it also seems to suffer from the association with the other big tech story of the moment: AI.

Grim warnings of the existential risk posed by AI are all over the news, but there is very little evidence to back them up

“People are asking the same questions about power and water everywhere right now, and it’s possible that they have connected [this with] the IQMP, assuming it’s a data centre,” says Gokhale.

Carroll says there couldn’t be a starker contrast between an AI data centre and the IQMP. Unlike data centres, which are largely filled with machines, she says the quantum park will be filled with people. This means there will be employment opportunities beyond quantum-specific roles, she says, similar to the variety of jobs that are available on college campuses.

Her colleagues are already involved with education and outreach programmes, some in partnership with local public schools and city colleges, that she says could help the neighbourhood’s young people become part of the city’s ambitions to become the leading quantum hub in the country. IBM is also establishing a centre at the IQMP that the firm says will bring 750 full-time jobs in cybersecurity, data science, quantum computing, AI and related technologies.

Quantum computing technology isn’t necessarily dependent on the large data-processing facilities AI uses, but to become more useful, quantum computers will have to become physically larger. Does that also mean that they will gobble up more power?

Earlier this year, Olivier Ezratty at the Quantum Energy Initiative estimated that future quantum computers could draw anywhere between 100 kilowatts to 200 megawatts of power, a range that goes from the current needs of a supercomputer at a moderately large research facility to a figure that tops the energy usage of a small city. In other words, the situation is complicated even for quantum industry watchers and analysts, let alone for people with no prior knowledge of anything quantum.

Recently, many who work in the quantum computing industry have also purposefully compared and conflated their technology with AI. Investors that may have missed out on AI are being urged to not skip quantum as the next big thing. Countless claims circulate online about quantum computers making AI better, despite the scientific reality being a lot less settled. Quantum computing and AI will surely be part of the same scientific workflows, but putting an equals sign between the two, or implying one, isn’t yet fully warranted.

For the past year, quantum technology firms have been switching into higher gears, getting ready to scale up and make their biggest splash yet. If all goes according to their roadmaps, they will be in the news more and more often, and the growing importance of quantum computing as an arena of geopolitical dominance – particularly in the technological race between the US and China – will only exacerbate this.

For activists like Sodicoff, quantum’s connection to the US military, such as through some of the IQMP tenants’ contracts and partnerships with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, is already a reason to be sceptical of the technology and participate in the pushback. So, quantum computing firms really can’t afford miscommunication. The technology can’t risk being confused with AI or any other technology that has already raised electricity bills, caused noise pollution or become attached to ideas like bringing decommissioned coal power plants back online to produce enough energy for computing.

Quantum computing may be facing a replication crisis

Certainly, the quantum computing industry also cannot afford to be a bad neighbour. If successfully scaled up and made useful, the technology stands a chance of making a big difference in the lives of not just those who live near research campuses, but people all over the world too. Whether it be by cracking the chemistry behind more efficient ways to produce fertilisers, advancing our understanding of materials for solar panels or shortening the drug discovery timeline, transformative uses for quantum computers are on the table.

“People get excited about quantum helping us address humanity’s challenges,” says Carroll. She shares a vision of the IQMP as a bustling campus that can be both an economic engine for Chicago’s south side and a place where researchers will work on solving some of today’s most pressing problems. The challenge lies in being accountable to the local community and addressing their concerns about the environment, infrastructure and what quantum technology will be used for.

Everyone I spoke to acknowledged that the IQMP is unlikely to be successful without the support of people who live nearby. “They are the people who are breathing in the dust that’s coming off these construction sites. They’re the people who are just wondering what’s behind this fence,” says Sodicoff. Simply put, it isn’t enough for quantum technology firms to promise that they will make the world better in the future – they have a chance to practise for a better world right now.

See Jim Al-Khalili at New Scientist Live 2026

National says it will start construction on stage one of Auckland’s long-awaited Mill Rd in 2028 if the party is re-elected next month.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon made the announcement in Auckland this morning, which is being livestreamed at the top of this article.

Mill Rd is a new four-lane, 21.5km corridor running alongside State Highway 1 from Manukau to Drury and is regarded as a Road of National Significance.

National will also progress route protection on stages two and three, the party’s Transport spokesman Chris Bishop says.

“South Auckland is one of the fastest-growing parts of the country and Drury is at the centre of that growth, but the roading network hasn’t kept up.

“People travelling between Drury, Papakura and Manukau are funnelled onto an already congested Southern Motorway, while roads like Redoubt Rd and the existing Mill Rd were built for a semi-rural community, not tens of thousands of new households,” Bishop said.

According to Bishop, stage one between Manukau and Alfriston, is one of the highest-ranked projects on the Government’s Major Transport Projects Pipeline and has a benefit-cost ratio of 3.1 if not tolled, or 2.2 if tolled.

“NZTA estimates stage one will reduce congestion by 30% on the corridor, cut journey times by 25%, and result in a more than 60% reduction in deaths and serious injuries,” Bishop said.

National would allocate $1.75 billion in Budget 2028 so construction can begin in the late-2028 construction season.

“The NZTA Board has endorsed the investment case, and NZTA is completing the design work and taking the project through the fast-track process to secure the consents it needs.

“After years of debate and discussion about Mill Rd, National in government is getting on with it.

“In addition to starting construction on stage one, National will allocate $100 million to progress route protection on stages two and three,” Bishop added.

H. pylori: The group one carcinogen lurking in Kiwi tummies and why NZ doesn’t screen for it

New Zealand Herald October 03, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

A tenacious bacterium has outlasted the stomach’s acid for thousands of years, mostly unnoticed. Finding and treating it could save hundreds of Kiwi lives. Mike Scott reports.

The human stomach is a pot of acid and enzymes churning and killing most of what you swallow.

For almost all microbes it is a Venusian hellscape, but not for Helicobacter pylori – a cancer-causing bacterium sublimely surviving in almost half the world’s population thanks to masterful evolution.

Over thousands of years, H. pylori, as it is commonly known, has perfected a three-part trick.

It converts urea in the stomach into ammonia, wrapping itself in a defensive cloud that neutralises acid around it.

Then, using whip-like flagella, it swims through the stomach’s mucus lining, using it like a blanket pulled overhead.

Once through, it anchors to the stomach wall and stays, lives and multiplies.

Most who carry it never know they have it, but for others it causes gastritis and ulcers.

But most concerning, it is behind about three-quarters of stomach cancers worldwide.

In 1994, the World Health Organisation (WHO) classified it as a group one carcinogen – the same category as tobacco and asbestos.

It is a discriminate killer.

Within the Kiwi population, it harms Māori and Pasifika at a far higher rate than Europeans.

In 2020, the Ministry of Health’s Cancer Action Plan put H. pylori on a shortlist of three cancers worth screening for, alongside lung and prostate.

Despite the intention, six years later no programme exists, and current detection of H. pylori in Kiwis is described as “opportunistic”.

While New Zealand waits for a screening programme, this common and largely unknown bacterium survives the stomach’s soupy acid, biding its time and, for some, killing.

Paul Misipeka, 84, reckons he’s one of the lucky ones – see if you agree.

In 2024, while tinkering in his beloved garden at his Warkworth home, he felt unwell.

He struggled inside and fell asleep. His wife, Nola, was concerned and called an ambulance.

This was Misipeka’s first trip to hospital. He was checked out and sent home. Sadly, over the next weeks his condition worsened and he returned to hospital.

“I was really sick ... I was vomiting blood,” Misipeka, who hails from Niue, says.

An endoscopy found a tumour in his stomach – he had cancer.

As far as killer cancers go, stomach – or gastric – cancer is right up there.

It is the fifth most common cancer in the world and the fifth most common cause of cancer death, Dr Cameron Schauer, a gastroenterologist and clinical senior lecturer at the University of Auckland, says.

In New Zealand, about 400 people are diagnosed with stomach cancer each year and around 270 die from it, according to the Gut Cancer Foundation.

“And we don’t pick it up early enough,” he says.

Schauer led a major study of gastric cancer covering 21 years of cases, analysing 1797 patients, the largest of its kind done in New Zealand.

“The vast majority of cases that we had, in fact more than 84% of cases, were very advanced.”

In his soon-to-be-published paper, 38% of all reports of gastric cancer reached stage 4, meaning the cancer had spread widely from the stomach by the time they were diagnosed. For Māori, the stage 4 figure was 44%.

For those patients, average survival was under four months.

Māori patients were diagnosed at an average age of 61 and Pasifika patients at 63, both about a decade younger than the New Zealand European average of 73.

“This is a disease that is inequitable,” Schauer says.

“It’s worse in Māori, Pacific and Asians, and is causing a huge amount of both morbidity and mortality in our population.”

And this is where Misipeka was lucky. When the cancer was found, it had not spread beyond his stomach, Misipeka’s wife Nola says.

Yet finding it was only a start. A later complication meant his stomach partly split open, needing emergency surgery. Ultimately, the tumour and about half of his stomach were removed.

“Luckily our doctor was very persistent,” Nola says.

Five months on, Misipeka is eating small portions, slowly regaining strength and easing back into a bit of gardening.

“I was pretty lucky that I went past 80s. A lot of young ones died a lot earlier.”

During her husband’s ordeal, Nola recalls doctors mentioning “a bug” in his stomach and putting him on strong antibiotics.

Misipeka had never heard of H. pylori. “It was a complete surprise,” he says.

Learning of the harm H. pylori can have, the couple are spreading the message, insisting their extended family get tested for the bacteria.

Schauer says the most effective way to decrease stomach cancer rates is finding and eradicating the greatest cause – H. pylori infections – before cancer forms.

“It requires a paradigm shift in thinking where we go from the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff waiting for patients to present with abdominal pain, bleeding, weight loss, inability to swallow, and shifting to a preventive mechanism where we know that we can prevent this from happening and prevent the cascade of inflammation and cancer.”

Whether a doctor finds an H. pylori infection in New Zealand comes down to ticking the right boxes and a bit of luck.

Finding an infection should go like this: a patient turns up to their GP with symptoms like burning or pain in the upper abdomen, bloating, nausea or general stomach discomfort after meals – conditions labelled dyspepsia – and that’s a tick in the check for H. pylori box.

If the patient lives in northern New Zealand, is Māori, Pasifika or Asian, was born overseas where infection rates are high, has a family history of stomach cancer or lives in a crowded home, that’s tick, tick and tick.

A combination of those check marks means a doctor should request a test, usually a stool sample sent to a lab.

If you have H. pylori but no symptoms, or don’t fit the risk profile, then nobody’s ticking boxes.

And even patients who do have both symptoms and the risk factors get missed, says Dr Andrea Teng, a public health researcher at the University of Otago.

“Māori and Pacific, we know, have the highest rates of infection and are actually less likely to get tested than European and Asian groups.

”The current approach is not reaching the groups that need it the most.”

Teng and a team of researchers have finished New Zealand’s first population-wide survey of H. pylori infection, testing 1107 people aged 12 to 69.

The results are preliminary but the pattern is clear.

Blood tests, which show whether someone has ever been infected, found 48% of Pasifika participants and 15% of Māori participants had been, compared with 9% of European New Zealanders.

Around 3% of people who carry H. pylori go on to develop stomach cancer, Teng says.

Trials that followed people for about 10 years found treating those who tested positive cut stomach cancer by almost half.

A real programme won’t match a trial, because not everyone takes up an invitation or follows through.

“We know that it’s effective from the trials, so it’s just implementation questions,” she says.

A working group hosted by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organisation, and including Teng, concluded that screen-and-treat programmes are cost-effective, and may even save money, in high-risk populations.

Modelling based on 2011 data and prices found screening and treating for H. pylori would be good value.

Aimed at Māori, it would cost about $12,000 for every extra year of healthy life gained.

Offered to every adult aged 25 to 69, it would cost about $24,600.

At the time of the modelling, the benchmark for good value was $45,000.

“It’s just really good value for money,” Teng says.

“That’s where I think New Zealand needs to be – piloting an H. pylori screening programme.”

And Schauer agrees.

“We have overwhelming evidence that this is an excellent thing to do, but it really has to be stratified based on risk,” he says.

“I think we should really consider seriously a screen and treat programme for high-risk populations in New Zealand.”

And the Ministry of Health has long agreed, making such a programme one of three priorities in the 2020 Cancer Action Plan.

So what is the hold-up?

Dr Karen Bartholomew, Health NZ’s director of health gain development, says a national programme has to be carefully considered, including research, the cost, impact on populations and whether any system is ready.

Yet, the National Screening Advisory Committee, which Bartholomew chairs and advises on whether new national programmes go ahead, “has not yet reviewed H. pylori screening for gastric cancer”.

“It is on the list for future consideration,” Bartholomew says.

Health NZ is running feasibility studies on adding H. pylori testing to bowel screening, she says.

The Cancer Action Plan was updated in 2026 and has set one dated H. pylori goal – make a plan to design a pilot scheme by 2027.

New Zealand’s delay isn’t unusual.

The international agency Teng contributed to has recommended countries consider screening high-risk groups since 2014, and a report in the New England Journal of Medicine this year found implementation has met with “hesitation and limited action”.

It counts just three population-level programmes worldwide.

Schauer believes New Zealand should mirror others.

“In New Zealand, we like to have ingenuity but I think what we should do in this instance is see if we can just copy and translocate what’s worked very well in other countries.”

It took a “crazy” scientist to prove the link between H. pylori and stomach diseases.

Doctors used to believe nothing could survive the stomach’s acid. Gastritis and ulcers were blamed on stress, spicy food, too much acid.

Research by Australian physicians Robin Warren and Barry Marshall started linking the conditions to bacteria discovered living in the stomach.

In 1984, after experts dismissed the research and animal testing failed, Marshall decided to become the petri dish and drank a broth swimming in H. pylori.

Within days, he was vomiting, with gastritis spreading through a stomach that had been clear a week before.

In 2005, Marshall and Warren won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for their work.

“People thought he [Marshall] was a bit crazy,” says Dr Tom Mules, a gastroenterologist at the Malaghan Institute.

Nearly everyone who carries H. pylori caught it by their 10th birthday.

“This is acquired typically in childhood, and typically from your family members you’re living with,” Mules says.

There are two main strains of the bacterium – a Western strain and a more aggressively cancer-driving East Asian strain, he says.

Because it’s passed down within families, a strain tends to stay within the same ethnic communities for generations. Māori and Pasifika populations are thought more often to carry the East Asian version, a possible factor behind New Zealand’s higher gastric cancer rates among those groups.

The standard Kiwi treatment to eliminate H. pylori is called triple therapy – taking two broad-spectrum antibiotics and an acid-suppressing drug for two weeks. The treatment works for most, with an 85% or greater chance of clearing infection.

However, H. pylori is growing antibiotic resistance.

“If we look at Clarithromycin, which is the main antibiotic that New Zealand uses to treat Helicobacter pylori, our resistance rates are probably sitting around maybe the 10% mark,” Mules says.

“If you go to some countries in the world, particularly Europe, like France, it’s sitting more around 40% and so they’ve abandoned that therapy completely.”

Mules, an expert in H. pylori’s biology, is racing to offset growing antibiotic resistance.

At the Malaghan Institute, they have developed a molecular test that can detect resistance genes straight from a patient’s stool sample, meaning doctors could prescribe the right antibiotic the first time, rather than guessing, he says.

Mules is also chasing the “holy grail” – a vaccine.

“Because we know what causes the stomach cancer, why can’t we prevent that cause?” he says.

“Kind of in the same way that we do with cervical cancer and HPV.”

Development won’t be simple – 30 years of attempts by researchers worldwide have failed to deliver – so far.

A vaccine, if it comes, would protect the next generation. For the people carrying H. pylori now, the answer is to find it and treat it.

Misipeka’s advice is simple.

“Just go to the doctor and get all checked out,” he says.

“If you leave it too long ... it will get worse and it’s harder to fix.”

Mike Scott is a senior journalist at the Herald. His work spans writing, photography and video and he has won numerous journalism awards, including Videographer of the Year and Best Documentary. He has worked in media for more than 25 years, producing stories across New Zealand and internationally.

By John Gerritsen of RNZ

Education Ministry whistleblowers, who contacted RNZ in the past week, plan to add their voices to an investigation by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The investigation was announced after publication of a video showing a ministry manager asking staff not to mention contact with the Education Minister’s office in writing.

Nine people with inside knowledge of different parts of the ministry subsequently contacted RNZ to corroborate claims that ministry managers routinely asked staff not to write down sensitive information, lest it be discovered through the Official Information Act.

Some were from the ministry’s curriculum centre, which was the subject of a negative report about workplace culture published last week.

Others said that a culture of secrecy and avoidance of written records was common in other parts of the organisation.

The ministry said the comments made in the leaked video did not meet its expectations, but it would not comment on claims made by the people who contacted RNZ.

It initially said it was investigating whether there was a wider problem, but told RNZ it had dropped plans for an internal inquiry in light of the Ombudsman’s investigation.

Three of the sources confirmed they would contact the Ombudsman to make a protected disclosure and others said they were likely to do so.

A 10th person – former ministry staff member Claire Coleman – told RNZ she had already offered to participate in the Ombudsman’s investigation.

This week, Chief Ombudsman John Allen said he had formally notified the ministry of the investigation.

“I will be looking at various practices, including whether the ministry’s curriculum centre staff have either deliberately failed to make records or have been told not to do so,” he said.

“My investigation will concentrate on administrative conduct, and whether the Ministry has met its legal obligations under the Official Information Act and the Public Records Act.

“I will not be considering any substantive advice or decision making relating to the curriculum itself.”

Coleman, who has been a strong critic of the Government’s approach to the curriculum rewrite, said she hoped the Ombudsman “might get to the truth of things”.

“I hope we can hold some people responsible and any future processes are transparent.”

Coleman also hoped the Ombudsman’s work might lead to a wider inquiry into the curriculum rewrite.

“There were far too many things that were done in a secretive and unethical way,” she said. “Too many financial interests that have no business in that space.”

Coleman previously claimed that work on the curriculum was heavily politicised and several of the ministry insiders who contacted RNZ made similar allegations.

One source told RNZ the new curriculums felt like a step back in time.

“It felt like I was taken right back to the 80s of ‘we don’t let brown people have any rights’ and ‘we’re going to whitewash everything’ and ‘we’re going to make sure that this is back to how things should be’,” they said.

They said the curriculum was too directive of what teachers must teach.

“Some of the prescribed nature is needed, in order to be consistent and to make sure that children have all got equity wherever they are,” they said. “I get that, but not to the extreme this is.

“New Zealand is innovative, creative ... yet we’re just throwing it all down the tubes.”

Another source said schools could teach the new curriculums with resources left over from 20 years ago.

“It misses how young people learn today and it misses what’s important for young people today,” she said. “It’s such a missed opportunity for what a good curriculum could look like.

“It’s devastating, actually.”

Another source said: “I think the public deserve to know, in no uncertain terms, that the quality of primary and secondary education in this country is being directly compromised and coloured by the government’s ideological position, that the people responsible are consciously aware of it and that the minister, ministry and related parties have taken steps to circumvent proper protocol, and intentionally obscure the truth about how they have been operating”.

Several of the nine whistleblowers said the Australian firm Learning First had a major hand in curriculum drafts and some ministry staff were flown to Melbourne to work with the company.

One said the primary school maths curriculum was completely rewritten by Learning First and other learning areas were heavily influenced by the company.

“The general feeling amongst internal staff was that the work being produced by Learning First was bad and unnecessary,” they said. “There was a lot of confusion about why they were involved at all.”

Another said Learning First wrote a lot of curriculum content, but ministry staff were told not to imply or say that the ministry was not the author of the curriculum.

“Learning First replaced everything we had done,” they said.

They also said Learning First’s understanding of the Treaty of Waitangi was “completely wrong”.

A third source said Learning First provided a lot of content for some curriculums, but not for others, and ministry staff rewrote much of it.

“A lot of it was wrong, literally wrong,” they said.

However, Learning First chief executive Ben Jensen denied the allegations.

He said the claim Learning First wrote most of the content for several curriculum drafts was not true.

“We did lots of research, benchmarking, provided advice and so on, but this is just completely false,” he said.

Jensen said his company did not write the revised version of the maths curriculum.

“We provided comparisons with other systems and made suggestions,” he said. “We do a lot of work on how to sequence foundational learning in maths and what this means for the curriculum, but as above, we were not even doing this work when the draft was written.

“A lot of the feedback we provided was rejected by the ministry, so the idea that we wrote most of it is simply not true.

“When we finished, a lot of writing was still taking place, so just don’t know how people can say it was mainly written by us.”

Jensen said he was not aware of Learning First content being rewritten due to errors and the company was up front about not having expertise on local knowledge and history, such as the Treaty.

The Education Ministry also defended the process and said it was responsible for all final content and decisions.

“Characterisations of the curriculum process based on individual recollections or particular examples do not necessarily reflect the full context of how curriculum content was developed, reviewed, and finalised,” it said.

“The ministry develops and writes the curriculum, drawing on input from teachers, subject matter experts, stakeholders and external advisers throughout the process.

“As previously outlined publicly, including during the Education and Workforce Select Committee scrutiny examination, external advisers may contribute specialist expertise and international perspectives.

“For example, ministry officials have previously explained that Learning First helped identify relevant international curriculum content, while the curriculum itself was written by the ministry.”

The Ombudsman’s investigation was sparked by a video showing a principal seconded to the ministry to lead work on the secondary school curriculum, warning staff not to mention in writing feedback from the Education Minister’s office.

The source of that video said they were outraged by the attempt to circumvent the proper processes for recording and providing information.

“These rigorous processes are put in there exactly to serve the children and to serve the schools, and us bypassing them is not okay,” they said.

They said they heard similar requests almost once a month.

Other sources who contacted RNZ shared similar stories.

“Verbal instructions were given for changes that were controversial and come directly from the minister’s office,” one ministry insider told RNZ.

Another source said the comments made by the ministry manager in the leaked video were not an isolated case.

“This was a routine and extensive problem before she was seconded,” they said. “The problem did not walk in the door with her.”

Another ministry insider told RNZ: “We have been told many times not to write things down”.

As RNZ reported last week, a person present at a ministry-run curriculum hui said ministry staff were present to take notes and one of those staffers revealed that they had been told to be very careful about what they wrote down.

“The things that they weren’t writing down were pretty obviously things that they didn’t want to be recorded as part of the feedback we were giving.”

She said that, later at the same hui, a ministry manager instructed their staff to stop recording what was being said, because it was beyond the scope of the meeting and because it could be discovered through the OIA.

Several sources told RNZ they witnessed repeated attempts to keep information off the record prior to the change of government in late 2023, but it became worse after the election.

One said ministry managers would respond to complaints or potentially critical queries with face-to-face meetings, a tactic that appeared aimed at avoiding a written email response.

“The whole ‘have meetings, keep things off paper’ is deliberate,” they said.

The source said there were frequent meetings where nothing was written down.

“It didn’t feel like there was any integrity.”

A separate source said they commonly heard “that you shouldn’t write things down, because they would then be OIA-able” prior to the 2023 election.

“Recording discussions and notes was sometimes discouraged, with people encouraged to have conversations instead,” they told RNZ.

Another source said that, before the change in government, reminders about the OIA and putting things in writing were light in tone and emphasis, but after the election, the term “OIA-able” was frequently used and, in 2024 meetings, became the preferred mode of communication.

Most of the sources told RNZ they were told to remove Māori words from curriculum documents or noticed that others had done so.

They said the word “Aotearoa” was used as a synonym for or alongside New Zealand in original curriculum drafts, but was later removed.

“This instruction was never written down and, in some cases, senior staff made the changes themselves, rather than relay this change to the writing teams,” one source said.

Another said Aotearoa New Zealand was the blanket term used in the curriculum, often shortened to ANZ, but proofreaders and editors were told to replace it with New Zealand.

One source said the push to remove Māori words began before the coalition Government had even taken office, with some managers indicating they wanted to make the change because “it was in the pipeline”.

Two other sources said some English words were also apparently unwelcome, with instructions to remove words including “culture”, “identity” and “wellbeing”.

The Education Ministry had previously denied that it sought to remove Māori language from the curriculum.

The source of the video said ministry staff were being asked to behave dishonestly.

“We’re public servants and we’re being bullied, which I would say strongly, we are being bullied,” they said. “The majority of people in the ministry are under a toxic environment.”

They said nobody felt safe to complain.

“If you speak up and ask a professional, polite question of ‘is this okay?’, you very quickly have your fixed-term contract ended,” they said.

Another ministry insider said staff felt they had to comply with Government demands or lose their jobs.

“There was a lot of fear within the ministry that our jobs were now at risk, due to the change in government, and this contributed to what I experienced as an overall feeling that we had to say yes to everything and not question whether proper process was being followed,” they said.

A report published last week showed staff in the ministry’s curriculum division were unhappy about favouritism, workplace behaviour and application of public sector values.

Battling nature and neighbours: Westshore surf lifesaving’s hopes for new home

New Zealand Herald October 03, 2026

Westshore Surf Lifesaving Club junior director Ed White at the Option 1 site for possible rebuilding of the club facilities. A single-storey development is being considered to replace the current two-storey structure, also pictured, which is threatened by the sea and erosion. Photo / Doug Laing

Westshore Surf Lifesaving Club is battling both nature and neighbours as it looks to build a new clubhouse away from coastal swells and erosion.

An institution in Napier since 1959, the club has dismissed the idea of moving its two-storey Westshore Beach Reserve clubhouse, built with extensive volunteer labour and opened in 1963.

At the time, the beach stretched hundreds of metres out to the wave-line, attracted thousands of bathers and hosted 800-1000 people for the national surf lifesaving championships.

In 2026, the club has spent 40 years trying to combat the elements, most of the beach is gone, and a 2m-high bund tries to protect the clubhouse.

It’s a losing battle, but both the reserve and parts of the beach remain popular.

A club building committee looked at five other options, with its preference a new single-storey building landward of the current building and closer to Ferguson Ave.

But neighbours are opposing the site, preferring the “No 2″ option about 400m to the north, off Fenwick St, the link from Ferguson Ave to The Esplanade.

Club stalwart and education director Brian Quirk – Surf Lifesaving New Zealand Distinguished Service Award recipient (2002), life member (2009) and recognised in 2016 for 50 years of service – has been raising the issues with authorities for more than four decades.

But he says he’s “given up” to concentrate on growing surf lifesavers of the future and let others take up the issue.

Keith Price, who represents the Napier City Council’s Ahuriri ward, chaired a council workshop about a month ago which included a discussion with club representatives, and he knows what he’d like.

“I’d like more sand,” he says, expecting greater beach nourishment after the expected December arrival of the new suction hopper dredge Kapuka, a joint venture of Port Napier and Port Otago.

Wistfully, he’d like to see the return of “something like the ping-pong ball drop”, a popular community 1970s-1980s attraction in which a helicopter dropped hundreds of balls on to the sand for hundreds of people hoping to link ball numbers to major prizes.

No one would disagree, but they do disagree over the club’s proposals, which were aired at a meeting the club called with residents last week.

Club building committee chair and town planner John O’Shaughnessy said no final decisions had been made.

The focus is on more discussions with residents, hoping to lodge resource and building consent applications early in the new year, and, with favourable Surf Lifesaving New Zealand funding decisions, starting building by the end of next year.

By that time the lease on the current dirt would have expired.

Opponents say they accept the need for the surf lifesaving club to relocate, survive and thrive, and a council wish to assist by making land available.

But, according to one submission at the public meeting, they say building on the site “less than 50 metres” in front of the current building will affect residents living “across the road”.

The unnamed submission cites the removal of open, shaded space, removing protected trees, destroying the views, a negative influence on property values, and further risk of inundation of the site, although it would have an elevation of at least a metre above the current footprint.

“There is very little sense in spending the millions of dollars required relocating the building less than 50 metres from where they are currently being forced to move from, and squeezing the building into a small strip of land bounded by two roads, a playground, and an eroding beach,” one said.

Quoting a coastal hazards report, a submission notes the preferred site is eroding at 32cm a year, while the No 2 site is growing by 73cm/y.

O’Shaughnessy says all the feedback is being considered, but, based on his experience with councils and the public in property matters when it comes to “the view”, he recognises the possible outcomes won’t please everyone.

All matters are up for discussion, including the height of the building and the “footprint” – the land area being about 10% greater – and O’Shaughnessy says the club is also trying to secure space away from the site for storage.

One resident who declined to be named said he believed people were prepared to go “all the way” in opposition, but they were “individual residents”, with no group yet formed.

“The residents feel just feel it’s a shame to just push it back so close to the road [Ferguson Ave],” he said, highlighting that it would take away a popular shaded area of the reserve and part of the road to it, and be closer to the reserve’s playground.

O’Shaughnessy is confident no pōhutukawa would be removed, although it is possible a couple of Norfolk pines would have to go.

The committee believes it has considered the options available, of which there were not many, but O’Shaughnessy said there was “still a long way to go”.

The Westshore residents’ association, which in the past has made submissions on erosion issues, and also developed and runs its own security surveillance system through the area, is awaiting further information.

Doug Laing is a Hawke’s Bay Today reporter, based in Napier, with more than 53 years’ experience in newspapers and more than four decades covering news and sports events and issues in Hawke’s Bay.

Work of student journalist who broke Cornell Uni story shows media’s power when it’s done right – Editorial

New Zealand Herald October 03, 2026

A sign outside the fraternity house of Chi Phi, which was shut down in 2024, at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York state on September 28 this year. Interviews and text messages collected during private proceedings revealed how Jane Doe spent weeks grappling with shame, humiliation and concerns about her reputation before she began to consider herself a victim of sexual assault. Photo / Heather Ainsworth, The New York Times

It was a student journalist who broke the story that broke the hearts of anyone who read it and had one.

The story: the alleged pack-rape in 2024 by seven frat boys of a first-year university student at the elite Cornell University. In their group Snapchat, they included pictures of Jane Doe, drugged and stupefied, in the frat room.

The journalist: Cereese Qusba, at the student-run Cornell Daily Sun, is a very brave woman. Crucially, she had the support of her editor, Sophia Dasser, first in criticising the university’s response, and then demanding transparent data, accountability, and ultimately shining so much light on this dark place that the district attorney decided to reopen the case. Except there never was a case to reopen, as such. It didn’t exist. He had decided not to bring criminal charges.

Qusba has been unflinching in her campaign for justice for Jane Doe.

When a campus notification of abuse came to light two years ago, what struck her, she told CNN, was the silence of the university administration and the failure of the campus police to act on anything. She wanted to find out what happened to the defendants, and the administration’s process. The administration set up a sex abuse “task force”, taking an educational rather than criminal approach to the issue and the abuse claims. Ignoring the fact that those who commit such atrocities are unlikely to join hands in a workshop. Ignoring, too, evidence that perpetrators go on to commit abuse and rape again. It is rarely a one-time thing, according to experts.

For two years, Qusba kept in touch with Jane Doe. She built trust. She kept in touch with her lawyer. She did not let go. Fifteen days ago, when Doe’s lawsuit was filed, Qusba published everything, including the names of the seven allegedly involved in the Chi Phi Frat group: Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, Scott Kretzschmar.

Her story has been picked up by global mainstream and social media. One post said Cornell was “not a university but a hedge fund, a daycare for the future Epstein class”. That it protects only its shareholders. There is a straight line from prestigious universities and institutions such as Cornell to the corridors of power.

It soon emerged that there had been 12,000 incidents of sexual abuse reported at Cornell from 2018 to 2024. In relation to those, seven people were expelled.

Jane Doe was a young woman who was failed, first by the 50 men in the group chat (“is the shop still open”), then by seven men who allegedly raped her, then by subsequent men – the university administration, the campus police who failed to take the proper steps to protect her, and finally by the District Attorney.

Men protecting men, status and reputations.

In New Zealand we have a vital student media community. Some of the very best still practising began their careers at university publications such as Craccum, Salient or Canta.

To say that such abuses don’t happen here because they are not reported is sadly naive. Fortunately, there are journalists like Qusba. To be in that environment as a student on campus, fighting for justice for a peer, is peak courage-under-fire.

She’s an example to us all, in all walks of life, whether students or professionals and in whatever field.

It’s a reminder, too, of the power of media to do precisely what it is tasked with: speak truth to power, unflinchingly and without favour.

Why the humble sausage roll deserves more respect: Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald October 03, 2026

Glenn Dwight reckons the sausage roll deserves the same respect as the iPhone. Photo / Christine Cornege

Over the past few years, I seem to have accidentally become something of a pie correspondent.

I’ve written about them more times than I can remember and, judging by the emails, comments and occasional strongly worded email in caps lock, it turns out New Zealanders are every bit as passionate about pies as I am.

Sadly, all that passion didn’t translate into much enthusiasm for my invention of the Hamilton Fog Pie, where it’s a “myst-ery” what’s inside.

For some reason it hasn’t caught on, which I find strange.

Imagine it, a “myst-ery” pie followed by a visit to the Hamilton Gardens.

The Gold Coast wouldn’t stand a chance as a holiday hotspot.

But all this pie talk did make me realise I’d been neglecting another great resident of the Kiwi bakery warmer, one that has quietly sat alongside the pie for generations without demanding anywhere near the same attention.

In fact, it’s been so overlooked that even the name “pie warmer” has denied it the glory it deserves.

The sausage roll.

And I feel a little bad about that because, while the pie gets the awards, the exotic fillings and grown adults driving across town because someone on Facebook reckons there’s an unbelievable steak and cheese at a bakery in the industrial part of town, the sausage roll has just quietly got on with the job.

So, in an attempt to right this wrong, I managed to get myself along to the NZ Bakels Legendary Sausage Roll Competition, where some of the best sausage rolls in the country were being judged.

And as you can probably tell from the photo below, I also managed to “borrow” a judge’s jacket, which immediately gave me a level of authority I neither deserved nor had earned.

I wasn’t actually judging anything, but there’s something about putting on a black coat and standing near a table of sausage rolls with a clipboard, also “borrowed”, that makes people assume you know what you’re doing.

So I created my own unofficial judging category: “These would go well at Nana’s 80th”.

Because that, to me, is the true test of a sausage roll.

They are the ultimate event food.

Kids’ birthdays, school fundraisers, work morning teas, twenty-firsts, weddings, funerals and, of course, Nana’s 80th.

Somewhere in the background, there will inevitably be a plate of sausage rolls, usually cut in half because apparently that makes them fancy.

And no matter what else is on the table, the sausage rolls always seem to disappear first.

You can spend three hours creating some elaborate canapé involving smoked salmon, dill, crème fraîche and a tiny leaf that someone has carefully placed on top with tweezers, and five minutes later it’ll still be sitting there untouched while three people are standing around an empty sausage roll plate asking the host, “Are there any more coming?”

I think that’s part of their appeal. There’s no ceremony involved.

Nobody has ever had a sausage roll explained to them by a waiter.

You don’t need to know what farm the sausage came from, what the pastry was fed or whether the tomato sauce has been hand-foraged.

You just pick one up, take a bite far too soon and burn the roof of your mouth.

Sadly, unlike the humble pie, the New Zealand Police have never seen fit to introduce an “always blow on the sausage roll” policy.

Which got me wondering how we ended up here in the first place.

The idea of wrapping meat in dough has been around for centuries, which makes sense because humanity has always been very good at discovering that if you wrap something in pastry, it generally improves it.

But the sausage roll as we’d recognise it started becoming popular in Britain in the early 1800s, when it was cheap, portable food for working people.

By the 1840s, recipes were appearing for sausage meat wrapped in pastry, baked and eaten hot or cold.

And, really, nearly 200 years later we haven’t messed with the basic formula too much.

Meat, pastry, oven, tomato sauce if required. Done.

It is simplicity bordering on genius, but then the cleverest things often are.

Look at the iPhone. On the surface it’s just a screen and a couple of buttons, but there’s an extraordinary amount of thinking going on underneath.

I reckon the sausage roll deserves the same respect.

Meat, pastry, seasoning. It looks simple, but getting all three exactly right is another matter entirely, which is why an award celebrating the people who have mastered it makes perfect sense.

And, as I discovered, the sausage roll’s claim to greatness doesn’t end at the bakery warmer. It has also played a surprisingly important role in world history.

Well, “important” may be stretching it.

In Gilbert and Sullivan’s 1896 comic opera The Grand Duke, a group of conspirators plotting against the miserly Duke Rudolph uses a sausage roll as its secret recognition signal.

Basically, if you knew what to do with the sausage roll, you were part of the gang.

Given we’re in an election year, I think there may still be something in this.

I can easily imagine Chris Bishop and Erica Stanford enjoying a sausage roll while standing behind the Prime Minister at some campaign event.

And we already know Chris Hipkins would be there for a munch.

The sausage roll’s cultural influence doesn’t stop with politics either.

We Built This City has already been successfully reworked into We Built This City on Sausage Rolls, so perhaps it’s time we had a New Zealand version.

Sir Dave Dobbyn, if you’re reading, a true Slice of Heaven is sitting right there.

But to get back to the reason I was wearing a borrowed black coat in the first place, the Bakels Sausage Roll Awards.

Once you get beyond my highly respected “Would these go well at Nana’s 80th?” category, it turns out there’s a lot that separates a good sausage roll from a great one.

The judges look at presentation, pastry, colour and filling, then there’s the all-important pastry-to-meat ratio, the seasoning, the bake, the flake.

This is sausage roll science, so the black coat is important.

As for me, I was there in my borrowed black jacket and, other than enjoying the odd sneaky taste, I couldn’t really tell the winners from the losers.

Luckily, there were some actual judges in the room who knew exactly what they were looking for, and eventually they came up with New Zealand’s best.

So, if you fancy a sausage roll road trip, here’s where to go.

You may agree with them, or you may decide it’s time they hung up their black coats and left the judging to those in high-vis.

So, here are the winners:

1st: Bunnarith Sao, Dairy Flat Bakery, Auckland

2nd: Patrick Lam, Patrick’s Pie Group, Tauranga

3rd: Michael Gray, Nada Bakery, Tawa, Wellington.

But after spending the day surrounded by some of the best sausage rolls in the country, I came away with a newfound respect for something I’ve probably spent most of my life taking for granted.

The pie may get more attention. It has more flavours, more awards and considerably more heated-cabinet real estate, but when the trestle tables come out, the paper plates are stacked, the tomato sauce bottle appears, and somebody walks into the room carrying a tray covered in tinfoil, there’s only one question anyone really cares about.

“Are those sausage rolls?”

And if you disagree with any of this, that’s fine. We can discuss it at Nana’s 80th.

I’ll be the bloke hovering near the empty plate in a stolen judge’s jacket.

Pastures Past: Stolen petrol, butter and other tales of theft

New Zealand Herald October 03, 2026

Rural properties were not immune from theft, as these 1930s and 1940s newspaper reports reveal.

Kem Ormond takes a look at the world of farming back in the day. In this week’s Pastures Past, she has uncovered newspaper articles from the 1930s and 1940s about theft, from stolen petrol to stolen butter.

Stolen goods, stolen petrol, and stolen butter!

Apparently, a little creative borrowing was alive and well in the 1930s and 1940s, and, judging by today’s headlines, it seems we haven’t completely outgrown the habit.

You might think stealing butter would be a particularly desperate crime, but back then, when many families were feeling the effects of the Depression, and later wartime rationing, even a pat of butter could be worth taking.

Times may have changed, cars may be faster and shopping baskets considerably larger, but the age-old temptation to acquire something without actually paying for it appears to be alive and kicking.

Below is a selection of historical stories from the Northern Advocate (1931), New Zealand Herald (1932), Rotorua Morning Post (1941), and the Central Hawke’s Bay Press (1948).

Woman discharges gun.

Intruders flee.

(Special to “Northern Advocate.”)

Northern Advocate, May 1, 1931

New Plymouth, this day.

On Tuesday night a severe fright was given to some thieves at a farmhouse by a woman who discharged a shotgun at them while they were in the act of removing stolen goods from the premises of Mr. J. Gibbs, of Wharehuia.

At 10 o’clock, when Mr. Gibbs and some friends were listening to the wireless, Mrs. Gibbs went to the back door.

As she opened it, she saw someone moving stealthily near the garage.

She called to her husband, who, however, did not hear her above the noise of the wireless.

Remembering that there was a shotgun just inside the door, Mrs. Gibbs rammed a cartridge into the breech and sent a shot a few yards in front of the intruders, who promptly dropped what they were carrying and made a hurried exit.

A search near the front gate revealed a tin of petrol, a grease gun, and a packet of butter.

Locks on pumps broken.

134 gallons removed.

Discovery in Wellington.

[BY TELEGRAPH.—Own correspondent.]

New Zealand Herald, June 27, 1932

Wellington, Sunday.

Thieves broke the locks of two petrol pumps in the city and stole 134 gallons of petrol yesterday afternoon or evening.

A group of three pumps, owned by Magnus Motors, Limited, stand in Opera House Lane, which runs down the side of the Grand Opera House from Manners Street to Wakefield Street.

The locks of two of the pumps were found by a nightwatchman to have been broken and the. fact that a large quantity of petrol had been stolen was soon discovered.

The third pump had not been touched.

After the locks had been broken the petrol was evidently pumped from the tanks into a waiting vehicle or vehicles.

The discovery that the locks had been broken was made at 9.45 p. m., but it is not known when the theft occurred, or how the petrol was taken away.

The attendant locked the pumps at noon, and between that time and the discovery of the crime, 134½ gallons of petrol were stolen.

Motor-cycle thief warned about seriousness of his offence

Young labourer fined £7

Rotorua Morning Post, March 1, 1941

The suspicious proximity of a motor-cycle to a car in Pukuatua Street and a strong smell of petrol attracted attention to a motor cyclist which resulted in the taking of his number, and, finally, his appearance in the Rotorua Police Court yesterday afternoon charged with the theft of two quarts of petrol.

The defendant, Leslie Terence Lang, aged 18 years, pleaded guilty, and was fined £1 by Messrs. J. J. Dillon and T. H. Sloane, Justices of the Peace.

Detective Sergeant J. White stated in evidence that the offence occurred last Saturday evening.

He had warned Lang of the serious nature of his offence and pointed out that the car might have belonged to a doctor, in which case the loss of the petrol might have had disastrous consequences.

He had advised the defendant to sell his motor-cycle as it was an expensive luxury to a farm labourer earning £2 a week.

Central Hawke’s Bay Press, February 26, 1948

Petrol thefts from cars, a prevalent wartime practice, are again being freely reported in Dunedin.

At least three centennial visitors who left their cars out at night found the tanks dry in the morning.

Automobile Association officers believe that with the reintroduction of rationing, thefts will recur to an even greater extent.

The heavy drain on service station supplies created this week by the centennial events, was the probable cause of the thefts.
