Carcasses, trespasses and a ‘Slink Mafia’: The strange and smelly saga of ‘Fast Eddie’ Zhi, ‘The King of Sheepskin’

New Zealand Herald October 03, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Every lamb and calf that dies at birth leaves behind a problem: a body that must be collected, buried or rendered before it becomes a source of contamination and stench. Around three years ago, Eddie Zhi built a business around taking those bodies from Southland farms, stripping away the valuable skins and finding a use for what remained. Now, after council orders halted the operation, Zhi is attempting to burn the hundreds of thousands of accumulated carcasses instead. Ben Tomsett reports.

Da Cheng “Eddie” Zhi says he came to Southland to revive a forgotten industry.

Instead, his Tuturau slink-skin operation has become the subject of repeated Environment Court orders, seven Environment Southland charges, a parallel Southland District Council case, angry protests, a formal trespass notice and thousands of emails.

It began with a practical problem of farming: what to do with lambs and calves that die before they can be sent to the meatworks.

Zhi’s answer was to recover their skins for export and turn the remaining animal material into organic fertiliser.

The councils believe that the business has operated outside its consent, with carcasses, skins, liquid and earthworks creating environmental risks.

Zhi spoke to the Herald by video call, his face marked with the words “SAVE JOBS” and “SOS” as he drove to the Environment Southland offices, where he planned to sticker their signs as a peaceful protest.

He calls the councils the “Slink Mafia”, blaming them for strangling the industry.

Before Zhi arrived, Newton Slinkskins had reduced its Southland service from about 140,000 lambs and 25,000 calves the previous season to an expected 50,000 to 70,000 lambs, amid the collapse of other operators and Lowe Corporation’s withdrawal from the South Island casualty-stock business.

When Newton shut the Tuturau plant in 2023, Zhi established NZAgri Development Ltd and restarted slink-skin processing at the site with help from Newton and former Newton staff.

Before Southland, Zhi was involved in the Australian meat trade where the nickname “Fast Eddie” followed him through a series of high-profile business disputes and legal battles – he tells the Herald he is an experienced international operator: “I was the king of sheepskin”.

“I turned myself into a meat trader.”

Zhi said he graduated from East China Normal University, became a university teacher at 20 and later studied leather technology at Sydney TAFE.

He said he had worked in the leather and meat industries in China, Australia and New Zealand and had been involved in major Australian deals - and that the Southland business was relatively modest by comparison.

“Today it’s a piece of cheesecake,” he said.

Zhi said he became involved in the Southland operation in 2023 after a friend told him there were no longer enough slink-skin operators in New Zealand.

He travelled to Tuturau and visited the existing plant, which he described as “pathetic, dirty” and “very, very, very, very, very sad looking”.

The slink-skin business is seasonal.

Lambs and calves that die around birth are collected, skinned and processed.

Their hides are exported for use in leather goods, while the remaining carcasses have to be disposed of lawfully.

Zhi said the original business model was too seasonal and labour-intensive. He believed it could be modernised.

He said the first year exceeded expectations: “I collected 162,000 lambs - 162,000 lambs,” he told the Herald.

“It’s only because there’s no bloody competition.

“Everybody else died.” One requires a sense of humour to understand Zhi, he explains.

Zhi’s solution for dealing with the remaining animal material was to convert it to organic liquid fertiliser.

He said he had told Environment Southland about the plan and believed council officials had responded positively.

In the second year, Zhi said the operation collected about 182,000 lambs and 33,000 calves.

However, that year two contractors walked off the job, stopping work for five days.

During that time, he said, animals continued arriving and a backlog developed.

“After one stop for five days, you have like 30,000 lambs piling up,” he said.

He said the backlog was worsened by severe weather and that animals had to be stored in different parts of the property.

Alyce Perkins lives with her husband and children about 250m from the plant and says the smell has become part of daily life.

“It’s horrible,” she told the Herald. “It just smells every day.”

Perkins said the previous operator’s season was unpleasant but short – the current operation lasted longer and the fertiliser production changed the experience of living nearby.

“It wrecks your little slice of heaven, really. It’s a pretty nice place here, but you’ve got to live next to that hellhole,” she said.

She said she supported finding a use for casualty animals, but believed the work needed to be done properly.

“There’s got to be a way of doing it that’s not detrimental to the environment and the people around it.”

By October last year, Environment Southland and the Ministry for Primary Industries were investigating Zhi’s operation.

Zhi said the labour dispute had been resolved and that processing was continuing normally.

A worker who has spoken to the Herald said they were owed $1200, which should have been paid by September 21.

They believed other workers were also thousands out of pocket.

Zhi rejected the account as “a total lie from suckers” and sent documents appearing to show contracts to sell 30,000 calf skins for US$450,000 and 40,000 baby lamb skins for US$300,000.

The documents did not show whether workers had been paid or directly address the alleged wage arrears.

Zhi said any smell may have come from the backlog, but denied there was a serious ongoing odour problem.

On October 31, 2025, Southland District Council applied to the Environment Court for interim enforcement orders against NZAgri Development Ltd, Zhi and Hui Xie.

Its evidence alleged offensive odour, blood discharges, possible contamination and vermin.

A monitoring officer described the smell as “overwhelming” and said she had at times been unable to breathe through her nose.

Officers also counted 283 intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) holding organic liquid fertiliser at the Tuturau property.

The court issued interim orders on November 21, requiring fertiliser production to stop, restricting the receipt of new skins and carcasses, and requiring existing animal material to be lawfully disposed of.

The orders were extended in December after a substantive hearing was delayed.

The parties later disagreed over whether Zhi could continue processing the material in the containers, with Zhi arguing further chemicals were needed before the fertiliser could be exported and the council arguing that would amount to an unconsented industrial activity.

Further orders were made in March after the council raised concerns about earthworks and a proposal to mix liquid fertiliser with soil to make a solid product.

The court ordered the fertiliser businesses to cease and required action over the earthworks and animal remains.

Initially, the judge declined to order the removal of the 283 containers, saying there was insufficient evidence of a likely adverse environmental effect from their continued presence.

But after council officers provided further evidence, including photographs showing dark marks around some containers, Judge Reid found that a number of the IBCs were leaking.

Leaving them represented a “significant ongoing risk to the environment”, the judge found, and the orders were amended to require their removal.

Zhi sought more time, citing wet and unstable ground, unsuitable lifting equipment and difficulties scheduling council staff.

The council opposed the application, saying officers had repeatedly attended the site but there had been “very limited progress”.

The court rejected the extension in June.

In July, Zhi applied to receive slink calves for skin recovery, arguing that the short season was important to farmers, collectors and seasonal workers.

The council said existing skins, carcasses and fertiliser containers had not been cleared.

On August 13, the court refused the application. Although Zhi framed the proposal as skin recovery rather than fertiliser production, the judge said it would still bring more animal material onto the site.

The court found the seasonal urgency was foreseeable and that any commercial harm arose while the respondents remained subject to orders they had not complied with.

Despite the decision, Zhi told the Herald the business had collected animals during the 2026 season.

This week, Zhi begun burning the the thousands of carcasses piled at Tuturau - which proved difficiult, as there was “too much moisture,” he said.

Asked why he was burning the carcasses, Zhi said it was intended to sterilise the surface, kill bacteria, reduce oxygen and encourage gradual degradation.

He said carbonisation would adsorb ammonia and claimed the process would deter rats.

He also said the burn was intended to draw international attention and condemnation, express his “freedom of scientific expressions”, mock what he called the “ignorant two fat rats”(ES and SDC), and celebrate China’s national day.

Zhi has also filed a judicial-review proceeding in the High Court against Environment Southland and Southland District Council.

In the filing, dated July 30, he alleges the councils failed to properly investigate historic offal pits, including their lining, construction, location and potential impact on groundwater.

He also alleges the councils failed to properly consider laboratory results, historic sources of contamination and alternatives to burying animal material.

It is a statement of claim and contains allegations that have not been tested in court.

Environment Southland has laid seven charges against Zhi relating to the operation between August 1 and September 26, 2025.

Six concern alleged discharges of blood, leachate or contaminants to land where they could enter water; the seventh alleges failure to comply with abatement notices.

The district council has also laid charges against Zhi and NZAgri Development.

On September 9, Environment Southland announced further interim orders requiring Zhi and his company to stop receiving and processing carcasses, cease unlawful discharges and remove carcasses, containers of minced animal material and contaminated liquid.

Both councils declined to comment because the matters remain before the Environment Court.

Zhi’s response has been anything but quiet, with his campaign of protest veering into performance art.

Since September 11, he has taken dead animals to council offices on the back of a truck, sat across a carpark entrance while removing his clothing and appeared in white overalls covered in red.

Before his Facebook account was suspended this week, Zhi was a regular poster in Southland community groups, using them to document his dispute with the councils and share graphic images from inside the Tuturau operation.

Facebook said the account had breached its standards on account integrity and Zhi had 180 days to appeal.

Zhi says he is exercising his democratic right to protest and trying to defend his workers and business.

Environment Southland eventually trespassed him from its offices.

The next major step is an Environment Court hearing in Invercargill on October 7, where Environment Southland is seeking further enforcement orders and Southland District Council is seeking to revoke the slink-skin factory’s resource consent.

The outcome could determine whether Zhi’s operation can continue.

Ben Tomsett is a multimedia journalist based in Dunedin. He joined the Herald in 2023.

‘Let’s get back to real food’: Adam Liaw’s new show is a long way from MasterChef

Sydney Morning Herald October 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In the middle of a barn, on the edges of a farm on Sydney’s south-western fringe, chef, author and TV producer Adam Liaw is biting into an Anzac biscuit.

“Whoarrrh,” he says in delight. “Excellent crunch.”

I take a biscuit too, freshly baked by contestants on the ABC’s new seven-part cooking show Recipe of the Year. The show is being filmed all around us at handmade wooden benchtops stationed against a backdrop of green pastureland beyond the barn’s wide open doors. Liaw takes my phone and films me breaking the golden, oat-flecked biscuit in two.

“Good?” he says.

It is. Perfectly crisp and, after a bite, nicely chewy. I explain my love for Anzac biscuits that are more chewy than crispy, but Ellice Schrader, a judge on the series and a member of the Country Women’s Association of NSW, overhears.

“It needs to snap,” she says of the biscuit being broken apart. She also confirms that the CWA advises Anzac biscuits must never, ever, be called “cookies”.

“Ellice is formidable,” Liaw says. It’s a label he also gives her in the series’ first episode to which Schrader replies: “I’m a pussycat.”

Recipe of the Year features 10 home cooks, drawn from 20 hopefuls in the show’s first episode, competing to achieve Australia’s “recipe of the year”. Hosted by Liaw and actor and food-lover Pia Miranda, it’s created and produced by i8 Studio, the Sydney production company Liaw runs with co-executive producer and director Josh Martin.

Liaw and Martin, whose company is known for shows such as Tonight at the Museum, The Cook Up with Adam Liaw and Adam & Poh’s Great Australian Bites, say this series is a departure from the usual competitive cooking TV show. Not only do contestants bring their own recipes to cook, they share the meals cooked in each episode around a table together.

“It’s a really familiar space for a lot of viewers, and we’re genuinely trying our hardest to do things that are different,” Liaw says. “Not just for the sake of being different, but because we felt there were important reasons to make the show feel accessible and more like cooking feels at home.”

Those reasons include the current cost of living, time constraints for everyday cooks and how and why people cook for themselves, friends and family. Unlike shows like MasterChef Australia (which Liaw won in 2010) or My Kitchen Rules, Recipe of the Year’s focus is on recipes rather than cooking.

“[Australians] love recipes,” Liaw says. “We love them in the newspaper, online and in books. We were really thinking through what’s the experience with somebody when they’re making a recipe? And, when they choose to cook something, is it a recipe that makes sense for the purpose that is being set for it?

“Then, when you actually make it, what’s the process of eating? There aren’t many circumstances in home cooking where three members of your family stand there in front of you and taste it, give stern expressions and then give you feedback. Even though it is a competition, there’s also an atmosphere of home cooking on the show around the way we instruct the challengers and the way we judge.”

Pia Miranda, a passionate cook and food lover, says making the show inspired great warmth and conviviality. “It’s one of the best experiences I’ve ever had, and I’m not just saying that because it’s about to come out,” she says. “It really was.

“Everyone who was there just had a great time … It felt like a fourth or fifth season, not like the first season of a TV show. It was a real celebration of life.”

The show’s location also resulted in a passing parade of animal life beyond the barn’s doors. “We had cows,” she says. “We had kangaroos. There were deer and beautiful, beautiful birds. Adam’s so cute: every time kangaroos went past, he got misty-eyed. He gets so excited by kangaroos. We had to stop and just look at them.”

Josh Martin believes the show’s focus on recipes, along with the contestants’ stories about their recipes’ origins and histories, will inspire a broad range of viewers.

“Adam and I have made a lot of food shows,” Martin says. “And don’t get me wrong: we love MasterChef, we love Bake Off. Six hours for a challenge to do something? That’s great. But we thought, let’s just get back to real food that people cook. In the second episode, the very first challenge they do is make a sandwich. But it really works.”

Recipe of the Year’s format features three challenges: the blue ribbon, the gold ribbon and a feature recipe section. The first is about creativity; the second focuses on precision and is judged by the CWA, with recipes ranging from a jam roll to scones and Anzac biscuits; the third is a recipe brought in by competitors.

Across the series, themes include comfort food, budget cooking, the big barbecue, weekend brunch recipes and more.

“The final challenge is the only one with stakes on it,” Martin says. “They all bake a dish and at the end, rather than the judges tasting and judging like a lot of other shows, everybody sits around the table and votes for their favourite to least favourite. Then we tally the votes. Because everybody’s opinion on food matters – not just the expert.”

Today, contestants are getting ready to bake more Anzac biscuits. They stand at benchtops fitted with ovens, cooktops and kitchen equipment while crew members bustle around them.

Rustic wooden walls display retro tea towels, souvenir teaspoon displays, hanging copper pans and ceramic jugs filled with eucalyptus and banksia branches. Contestants have been given tea towels printed with the Anzac biscuit recipe (“Bake at 175 degrees for 15 to 20 mins or until golden brown”).

The contestants – who have a wide variety of ages, experience and cultural and geographical backgrounds – include a 19-year-old aspiring chef who experiments passionately with cannoli, and a builder from Sydney celebrating his mother’s cooking. There’s also a Malaysian-born home cook sharing flavours of her homeland, and a teacher who, expressing the importance of connecting with family via food, shares her late mother’s recipes.

Schrader, decked out in pearls and a total natural in front of the cameras, judges the gold ribbon category with warmth, generosity and strict CWA criteria. As with food competitions at major Australian agricultural shows, judging cakes, slices, biscuits and other baked goods is not done lightly.

In one episode, she wields a tape measure to assess the talents of a scone. Contestants are told that a good jam roll must have “no cracks, no skin missing and a neat roll”. Schrader slices one open to show a perfect, evenly layered swirl of jam inside the sponge.

“Ellice was the biggest surprise for us,” Martin says. “She had never done television before in her life and really has not much interest in it. But she was such a natural, such a joy, and at times quite scary. She’s like the Margaret Pomeranz of cooking, or a Simon Cowell-esque role. It’s hard feedback, but done with a completely different approach.”

Martin also applauds the ABC for supporting a show with an original format like this.

“A lot of the main shows that we have on air in Australia are imported formats,” he says. “There are very few original formats and that’s fine, they’re popular. But the ability for Australian IP and ideas to be created here, and then, if successful, exported to other countries … that’s what the ABC should be doing, that’s what all our cultural institutions should be doing: supporting Australian IP.

“I’d love to see a UK version or an American version or a Japanese version, or whatever it might be, of the show.”

What Martin loves most about Recipe of the Year is its blend of modern Australia: diverse food, shared community, nostalgia, creativity. He calls it intentionally analogue and an antidote to today’s AI-saturated world.

“I feel like people want to try something new in the kitchen or mix up their repertoire,” he says. “And this show gives them ideas that are achievable.”

Recipe of the Year premieres 7.30pm, October 11 on the ABC and ABC iview.

After an unforgettable career, Kate Ceberano has few regrets – but there is one big one

Sydney Morning Herald October 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

After more than four decades on stage and screen, singer Kate Ceberano has few regrets. She’s crafted 31 albums (11 platinum, eight gold), won five ARIA awards and been inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame for her performances, which span rock, soul, jazz, pop and classical.

In the 1980s, she won three Countdown awards, in the 1990s she played Mary in a record-breaking run of Jesus Christ Superstar and won a Logie for the video clip for the song Everything’s Alright. She was the first woman inducted into the Australian Songwriters Association Hall of Fame in 2014. On top of that, in 2007 she won Dancing with the Stars, and portraits of her have been chosen as finalists in the Archibald three times, with two winning the Packing Room Prize (in 1994 and 2021).

From fronting the band I’m Talking in 1984 to her successful solo career, for which she was made a member of the Order of Australia in 2016, Ceberano is one of the best-known voices and faces of the Australian entertainment industry.

“I’ve come to an age where I can’t be ‘un-Kate Ceberano’,” she says. “Like Chrissy [Amphlett], Renee [Geyer], Kylie [Minogue] and Delta [Goodrem], we’re all on a one-name basis with our audiences. That’s quite a rare and privileged place to get to in Australia and you only get there by being yourself.”

But there is one missed opportunity that hounds her still. It was during her serious flamenco phase, a dance form she took up at the age of 12 to understand more of her Filipina/Spanish origins. Her Filipino/Hawaiian father Tino was known as “the father of Australian karate” after his 1970s morning-TV appearances teaching self-defence. “My dad is the highest-ranked of his style in the world. He’s not just a karate master, he’s like Kung Fu Panda,” she jokes.“I first found out about fame and being in the public eye thanks to my dad.”

Her mother Cherie, whose ethnicity is Swedish and Welsh, was also one of the first women to hold a black belt in karate in Australia.

“At our house, at any given time, there was anywhere between 50 to 100 black belts. The only reason I didn’t do it was because I didn’t love the sound of women sparring. I found it very unfeminine.”

Instead of karate, the youngest of three, and only girl in her family, took up singing and dancing. At about the age of 12 she joined a dance group with the Filipino Association – “flamenco without the frilly dresses” as she calls it – and became obsessed. So much so that a young filmmaker called Baz Luhrmann approached her in the early 1990s to become involved in a film he was making about ballroom dancing.

“To my absolute shame, I declined the offer to be part of Strictly Ballroom because I didn’t know what the film was about. I didn’t understand that it was actually going to be exactly about the very thing that I was being a purist about,” she says.

“I found ballroom’s version of flamenco to be kind of like an aberrant version of flamenco because it wasn’t the true ethnic flamenco that I was into. But as it turns out, that was a lost opportunity of the highest degree. When the film came out I just wanted to bite my arm off.”

So since then she’s said ‘yes’ to everything, which is one of the main reasons she’s headed back on tour for the Australian Made encore tour. It began in London on August 8 and will end in Shepparton, Victoria, on November 20. It will take her to venues throughout regional Australia, as well as the Sydney Opera House (October 11) and Melbourne’s Hamer Hall (October 23), on the back of her 2025 21-date Australian Made tour, 2024’s Superstars Live with Jon Stevens, and the 2023 orchestral collaboration with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, My Life Is a Symphony. All three tours were sell-outs.

The Australian Made tour of 1986-87 was a watershed moment in Australian music, showcasing local talent in major stadiums and acting as a precursor to festivals like the Big Day Out. Ceberano was barely 20 that summer when, as lead singer of I’m Talking, she joined the stellar line-up of INXS, Jimmy Barnes, Divinyls, Models, The Saints and The Triffids.

The idea for a 2025 tour and live album came after a discussion with her husband and manager Lee Rogers after the 2016 re-release of Richard Lowenstein’s film Australian Made: The Movie.

“We bemoaned the fact that almost all of the performers are now dead,” she says, listing the tally of fallen fellow musos, from INXS’ Michael Hutchence to Divinyls’ Chrissy Amphlett, The Saints’ Chris Bailey, Models’ James Freud and now James Valentine. “I was kind of like the last of the Mohicans, along with Jimmy Barnes and Sean Kelly from Models.”

She felt it was time to tell her old friends’ stories to new audiences (or old ones keen for a dose of nostalgia).

Looking back, she remembers she was slightly terrified by the Australian Made cohort, especially Amphlett.

“What she taught me was you need to be bold enough to be yourself,” Ceberano says. “I wasn’t sidling up to any of my peers, like Renee Geyer or Chrissy Amphlett, for any badge of approval. But what they did teach me is that if you come too close to imitating or trying to become your idol, you have to pay the price … No one wants a poor imitation of another person.”

For a girl who left school at 15, whose band won the Victorian Battle of the Bands at 16 and who not long after opened for Vince Jones, jazz was a focus of her early career – thanks in part to Melbourne restaurateur Mietta O’Donnell. “She saw me as a sort of Josephine Baker singer and put me on her menu at [the restaurant] Mietta’s as a dessert – a warm chocolate tart.”

Ceberano credits her love of singing back to a childhood illness. “I got a very severe case of glandular fever around 13 and I sat and watched midday movies for about three months, and mostly they were musicals. And then I reckon I just started sort of hallucinating with fever and imagining I was singing in musicals.”

Like it or not, she is best known as a rock singer whose name will be eternally linked to those giddy days of Oz-rock in the 1980s.

“I always really loved the entourage of the bands that were on the Australian Made stage,” she recalls. “Michael Hutchence was going out with [model] Helena Christensen. Backstage there were a lot of his beautiful acolytes who were beautiful spirits as well. Among them was Jane Barnes, who had baby Mahalia on her hip through most of Jimmy Barnes’ wild gigs.”

That baby, Mahalia Barnes, has since gone on to play Mary Magdalene in Jesus Christ Superstar, the same role Ceberano played next to John Farnham in the 1990s, and Ceberano’s own daughter, Gypsy, has also gone into a career in music, as next-gen Australian Made offspring. Ceberano welcomes the fact there are more professional female musicians than when she began.

“Barbara Hogarth, who was the first woman that I’d ever worked with or had known of in the music business, was on bass in I’m Talking, When you consider that of all of the bands on that tour, there were only two bands with women in them, you can see how far we’ve come in the music industry.”

Despite early warnings that “girls don’t play the drums” (“The Go-Betweens’ Lindy Morrison was the first woman I’d ever seen on drums”), for this tour, like the last one, she plays the drums.

“The reason why I drum on this particular tour was because we wanted to travel light in two cars with [support acts] Kathleen Halloran and Dusty Lee and our crew as well, and we wanted to be able to be very nimble when coming into regional gigs,” she said.

“I also wanted the sounds to be big and I wanted that to be rock, so it has the same visceral impact. The body has to feel like you’re shaking, and the roof is shaking, and you need to be able to make it big.”

Ceberano developed a passion for sewing during the COVID lockdowns and has a clothing line she sells online, including flamenco-like frilly skirts that she embroiders with song lyrics.

In between songs in the show she will tell anecdotes about her former 1980s muso friends, but insists it is not a tribute show; just an old friend singing songs to remember an amazing time in Australian rock history. As a prelude to the show she uses the same music INXS used to come on stage to every night during the original Australian Made tour.

“It’s fantastic warm-up music,” said the singer, who will turn 60 in the final month of this tour. “The minute it starts I feel like the child that I was at 20, watching at the side of the wings for Michael and the boys to launch into their first hits. I hope my own enthusiasm and nostalgia for this era can bring the audiences along with us.”

Kate Ceberano’s Australian Made encore tour reaches Canberra’s Playhouse on October 10, the Sydney Opera House Concert Hall on October 11 and Hamer Hall in Melbourne on October 23. kateceberano. com/home#tours

Barnyard punks in Orange, empty stages in Byron Bay: The NSW towns where live music thrives or dies

Sydney Morning Herald October 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In showground barns usually reserved for cattle on the outskirts of Orange in western NSW, Mitch Colton awaits hordes of hardcore punk and metal fans ahead of his inaugural two-day music festival, The Gig.

Speaking to the Herald under a corrugated iron roof two hours before the scheduled start time, Colton appears unbothered but is apprehensive. “Two weeks ago, the ticket sales were awful,” the co-organiser and seasoned event manager says. “Tickets are getting better now.”

“I was talking to the guy that owns Mojos, which is a really famous live music venue in Fremantle, and he’s like, ‘Yeah, we do 80 per cent of our tickets on the day now’.”

Dozens of punters as young as 12, clad in leather garments, with spiked hair and face piercings, stream in throughout the first frosty Friday night. “Even if it’s not packed out, as long as it’s a good turnout and there’s a good crowd [that’s a success],” Colton says.

Colton had hoped for 500 patrons. Instead, about 190 came through. The following Saturday night, 250 did. “Obviously, we’d like it to be a commercial success, but the reality is, as long as it feels good – because the joke of the sign is that nothing ever happens in Orange,” he says, referencing the festival’s poster, which in the spirit of punk declares just that.

Live music scenes across the state are evolving. Musicians are struggling to get stage time in the Northern Rivers’ once-bustling scene, while the Central West is remaking the model and Newcastle is emerging as a hotspot. Meanwhile, in Sydney, venues are shutting as punters’ behaviour changes amid the cost of living crisis and the decline of alcohol consumption.

Over the years, the regions have nurtured some big names. Singer-songwriter Shannon Noll was born in Orange, while Lismore delivered Grinspoon and Skunkhour. Country stars Keith Urban, Lee Kernaghan, James Blundell and Beccy Cole got golden tickets at Tamworth’s annual country music festival.

Byron Bay has cradled Parcels, Skegss, Parkway Drive, Tones and I and Pete Murray and Newcastle claims the likes of Silverchair, The Screaming Jets, Morgan Evans and Catherine Britt.

Colton’s festival is one of the increasing number of independently organised cultural events in NSW’s regions. On the festival’s first night, pub-rock Orange-born band Where’s Jimmy performs an electric set.

The high-school mates moved to Newcastle for better opportunities after exhausting the “same two pubs” in Orange soon after forming in 2020 amid the pandemic. Now, they regularly book gigs in Newcastle, occasionally in Sydney and are fresh off a European tour.

“It’s special for our first show back to be at home,” the band’s bassist James Pansini says. On stage, lead singer Hugh Westcott squirms erratically and jumps around barefoot, before launching into an acrobatic midair split. In the band’s music video for the song KICK IN THE HEAD, he takes it further, running barefoot around a barn with animal faeces strewn across the straw ground.

Since the band relocated, Orange and the rest of the state’s Central West towns have embraced an experimental attitude towards their live music landscape, says Sophie Jones, the region’s Music NSW coordinator.

“People are wanting to step away from the pubs and clubs where there are pokies,” Jones says. Orange’s Badlands Brewery’s ticketed gigs include acts such as Alex Lloyd, Meg Washington, Josh Pike and The Whitlams. But the most exciting event, says Jones, is the “little blues festival in the car park” the venue runs.

“It’s so cool to see these smaller venues doing these non-council-run little one-day festivals,” she says. “My band’s been playing together for 12 years now, and we started here in Bathurst, and there was nowhere for us.

“Now it’s taken this kind of turn where a lot of people are really wanting to come to Bathurst and play at venues like Reckless, The Victoria and Keystone … There’s still a challenge of getting people along to ticketed original shows, but it’s definitely got better in the last 10 years.”

Beyond towns and in the outback, music scenes are also pushing boundaries. In Lightning Ridge, musicians perform, record and collaborate out of a “tinny”, or a performance space modelled on the housing in the typical 1950s Aboriginal “tin camp” and designed by First Nations musician Warren Mason.

“He’s got a permanent one set up at [venue] Hungry Spirit ... but he takes the tinnies all around and, oh man, it’s so cool! And all original music,” Jones says. “Warren’s toured all across the outback and then around the bottom of Victoria, like Mildura.”

Newcastle’s talent pool and hunger for gigs has never been higher, Joab Eastley, that city’s coordinator for Music NSW, says.

“I feel like we’ve punched above our weight for quite a while here in Newcastle,” he says. “Every time you go somewhere like Big Sound and Music Conference, or get out to another city, everyone’s like, ‘Wow, what’s going on in Newcastle?’ Or everyone’s got a story of, ‘I saw this band from Newcastle in Brisbane the other week, and they blew my socks off.’ It’s a very common line.”

Eastley says it’s natural there are more opportunities in a bigger city like Newcastle for acts such as Where’s Jimmy than in other regional towns. But, as with Orange and Lightning Ridge, venues and event organisers are experimenting with how to deliver gigs.

“A lot of our bigger festivals have seemed to have gone by the wayside; that was sort of post-COVID,” he says. “Instead, it’s more like boutiquey-niche things are what’s happening. Claire O’Brien, who’s an amazing DJ from Newcastle, Mulubinba, puts on a thing called Ode events, which are raves in all different unique places, and they absolutely slap.”

As the NSW government expands its music and nightlife agenda through its $150 million hospitality nightlife reforms and new live music laws, funding and policy ideas are being fed into the regions. Tamworth has become the first regional town to trial Labor’s “special entertainment precinct” scheme that allows councils to set more relaxed planning rules in a designated nightlife area.

But some regions in NSW are still struggling. In the Northern Rivers, Byron Bay has become a victim of its own success: creatives are being priced out of the bohemian capital, says Music NSW Northern Rivers coordinator Niño Haggith. Meanwhile, its music events – Falls Festival, Splendour in the Grass and more recently, Bluesfest – have been cancelled.

“I was the general manager of a local festival, Mullumbimby Music Festival, and we also had the Bellingen Winter Music Festival down in the Mid North Coast, and we froze those purely because of COVID, and [they] haven’t come back yet,” Haggith says, adding the region has also suffered from a spate of natural disasters, including the 2022 floods.

While the region is “voluminous” with artists, Haggith says they’re moving to more affordable towns such as Lismore and Ballina. “Just looking around Byron, you can see priorities in these big, huge hotels that are coming up, and I just don’t know how sustainable it’s going to be,” he says.

“Obviously, it’s not conducive to affordable living, especially for artists and arts workers.”

Mayor Sarah Ndiaye says cost of living price rises and weather events have pushed Byron Bay’s music scene “through the eye of a needle”.

“Festivals are having to come back into the towns where they were often first born from, and got too big for, and had to move away from,” Ndiaye says. “I think we’re having to rethink how we deliver festivals.”

The Northern Rivers needs to utilise more of its infrastructure and invite local businesses to take part in the live music scene to become sustainable, Haggith says. As in other NSW regions, this approach is manifesting in a rise of DIY, all-ages and experimental scenes less reliant on the local pokies pub.

“They can be a bit more creative with spaces … people are also teaming up with each other on putting gigs on in different spaces, community halls, shopfronts,” he says.

In Lismore – where, Haggith says, “is actually where the music community is” – venue Blah Bar, a dedicated space supporting local independent musicians, closed after less than a year due to planning difficulties and licensing costs.

“I don’t have the money to keep going any more,” co-owner Pat Stanton told the Lismore Times. “I’ve been operating for a couple of months now with BYO, and unfortunately alcohol is where you make your money ... I don’t take money off the bands because I don’t believe in that.”

NSW Greens MP Cate Faehrmann asked Nightlife and Music Minister John Graham in August budget estimates whether Labor’s latest $3.8 million funding round could assist. “That specific funding that [Faehrmann] referred to is in relation to core music venues,” Graham said, adding that the changes to planning rules and liquor discounts were designed to help new venues.

“We’ve got to back the music venues doing most of the programming as new venues open up; otherwise we’ll lose those original ones,” Graham said.

In response to an on-notice question, Graham said Blah Bar had never applied for government grant funding and therefore did not receive any.

Back in Orange, The Gig co-organiser, Colton, isn’t fazed by its low turnout. In fact, he believes the event was a total success. “Everyone who came thought it was awesome,” he says.

“There’s a huge metal scene down here, and there’s just not a lot of good performance opportunities. And we’re like, we should do something for them.”

Forget the men, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles carry the true love story of this film

Sydney Morning Herald October 04, 2026

The two actors are the perfect pick to play sisters in this latest Austen reboot.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A decade before anyone put them in bonnets, Daisy Edgar-Jones met Esmé Creed-Miles on the 2017 Yorkshire set of coming-of-age drama Pond Life. “I was so blown away by her,” says Edgar-Jones, who was then 19, of her co-star, then 17. “[She] has this energy that is so compelling. She’s a wonderfully intelligent and sort of wild person, in the best way.”

The teenagers became fast friends and “had a really great summer of watching Love Island and shooting this indie film”.

Creed-Miles’ first impression of her co-star is equally vivid: “Daisy was unbelievably kind and talented. She put me at ease and I could tell I had a friend in her.” Admittedly, “it would be hard not to get on with Daisy. She’s just one of the loveliest people.”

Almost a decade on, the women are reunited on a much grander stage: Georgia Oakley’s gorgeous adaptation of Jane Austen’s 1811 debut novel, Sense and Sensibility, in which they star as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood. “To already have that shorthand with Esmé and to feel a sort of sisterly feeling, made it so seamless,” says Edgar-Jones.

An Austen adaptation is a world away from a small budget indie, but this is no polite costume drama either. It’s a kaleidoscope of undone hair, mud, rage and running.

“I was really trying to get into what it might have felt like to live in Devon 200 years ago,” Oakley has said of her film’s unbridled aesthetic. “Steering away from this preconceived idea we have about Austen, that everything takes place in a stuffy drawing room.”

When Edgar-Jones, 28, appears on our video call, it’s 11am in London. She’s just off a call with Australian writer Tony McNamara about Mosquito, their upcoming comedy series. What does a Gucci, Boucheron and Estée Lauder brand ambassador wear when working from home? As it turns out, a striped rugby jumper, no discernible make-up and “sports shorts” from a morning workout: “It’s not my best look!”

A few days later, Creed-Miles, 26, is similarly casual when she Zooms in just after 1pm. “I woke up quite recently,” she says, wandering around her London home, earbuds in, breaking off to answer the door: “I think it’s some food.”

Seeing the pair like this – using tech, in athleisure wear, waiting on deliveries – is faintly surreal after seeing them as the Dashwoods, physically and emotionally entwined as they braid hair, share a bed and absorb each other’s heartbreaks. With apologies to Edward Ferrars (George MacKay) and Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum), they’re the heart of the film and its true love story.

“I’m really glad that you say that because I remember that being such a clear piece of direction that Georgia, our director, wanted to follow,” says Edgar-Jones. Growing up an only child, she “had to outsource that sisterly or that familial sibling bond to friends”, and found it here. “It’s just a really lovely thing that the love story is the two women and how much they gift each other.”

To Oakley, the Dashwoods “represent these two opposing forces that a lot of women have within themselves that are always at war”. For Austen-era women with few ways to support themselves and little control over inheritance, says Creed-Miles, “the bond of motherhood or sisterhood becomes more prescient”.

In Austen’s world, marriage was survival – do it or sink. So in 2026, when women have careers, best friends and their own front-door keys, what is romantic love actually for? “It’s a great question, and I think it’s one we’re always asking,” says Edgar-Jones.

In a relationship with photographer Ben Seed for nearly four years, Edgar-Jones says she “loves love” and that modern romance is “for friendship and companionship and support”. But her longer answer is pure Elinor: “What Austen does so well is explore the variety of love we can experience in a life – be it platonic, familial, romantic – and how valuable all of those are. The same exists today. It’s so magic to cultivate love in all those different areas of your life if you can.”

Asked about the same topic, Creed-Miles admits defeat – “Oh gosh. Literally, that is just too big a question for me”. There is romance in her life, though, in the form of an engagement to musician Daisy Maybe – yes, another Daisy. “I love going for a walk with my fiancée,” she says. “We take our dog to the park. We might cook some nice food and watch a bit of telly and chill out. Very simple.”

In real life, which of the pair is sense and which is sensibility? Edgar-Jones says she is “probably a mixture, honestly”, adding “I don’t fall in love very easily” while admitting to being “a massive romantic”.

Creed-Miles, gloriously vulnerable and untamed as Marianne, leans “more towards sensibility, internally. I definitely experience that sort of crushing depth of feeling.”

Marianne is the kind of woman Creed-Miles always wanted to be, someone “outgoing and with a passion for life who took risks”, whereas she describes herself as “quite reclusive”. That introversion is something she’s “constantly reconciling” with her other day job as singer and guitarist in UK duo Cusk.

Edgar-Jones is a devotee of Ang Lee’s 1995 version of Sense and Sensibility, describing Emma Thompson’s Elinor as “one of the most beautiful performances in cinema”. The successor to Kate Winslet’s Marianne, Creed-Miles has never seen the 31-year-old film, but says the new incarnation will “hopefully do [Winslet] and Emma and Ang Lee proud”.

The storyline, of course, is awash with yearning: Elinor and Edward for each other, Colonel Brandon for Marianne, Marianne for Willoughby, mothers and relatives for weddings. It’s a mode Edgar-Jones perfected as another Marianne, opposite Paul Mescal’s Connell in the 2020 smash TV series Normal People, which made her a household name and garnered her Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations.

Does she ever wish we’d forget Normal People? “Oh no, I’d be so sad if that happened,” she says. “I love those characters so much, and I love that show. I mean, perhaps the thing I love most in the world is a good bit of hardcore yearning, and I do think Sense and Sensibility and Normal People really tick that box.”

MacKay’s Edward also extends a streak she copped to in Elle last year: “I have worked with basically all of the internet’s boyfriends,” she said, citing Mescal, Sebastian Stan and Jacob Elordi. “Just Timothée Chalamet and Austin Butler left!”

Born in London to Wendy, a film editor, and Philip Edgar-Jones, a television executive, Daisy acted in school plays before studying at the National Youth Theatre. Teenage TV roles in Cold Feet and Silent Witness led to Normal People, then Where the Crawdads Sing, Under the Banner of Heaven and Twisters.

The daughter of actors Samantha Morton and Charlie Creed-Miles, Esmé made her showbiz debut at seven as a tiny Shirley Temple impersonator in Harmony Korine’s 2007 film Mister Lonely, before moving on to three seasons of snapping necks as the title assassin in Amazon’s Hanna and a role in Kristen Stewart’s 2025 directorial debut, The Chronology of Water.

Both women talk glowingly of the fun and shared knowledge on Sense and Sensibility’s female-led set: director Oakley, writer Diana Reid, a cast including Fiona Shaw (Killing Eve, Andor) and Caitríona Balfe (Outlander).

Were gossip and tips swapped around the catering table? “It was wonderful to learn from Fiona and Caitríona, but I think less to do with the industry and more just to do with their attitude towards life and storytelling,” says Creed-Miles. “Even if it was like a squeeze of the hand or a moment of eye contact, to feel like you were held in those spaces was really precious.”

The shared experience extended to the costumes. Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles raided each other’s on-set wardrobes, just like real sisters, and covet each other’s actual things. Edgar-Jones– whose off-duty staples are jeans, a “really good” white T-shirt and a “woolly jumper” – loves her friend’s vintage loafers. What would Creed-Miles steal in return? “Daisy is the chicest,” she says. “Probably one of her really cool coats.”

The day we speak, Edgar-Jones is heading to a pub to see Creed-Miles’ band, although Esmé says that Daisy, a fan of Sarah J. Maas fantasy novels and personalised stationery, is the better after-dark girl. Edgar-Jones laughs at that. A DJ, she runs through what makes a great party – “the lighting has to be dark” – while on the decks “I’m still obsessed with Charli XCX. But then, I love a bit of Motown.”

The film’s PR tagline is, “No one knows your heart like a sister.” Creed-Miles says it’s true, adding, “Daisy is family to me. That kind of sisterhood is really important in this world and in this job. I’m very grateful.”

Marriage plots come and go. This is the love match that stuck.

Sense and Sensibility is in cinemas on October 15.

The lonely boy with the sad eyes finally got to come back to Australia

Sydney Morning Herald October 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The tale of the lonely boy left at a Sydney orphanage broke the hearts of a nation. Described as a war child of mixed race with “sad eyes”, Geoffrey Joiner was the result of a wartime romance between an Australian woman and an African-American man who met at a Sydney nightclub.

Joiner was born in Sydney on the day after his father, Trennon, a US Navy sailor, was shipped home in 1944.

Three years later the boy was surrendered to Dalwood Children’s Home at Seaforth on Sydney’s northern beaches by his mother, Jean Aughey.

Joiner had no other home and was stateless. He was not the only one.

“There are potentially thousands of children [like Joiner] born of war who have been neglected by the United States and Australia,” said historian Dr Victoria Grieves Williams, who developed an Australian Research Council project looking into such cases. “We have almost 40 of the children and their families in the project, and every story is different.”

Most were love stories.

“People fell in love and wanted to marry,” Grieves Williams said. “Many were bitterly disappointed by the two racially segregating regimes [Australia and the US] not allowing them to marry and form families for their children.”

Like Joiner, many were never issued a passport or any papers.

The story of five-year-old Geoffrey Joiner’s abandonment, his loneliness and the generosity of the public and a prominent philanthropist and trustee of Taronga Park Zoo, Sir E. J. Hallstrom, who funded Joiner’s reunion with his father Trennon in the US, made gripping news.

Like a real-life soap opera, it prompted daily coverage by newspapers to quench readers’ interest in the boy’s fate.

By March, the five-year-old was reunited with the father he had never met. Joiner never made it back to Australia before he died, aged 79, in Ohio in 2023, and did not ever see his mother or his older sister Betty again.

This year, though, his son, Geoffrey Joiner jnr, of Virginia Beach, US, brought his late father’s ashes back to Australia.

Before his father died Joiner jnr asked: “Would you like for me to take you back to Australia and dump your ashes somewhere? And he was like … ‘That’ll be the best thing that could ever happen. That way I’ll be back to where I started from’.”

Joiner’s remains were spread at Dalwood, no longer a children’s home, and at Aughey’s grave.

His family sprinkled more ashes at Taronga Zoo, where Hallstrom’s archives are held. A long-serving director and trustee of the zoo, Hallstrom made his fortune selling Silent Knight refrigerators. He wrote a blank cheque to cover the costs of sending Joiner to live with his father in the United States.

Hallstrom’s philanthropy also included bringing three boatloads of animals from Africa, South America and Papua New Guinea after the war to Australia, which he had bought and donated to the zoo.

In correspondence, Hallstrom marvelled that Joiner had grown to more than two metres tall.

The boy may have remained at Dalwood for his entire childhood if it wasn’t for a report by The Daily Telegraph on the eve of his fifth birthday in 1949, and headlines describing him as “the loneliest boy in the world”.

“Geoffrey never has a visitor, and nobody contributes to his support … he gets all dressed up and sits waiting for someone to come see him, but no one ever calls,” the report said.

It included a plea from Trennon Joiner, writing from Ohio. “Won’t you please send my son to me? Why should he suffer for what was wrong?”

The next day the boy with no visitors had crowds of them, and a mountain of toys. Soon after, Hallstrom gave him the blank cheque to get him home.

Later in life Geoffrey Joiner wanted to return to Australia, but he had been scared that if he left the US he would not be able to come back.

And when the boy arrived in the United States he was detained until the paperwork for his entry was complete. He was not issued with a passport.

Joiner jnr said his father never recovered from his experience in Australia.

A fear of abandonment had haunted Joiner snr’s life, making him insecure in relationships and unsure of his citizenship.

In an undated letter, he writes to his half-sister Betty in Australia, apologising for not being in touch: “I had no way of corresponding with mother and you.”

He writes that he doesn’t know how they were separated, and adds, “please don’t let it happen again”.

“He didn’t really know if he had proper citizenship in the United States, and he had been living under the radar his entire life,” Joiner jnr said.

“The biggest question we all have is why Jean didn’t come. Sometimes I ask myself if it was the military, or if she had a change of heart. Maybe my Aunt Betty wasn’t allowed to come and she didn’t want to leave her behind. Or perhaps some paperwork was required for her because from that point on it’s where [Hallstrom] steps in.”

Letters between Joiner’s parents, who had met at Booker T. Washington Club in Darlinghurst during the war, show they wanted to stay together.

Aughey was unfairly criticised by people, Grieves Williams said. “Women like Jean who were left holding the baby were commonly not thought well of. Placing your child in an orphanage when you had no family support to allow you to work was a common option for single mothers at this time.”

Some reports said Aughey would often stand at a distance to glimpse her son, and Joiner thought he occasionally saw her. She was reported as saying he would be better off with his father.

If Trennon Joiner had applied for permission to marry Aughey, it was probably never approved. Grieves Williams said military command generally did not action requests by African Americans to marry Australian women. Only two cases she knows were approved, including an under-age and pregnant woman whose family insisted on a marriage to avoid a scandal.

Prospective war brides were encouraged to write to their fiance’s family, and Aughey had been writing to Trennon Joiner’s mother.

Wakefield dominate Warrington in Grand Final to claim fairytale Super League title

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 20:51:55 GMT

Grand Final: Warrington 10-23 Wakefield

Trinity are champions for first time since 1968

Do not let anyone tell you fairytales do not exist. This is not just a maiden Super League title, or indeed a first major trophy for almost 60 years. This is the culmination of one of the most remarkable sporting stories of our time: from the unfashionable, second tier side nobody really spoke about to the champions of England.

Matt Ellis promised things would change. When he took ownership of his beloved Wakefield Trinity in 2023, he inherited a club on its knees. Just relegated to the Championship, with a stadium that resembled a building site and a squad of players nobody wanted a piece of. But he insisted that within five years, Wakefield would win their first major trophy since 1968 with his investment.

In the end, he lied: it only took him three. As Wakefield lifted rugby league’s most prestigious prize aloft inside Old Trafford on Saturday evening, surely not even Ellis could have foreseen how quickly all this could have happened. It is not an exaggeration to suggest Trinity have long been seen as one of Super League’s laughing stocks; now, they are the club everyone has to catch.

Most of their recent history has been dominated by financial problems, and, year after year, simply surviving was seen as an achievement. That is not an indictment on those who came before Ellis, with the previous custodian of Wakefield, Michael Carter, playing just as key a role in this moment. Without him, this night does not become a reality.

Two years ago this week, Wakefield were preparing for the Championship play-offs with promotion to Super League the prize. Just making the playoffs this season would have been regarded as an achievement but, instead, Trinity have defied all odds and, in truth, all sporting logic to win their first trophy for a long, long time.

Perhaps the most staggering thing about this night though was how Wakefield managed the occasion. After dismantling Wigan in the semi-finals last week, the biggest question mark over Trinity was their inexperience in games like these. But they looked like a side who have been walking out in Grand Finals for years.

They comprehensively outplayed Warrington from start to finish, leading 19-0 by half-time and never really looking back. Tries from Cam Scott, Isaiah Vagana and Jazz Tevaga put Trinity in complete control – with Jack Sinfield’s drop goal in the moments before the half-time hooter establishing a four-score lead. In games like these, they are often insurmountable cushions. That proved true here.

What a moment for the Sinfield family too, with Jack winning his first Super League title on the day his father, Sir Kevin, seven times a winner here himself, delivered the match ball after completing his latest ultra-marathon fundraising challenge. That story was just one of several on the night: with seven of this team with Wakefield in the Championship just two years ago.

“It’s pretty sweet for me as an individual but for the club, the players, everything we’ve built up over the last three years is phenomenal,” said Powell, beaten here in 2017 with Castleford. “This club can go as far as it wants and do anything it wants. It shows you that special things can be achieved.”

Sign up to The Recap

after newsletter promotion

For every winner though, there is a loser. Warrington were looking for their first league title since 1955 themselves but they have now lost five straight Old Trafford deciders. It is hard to imagine when a better opportunity will come around. “It’s not the result we were after,” Sam Burgess admitted. “The further you go, the deeper the wound. There’s a lot of disappointed men.”

There was no shortage of effort from his side after half-time, epitomised by the early Arron Lindop try which briefly raised hopes of the greatest of comebacks. But Wakefield extinguished any momentum quickly, reasserting their control on the contest as Johnstone – who won the Rob Burrow Award for man of the match – finishing a fine move for his second try and putting the game beyond doubt.

1968 was the latest time the Wakefield City Hall steps were filled with a Trinity squad celebrating silverware. They will finally return on Sunday as heroes. You would suspect it will not be 58 years between drinks this time around. This club are here to stay.

Tuchel convinced England have buried World Cup woes with Croatia thrashing

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 19:50:01 GMT

‘We’ll always have a scar, but this is how we move forward’

Manager praises ‘complete package’ Scott on full debut

Thomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side deliver a statement performance in Rijeka and hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat.

Tuchel was delighted after his front four combined to devastating effect at Stadion HNK Rijeka, where 6,200 local schoolchildren were allowed in free of charge even though the game was supposed to take place behind closed doors after Croatia were punished by Uefa for racist and discriminatory fan behaviour last year.

England, who have a firm grip on second place in their Nations League group and are confident of reaching next year’s finals, saw Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka each score twice and Jude Bellingham become the first midfielder to register four goal involvements in a game since David Platt against San Marino in 1993.

Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on the scoresheet and Tuchel believes his players have used this extended international break to consign their limp World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina to the past.

“If you feel pain you have to lay with the pain,” the manager said. “The same with disappointment. It was not easy at the beginning of the camp. We had an excellent performance against Spain. The focus in the meetings, the translation of the meetings on the pitch, to bring it within these circumstances in Croatia, to win this dominant performance is the way to move on. We’ll always have a scar, feel pain, but this is the way to move forward. We’ve played in the same manner all three matches.”

Tuchel called it a complete performance. England pressed hard, offered invention in possession and were rapid on the counterattack. Kane, who will equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps when England host Czechia in their and fourth final game of the camp on Tuesday, felt it had the power and physicality of a Premier League performance.

“They just want to play like this, it’s their belief and wish, their conviction,” Tuchel said. “We don’t have to convince them. Harry plays a very intense game at Bayern. We still think we have a certain edge if we play on the front foot. If we push as often as possible in man for man it’s what the team likes. We have to manage these risks.”

There was also an impressive performance from Alex Scott, who made his full debut in midfield. “First start and what a start,” Tuchel said of the 23-year-old. “He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making. He plays with so much confidence. He is so active. The work rate off the ball makes him the complete package. We had a lot of variety in the centre of the pitch.”

Scott was buzzing about facing Luka Modric, who struggled for Croatia. “It’s pretty surreal,” the Bournemouth midfielder said. “Probably one of my favourite players growing up because I had seen him as a boy. One of the best players in the world on his day. To be on the pitch with him and competing is a great honour and thankfully we got the win today.”

Kane, who is up to 89 international goals, was delighted with England’s attitude. Croatia, 13th in the world, were looking to bounce back after losing 4-1 to Spain on Tuesday.

“Every man was at the highest level,” the captain said. “They rested a lot of players on Tuesday. I feel they saw this as their best opportunity to get into those top two spots. During the week it was beautiful weather, an amazing hotel, looking out to the ocean. We could have fallen into that holiday mode.”

OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 19:41:21 GMT

David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology

A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.

David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.

Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.

Writing in The Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”

Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”

OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models.

Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.

Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation.

“I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”

Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified.

Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.

“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.

Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.

“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.

An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.

Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 19:00:08 GMT

The spaces can stand both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justice

At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.

Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.

But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led to Premier League consolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.

Should Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?

These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.

Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.

I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.

Others may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.

Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.

As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.

Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.

That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).

How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?

after newsletter promotion

The argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.

Euphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.

That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.

Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.

And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.

Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.
