‘There’s a lot of silence’: have we created a new ‘Lonely Generation’?

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 19:00:07 GMT

Learning to be one human among many has always been a little lonely and discombobulating. But young people around the world are lonelier than ever. Why?

In September, a Reddit user identifying themselves as a 25-year-old man turned to the r/ForeverAlone subreddit with a question: How do you deal with touch starvation? “It’s becoming obvious to me that I’ll probably be alone forever,” he wrote. He used to be worried about missing out on sex, but now he just misses hugs. Cuddles.

“I don’t have many friends and none with that kind of physical relationship. I don’t really hug family either anymore. Some days, I feel so desperate for a hug with someone I love.”

On another thread, a user identifying as a 20-year-old woman took to the platform to ask if anyone else had experienced university as one of the loneliest times in their lives. “I eat lunch alone, go to class, drive home, study, and repeat,” the user wrote. “Evenings and weekends are the hardest because I crave social connection, but there’s no one to go out with or even talk to.”

Another user, on another subreddit thread, expressed that they had tried to ease their unwanted solitude, but failed. “The loneliness is unbearable,” they wrote. ‘Is anyone else experiencing this” No question mark. No full stop.

The answer is yes.

Around the world, young people, according to the 2025 World Health Organization Social Connection Commission report, “feel the loneliest”. Between 17 and 21% of 13 to 29-year-olds report feeling lonely, a greater proportion than any other age group, the report found. Another study, based on a survey of more than 1 million young people from 38 countries found that youth loneliness had increased in many regions between 2002 and 2022. From Germany to Australia to the UK, studies are showing an uptick in loneliness and social isolation among teenagers and young adults.

That much of the world has produced a generation in which so many regularly feel unable to meet their needs for social connection is a curiosity which has propelled years of work for Dr Michelle Lim.

The act of learning to be one human among many has always been a lonely, discombobulating exercise in parts, she says. But in her new book, The Lonely Generation, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist examines exactly what has happened over this century to make many young people even lonelier.

In short, she writes, “It must be said that the nature of childhood has changed dramatically over the past few decades.”

The list of aggravating factors Lim identifies is long: our hyper competitive education culture, digital technology, the long tail of Covid (“they’re grieving”), the shift towards smaller families, the decline of third spaces, the high cost of living, hybrid working, hybrid learning, the decline of religion, and the rise of automation which means that a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human. Young people, she argues, are being offered fewer and fewer opportunities to form meaningful connections.

“What I fear is social atrophy,” she writes. “People are getting used to being alone.”

Lim is one of the world’s pre-eminent loneliness scholars. Alongside her work as a psychologist and researcher, she leads the University of Sydney’s School of Public Health’s Social Health and Wellbeing Group, is CEO of the Australian Ending Loneliness Together campaign, is on a loneliness advisory panel to the World Health Organization and in 2020 cofounded and led the Global Initiative on Loneliness and Connection, which has since expanded to six continents.

In The Lonely Generation, she seeks to dispel myths around loneliness and expound on its many individual and societal consequences. But it is in diagnosing the cause of the “crisis” levels of youth loneliness that she spends the most time. And the first among the culprits she identifies is education.

“The current education systems are built to prioritise academic excellence from children and adolescents,” she writes. And this focus entails “hidden costs”.

After-school tutoring, high-stakes testing, and well-intentioned enrolments in extensive extracurricular activities are the hallmarks of a 21st-century education. Lim says that parents tell her: “If I stop, then [my child] will fall behind and I’m not doing the best job I can.”

However, children need rest, free play and empty time in order to practise organic social interactions, says Lim. Interactions which are essential to developing their fledgling social skills and a sense of identity outside their family.

“The more time you spend studying, it will come at the expense of [other] important skills,” she says. “We run the risk of raising them to be academically strong, but not socially well-equipped to manage the challenges of adulthood.”

The idea resonates with Usha Makkena, a 22-year-old student at university in Sydney.

“I think when you’re growing up with school, extracurricular activities and then later study and work, a lot of your time can become very structured and goal-oriented,” she says. “Something I realise as I’ve gotten older is that meaningful connection often develops in quite unstructured and almost unproductive times.

“And for me, being very busy certainly didn’t protect me from loneliness.”

Makkena, who is now a national reference group member for Australian youth mental health charity headspace, first started experiencing loneliness in her late teens, around her last year of high school. She did a lot of extracurricular activities and had an active social life, but she had a persistent feeling of disconnection. “What I was missing wasn’t necessarily having more people around me, but that deeper sense of feeling understood and genuinely connected to people.”

Her life did not have the contours of a lonely life. “And I think that can make it harder to recognise,” she says. “When you look at your life and you see all this happening, sometimes it makes you think ‘I shouldn’t be lonely.’”

At the high rise campus of the University of Technology Sydney, in the centre of the city, students wander through chatting in pairs, threes. Some, solo, walk or sit with earbuds in and eyes fixed on their phones. Across the flight of stairs in the foyer of the main building are cast the words “MAKE NEW CONNECTIONS”.

Nenyasha Dongo has struggled to do as the stairs advise.

The Zimbabwean 18-year-old was excited to move to Sydney for her studies. She is a friendly person. She doesn’t want for a huge group of friends, or for parties. Three good friends would do it. But at the end of a day of classes where she didn’t really establish relationships with peers, she would return home to where every one of her five housemates were either out or had retreated to their bedrooms. “There’s a lot of silence,” she says.

“When I do get home, the loneliness,” she shakes her head. She would watch movies and TikTok to fill time until she could call family or friends back home. She carried on like this for six months. “You just have to get used to it.”

Dongo sits with Mihindi Pathinyake at a table in the sun outside a campus cafe. Around them, students and staff mill in and out. Often what the pair describe might have been a situation transplanted from university halls decades ago; the trepidatious step into a lecture hall, scanning to see who might be open to a greeting by a stranger, watching the one big group of old high school friends chat together in the front row, wondering whether the person you just spoke to might like you, might be interested in hanging out one day.

“Just to be clear, young people are just generally awkward,” laughs Lim. “They’re really awkward.”

And the transition from school to university, vocational training or work has always been an inflection point for loneliness, Lim says. Individual young people leave their highly structured environment of high school, with a set cast of characters with whom they are familiar and enter a new world populated by new – and often a vastly greater mass of – people. It is also a time when, often, the desire for a great deal of social interaction and a volume of connection is at its highest. Add to this their prefrontal cortex is still developing and adolescence has yet more years to run its course, the period can be one of flux, confusion, self-questioning and, of course, loneliness.

But this awkward rite of passage is now charged in a new way, says Lim. “Our young people in this generation are living in a world that is very different.”

“You meet new people every day,” says Pathinayake, an exceedingly bright-eyed 20-year-old student from Sri Lanka. But she describes a new social script to developing friendships in 21st century adolescence and young adulthood.

“They take your Instagram and then you never talk to them again.”

Due to the hybrid online-real life attendance structure to many tutorials and lectures which has proliferated since Covid, it can be difficult to be sure that you may run into the same people with the frequency needed to establish organic connection.

“Sometimes following someone or reacting to something that they post can almost be a substitute for reaching out, even though those interactions don’t meet the same need,” says Makkena over a video call in late September. “And then there’s also that element of comparison.

“For me, when I was already feeling lonely, constantly seeing other people’s friendship groups or social lives could sometimes create the impression that everybody else had found their people and I somehow hadn’t.”

She is, however, wary of narratives which pit technology as the silent assassin of social connection. “It also helped me maintain relationships.”

“Social media has not been an entirely negative development”, writes Lim. While the professor is concerned about the dopamine hit from social media blunting the rewards we feel from other interactions and that, for people who are already lonely, it can embed an aversion to real life connection, her own research has shown it can fortify young people living in communities that don’t accept them, or help others to learn about the world. “Digital use is not the enemy.”

However, she openly imagines (not happily) a future in which her own daughter might tell her that her best friend is an AI avatar. It does not feel like a big leap from what she already sees in her clinical practice, where she might be helping a young person navigate problems in their romantic relationship only to realise that they have never met their boyfriend or girlfriend in real life. “It’s really common,” she says.

These virtual relationships, whether remote between human beings on separate continents or between human and AI avatar, are lower in the friction typical of in-person relationships, and entirely absent of touch.

“Humans are hard,” says Lim. “But that’s actually the beauty of relationships as well. We are being challenged, we are being pushed. Our ability to think more diversely, be empathetic are challenged by other humans.”

“Do we run the risk of getting de-socialised with real humans?”

Anxieties about the decline of social fabric and interaction – particularly for young people – have abounded for decades. Telephones and televisions were derided for their antisocial powers long before the term the “antisocial century” was coined by US writer Derek Thompson.

“But there is a sense of feeling unsafe right now, generally, whether it’s political safety around the world, or the lack of community,” says Lim. “It affects the way we see our relationships, the way we relate to people, what we choose to do.”

Lim writes about the “loneliness loop” – a particularly nasty trap for young people – by which experiencing loneliness causes the lonely person to perceive social interaction as more threatening, and so they retreat, reduce their social interaction and in doing so become more lonely.

But there is a bigger, community wide loop too. We have settled, she writes, into a social disconnection crisis.

In The Lonely Generation, Lim imagines a world where social interaction becomes something like exercise has become today: something we once did as part of daily life, but which now we need to make a concerted effort to schedule in our diaries.

“We already see this,” says Lim. Paid-for services coming on to the market as apps or activities in order to facilitate human interaction and combat loneliness. Lim herself receives “so many” requests to endorse different offerings.

“People are capitalising on that,” she says. “This is not to say that they are not a good thing, but I think that it’s really reflective of the erosion of other kinds of social life that we once had.”

Loneliness, particularly youth loneliness, writes Lim, is a signal. A sign that we need to reassess our social world. “There is an ‘us’ problem here.”

“People just go, ‘well, it’s not my responsibility’. But the problem is, actually everyone’s responsible,” she says.

“If everyone says that, then we are going to be living in a world, and raising kids in a world, where healthy social connection is ‘a nice to have’.”

The moment I knew: As a reality TV contestant, I was allowed one 15-minute call a week. Even at 3am, Chris would always pick up

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 19:00:06 GMT

Conor Curran’s first date with Chris lasted nine hours but their relationship remained casual. Then, when Conor was at his most vulnerable, Chris was there for him

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

At 29 I had lost my career in hospitality because of Covid and decided to throw my hat in the ring as a contestant on MasterChef Australia. By the time I was eliminated in 2021, restaurants still weren’t open and I didn’t know what to do with my life. My lease was coming to an end in Melbourne and I wasn’t doing well with the lockdowns and people recognising me from TV. So I decided to retreat to my father’s place in Adelaide for a while.

By early 2022 I was dating a guy but, after a few months, he ghosted me suddenly.

One sunny autumn weekend as I was miserably assembling some flatpack furniture at Dad’s, I realised I had to get out of the house. I got on Grindr and this lovely guy, Chris, fresh from England, started messaging me.

I’d lived in the UK in my early 20s and I knew how hard it was to make friends in a new city. Still processing the shock ghosting, I invited Chris for a drink – just as mates – so neither of us had to be lonely on such a beautiful day. He said he couldn’t imagine anything better.

We met at Brighton beach and had a beer. What followed was one of the most wonderful and unexpected dates of my life. It went for nine hours! We chatted and chatted, not wanting it to end. I wasn’t anticipating any chemistry but it was there, and we spent the night together.

The next day I took him on a tour of Adelaide’s wine regions and then sent him on his way. He was only in town for two days, en route to his new life in Sydney. I didn’t think I’d ever see him again.

But we stayed in touch as he settled into the harbour city. One thing led to another and, by May, little more than a month after we’d met, we both wound up in Melbourne. Chris had been offered a job and I had always planned to return at some point. So without ever having discussed the details, or even admitting to ourselves we’d caught real feelings, we’d moved to the same city and became a sort-of-couple, while still keeping things casual.

In July I was scheduled to be on this reality show, The Challenge, that was filming in Argentina. The show had a Survivor/Big Brother vibe and I didn’t think I was going to do very well. I figured I’d be eliminated within a week but, much to my surprise, I turned out to be quite the Challenge beast and made it all the way to the final.

We were only allowed one 15-minute video call a week and in that month I used 53 of my 60 allotted minutes talking to Chris.

I’m not a person who likes to show vulnerability but the demands of the show broke me in ways I wasn’t expecting. Being filmed 24/7 and doing all these insane challenges put my mental health on a knife’s edge. We weren’t even “official” but Chris would pick up the phone at 3am and just be there for me. No games, no bullshit: he was my support when I needed someone the most.

In the final week of the competition we were given time to write a letter to someone in our life. I wrote to Chris and all my feelings came flooding out. I told him I was falling for him and that if he ever read this letter it meant I was no longer just falling. I was, for sure, in love. I tucked it away and made my way back to Melbourne to recover.

Once home it became clearer that the reality TV filming had taken a real toll on my mental health and the network started paying for my therapy. Chris was with me all the way.

A few months later I gave him the letter. And he told me he loved me too. I didn’t know it at the time but those weekly therapy sessions were a blessing in disguise: they really set me up to be the best partner I could be for Chris.

When I lived in the UK, my dream was to find the love of my life and stay there for ever. Chris had his own ideas about what his time in Australia would look like – and they definitely did not include meeting his future husband in the first week!

We might not have got what we thought we wanted from our big solo adventures but in a roundabout way we have both found exactly what we were looking for. We’re engaged and plan to move back to England together next year.

Conor Curran’s cookbook Eat More Greek is available now through Murdoch (A$45)

Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during his visit to the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans.

The 76-year-old – who has been criticised by supporters for an apparent lack of progress on the pitch – was taking part in the pro-am event on Saturday when the disruption happened on the green of the 15th hole.

Martin O’Neill’s side – who claimed the Premiership title ahead of Hearts after a final-day decider last season as part of a domestic double – currently sit top of the table, two points clear of rivals Rangers.

Louis Rees-Zammit scores two tries as Bristol defeat champions Northampton

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 18:34:44 GMT

Prem Rugby: Bristol 41-26 Northampton

Bears win opening two games for first time since 2023

Louis Rees-Zammit may have been denied a hat-trick against Northampton but there is no doubting who stole the show as Bristol maintained their flying start to the season by downing the champions. The Wales winger scored twice, earned the Bears’ late penalty try and, just to make clear that there is more than one showman in town, produced his own version of Henry Pollock’s pulse celebration.

“I obviously know Pollock has done that before so I thought I’d just give it a little bit back,” said Rees-Zammit. “Me and Pollock are really close. He’s doing great things for the sport. If we’re going to grow this game we need personalities, he’s definitely one and he’s got to do something next week after the forfeit we spoke about yesterday.”

All things told, it was a fine day for Bristol – a nasty-looking head injury to Benhard van Rensburg aside – and a pretty miserable one for Northampton. The Bears helped themselves to six tries with Gabriel Oghre, Tom Jordan and the excellent Harry Randall also on the scoresheet but it is the defensive resilience that will please Pat Lam most. Back in May, Bristol shipped 94 points to the Saints at Northampton but there is far more steel about them on this evidence.

“I’ve watched that game five times,” said Bristol’s director of rugby Lam. “I never watched a game five times in the off-season. Though it hurt, I watched it and built the whole pre-season around that in a sense.”

The downside was Van Rensburg’s injury. He received lengthy treatment and was taken off on a stretcher just before half-time and appeared to be knocked out cold. The South-African born centre is all-action but suffered the same fate during England’s summer victory over Argentina. He was seen by the Bristol dugout in the second half, however, allaying fears that the injury was serious.

For the champions, it was a day to forget. For the first hour, pretty much everything that could go wrong did. Balls were dropped, sitters were missed, tries were disallowed and the lineout went horribly awry. Pollock began brightly but endured a disappointing afternoon too, taking a painful looking low blow in the first half for good measure.

Then came Alex Mitchell from the replacements bench and Northampton briefly threatened the unlikeliest of comebacks but two late yellow cards – the second for Tommy Freeman for a bodycheck on Rees-Zammit which led to a penalty try – put paid to that. “I’m not going to lie, I was devastated,” said Rees-Zammit. “It was just fire in my belly to score a hat-trick. I’m good friends with Tommy and it’s all love after but in the moment I was a bit gutted.”

Fitz Harding was a constant presence at the breakdown for the Bears and his early turnover gave Bristol a lineout deep in Northampton’s 22, from which there was no stopping the lineout drive with Oghre dotting down. However, Northampton hit back almost immediately with George Hendy going over on the left after a burst from Pollock.

Bristol seized the initiative thereafter and Rees-Zammit eventually went over after a smart pass from Oghre. Northampton had endured a pretty torrid first 39 minutes and Ollie Sleightholme’s fumble on the right with the try-line beckoning just about summed up their first-half performance. They probed just before the interval, however, and it was then that Van Rensburg’s head struck a stray knee.

The match restarted with a Northampton scrum. Another strike move, another try for Hendy and suddenly it was a one-point game at half-time. To the Bears’ credit, they raised their game again with Jordan stretching to the line before Randall sniped over from close range. Rees-Zammit splashed over for his second to give Bristol breathing space after a touch of good fortune, with James Williams’ penalty striking a post before Mitchell inspired a mini-revival from Saints.

First he scooted under the posts before teeing up Josh Kemeny in the left corner, but Fin Smith pulled the conversion to keep Bristol’s lead at eight points. And after Northampton’s replacement prop Ion Neculai was shown a yellow card, the Bears finished the game on top.

Max Pepper had a try disallowed before Rees-Zammit was cynically denied a hat-trick by Freeman, who was sent to the sin-bin, with the referee, Ian Tempest, choosing to award a penalty try. “I’d hate to think we would ever panic, regardless of the result,” said Northampton’s director of rugby, Phil Dowson. “The overwhelming feeling is frustration. There’s no panic but we don’t want to make the same mistake twice.”

Kane and Saka double up as England school Croatia in historic Nations League rout

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 18:04:02 GMT

It had all the edge of a pop concert in the stands but England looked ready to steal candy from a baby. The 6,200 Croatian under-14s allowed inside Stadion HNK Rijeka were invited free of charge and this was a priceless footballing experience. England ripped Croatia to shreds to take a firm grip on second place in their Nations League group, boosting their hopes of reaching next year’s quarter-finals, and anyone supporting the home team could at least find consolation in watching Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham combine to devastating effect.

Perhaps the ticket should have come with an adult age rating. This was grisly viewing for the locals but Thomas Tuchel delighted in England’s most complete performance since surging to a 4-2 win over Croatia at the World Cup. Kane marked his 124th cap with his 88th and 89th international strikes and had plenty of help. Three assists and a goal decorated a scintillating display from Bellingham and Tuchel found satisfaction in the other members of his ruthless front four getting on the scoresheet.

Everything clicked. England could have had double figures against opponents ranked 13th in the world but they settled for seven. Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka were in lightning, goalscoring form on the flanks and another story was an exceptional full debut from Alex Scott. The 23-year-old proved that he belongs, impressing with his tenacity and quality on and off the ball, and made it hard to shake off the sense that Tuchel missed a trick by not taking him to the World Cup.

One gorgeous, defence-splitting ball from Scott to release Gordon emphasised that this is a player with a big England future. This was the Bournemouth youngster’s second cap and it said much about Tuchel’s belief in Scott that he deployed him against Luka Modric, even if the great Croatia midfielder has seen better days.

The occasion was nowhere near as surreal as when England played here with no supporters present in 2018. It was meant to be behind closed doors again – Uefa had punished Croatia after discriminatory and racist fan behaviour during last year’s Nations League quarter-finals – but the rules allow tickets to go to local children and the constant high-pitched cheers were a reminder that much of the crowd were not alive when Modric first faced England 20 years ago.

Tuchel knew youth was on his team’s side. Modric is 41 and, given that he was accompanied by another old timer in Mateo Kovacic, it not a surprise that Scott and Elliot Anderson, resuming their partnership when England won the Under-21 European Championship last year, dominated.

Anderson, Scott and Bellingham were superb. Bellingham, back in the side after being rested during Tuesday’s 2-0 win over Czechia, was still going near the end, sending the England substitute Morgan Rogers through to make it 7-0.

The mind went back to when these sides met in their opening game at the World Cup. Anthony Barry gave an impassioned half-time interview and, having struggled in defence during the first half, England emerged triumphant after producing one of their best spells of attacking football under Tuchel.

Replicating those levels has been hard since then, but this was like Dallas. There was a moment when Bellingham went shoulder to shoulder with Modric and just eased his former Real Madrid teammate aside. England were quicker and stronger. The press was aggressive and Croatia were in damage limitation mode by the time Bellingham made it 2-0 in the 21st minute, stabbing past Dominik Livakovic from close range after Gordon plucked Saka’s cross out of the sky before cracking a low ball into the six-yard box.

Slaven Bilic, back in charge of Croatia for a second spell, was powerless to respond. England led after eight minutes, moving in a blur when Marc Guéhi cut out a loose pass from Josko Gvardiol. Bellingham scanned, turned and chose the logical option. He shovelled the ball through a gap; Kane, free of Gvardiol and Luka Vuskovic, set himself and rammed a shot past Livakovic.

The kids booed and gave a collective thumbs down as England’s captain celebrated, but they were watching greatness. Funny, of course, to think there was a time when Kane and Bellingham barely passed to each other. There is no problem with their relationship these days.

Gordon, again linking well with Lewis Hall, was a constant outlet on the left. He kept bursting beyond Josip Stanisic and now has a goal or assist in each of his last seven England games. It was 3-0 when Jarell Quansah, in for Trent Alexander-Arnold on the right, hit back at criticism of his crossing ability by whipping in a ball for Gordon to head past Livakovic.

Quansah was one of five changes by Tuchel, who also restored Jordan Pickford in goal. Pickford remains the No 1 and made a key intervention at 1-0, rushing out to smother as Ivan Perisic threatened.

England dozed off after Gordon’s goal. A rare misstep from Anderson led to an opening for Kovacic, who somehow shot wide after rounding Pickford. England responded on the stroke of half-time. Kane dropped back to help out and start a counterattack which ended with Bellingham toying with Croatia before crossing for Saka to score.

The 100 England fans given tickets enjoyed their evening. There was no let-up after the break. Anderson zipped down the right and crossed for a stretching Kane to score.

It was not long before Croatia, who suffered their biggest ever defeat, removed Modric. The night belonged to England’s stars. Kane, who set up Saka to make it 6-0 in the 68th minute will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record when England host Czechia on Tuesday. The 33-year-old is not slowing down.

Tennessee’s top prison official is stepping down in the aftermath of the failed execution of death row prisoner Christa Pike, the state’s governor Bill Lee announced Saturday.

Frank Strada, the department of correction commissioner, will leave his position later in October as the state launches an independent investigation into what went wrong during Wednesday’s botched execution of Pike, according to Lee.

Strada for his part said his resignation would allow that review to move forward in the best interests of Tennessee.

“Serving as commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction has been a great honor, and I continue to believe the department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” Strada said in his resignation statement.

“Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward,” he said. “I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”

Strada handed in his resignation amid intensifying scrutiny of Tennessee’s closely guarded execution procedures after Pike was injected with lethal drugs on Wednesday but survived. She became the first death row prisoner in the US to undergo such an execution attempt and live.

Pike’s attorney Randy Spivey, who witnessed the procedure from inside the death chamber, described what happened as “cruel and torturous”. He said he personally counted seven needles inserted into Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.

Attorneys have alleged that Pike’s failed lethal injection was the fifth “botched” execution carried out under Strada’s leadership in two states since 2022, as the Guardian reported on Saturday, hours before his resignation was announced.

Pike remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital as of Friday, according to a court filing submitted by her attorneys. Her lawyers said hospital personnel were trying to save her life and, as of late Thursday, were working to clear the two doses of the execution drug from her system.

Wednesday’s extraordinary breakdown inside Tennessee’s execution chamber has triggered demands for an explanation from people on both sides of the death penalty debate. Besides ordering the independent review into case, Lee has paused the scheduling of executions in Tennessee.

Pike’s attorneys said they believe complications involving intravenous lines caused pentobarbital to enter her body rather than her bloodstream.

“Frank Strada’s resignation does not change the fact that Tennessee is shrouding its executions in secrecy,” Kit Thomas, a death row attorney in the federal public defender’s office in Nashville, said in a statement. “When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known. Strada then oversaw the implementation of a new protocol that ignored the recommendations of the independent investigation and weakened protections leading to a string of problems in Tennessee, including this week’s horrific botched execution attempt and another one in May. Until there is transparency and accountability, botched executions will keep happening.”

Laura Porter, the executive director of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said in a statement: “Hopefully this is the beginning of accountability and an end to secrecy that enables these debacles.”

“Attorneys and community leaders across Tennessee have been trying for some time to get the Governor and the administration to take seriously the huge problems with the competency of the state’s execution process,” Porter’s statement continued. “They were ignored.”

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of teenage classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville.

A pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.

After the murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

Had her execution that day succeeded, Pike on Wednesday would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 15:00:02 GMT

In the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-ticking

Andy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s.

Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government.

A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election.

There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost.

The economist Sir John Kay, a fellow of St John’s College, Oxford and former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, is a keen advocate of organisations that remember for whose benefit they exist. That means their primary aim should be to achieve customer satisfaction. In the private sector, profits will follow. In the public sector, there will be savings.

In his book Obliquity, Kay shows how those companies that pursued shareholder value as their primary aim failed. And those that wanted to produce the best product secured long-term success.

Just as a devotion to shareholder value – a financial metric of the benefit to investors -proved a blind alley for thousands of now-deceased companies, so the reliance on protocols in the public sector as a substitute for understanding the task in hand leads to failed outcomes and wasted money.

You can see it now in the NHS, where satisfaction levels are rising in relation to GP and hospital visits. The new system for booking appointments has its drawbacks, but people are finding doctors are available more quickly, especially for GP and outpatient appointments.

You can see the failures in the NHS from the cover-ups by maternity unit managers of rising mortality rates.

Neither the success nor the failure can be attributed to the regulation of the health service. Regulation is an extra layer of cost that has, time after time, been shown to undermine productive behaviour, either because private providers and managers find they can game the system or it stifles innovation.

Another example can be found in two unconnected government agencies. Last week, the Environment Agency said it would fund the planting of half a million trees, giving funds to councils and mayors and other government bodies to carry out the work. Surely this is a good thing?

On the other hand, you might think it a complete waste of time and money when National Highways, the main road builder in England, planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge, only to report three years later, in an internal review, that three-quarters of them had died.

These failures are about the way public sector departments and agencies go about their work. Regulation only adds to a tick-box culture that asks: “Did you follow the protocol? If so, everything’s fine.”

Eminent figures in Whitehall, from the former mandarin and Bank of England deputy governor Sir Jon Cunliffe to the House of Lords industry and regulators committee believe the answer is more intensive oversight.

after newsletter promotion

Kay has many examples of companies that grew because the boardroom was dominated by people who were more obsessed about delivering the best service or product than rewarding their shareholders as the chief metric. Profits and improvements in things such as market share were not the dominant metrics in companies that expanded.

The aircraft maker Boeing succeeded before it lost its way chasing quarterly profit targets. ICI, once the UK’s largest industrial company, was broken up and faded away after a higher stock market value became the main target.

The management consultant John Seddon, whose Vanguard consulting firm has adapted the Toyota systems method, supports Kay’s studiously well-informed analysis of what it takes to make a successful organisation. Seddon puts flesh on the bones with the kind of practical systems approach that has helped Portsmouth city council’s housing department win international awards for its repairs service.

He has seen many new initiatives in public sector management from grand strategies to more prosaic schemes for benchmarking services against the private sector. All have failed to improve services.

Seddon is not in favour of ditching regulation altogether. Regulation based on how well an organisation achieves the purpose will, he says, avoid the persistent problem of regulation “running behind events, shutting the stable door after another horse has bolted”.

He adds: “Having a clear statement of purpose will enable regulators to apply sanctions immediately if and when an organisation is found to be undermining its allotted purpose.

“It is time to liberate public servants from the prison of suspicion and distrust that our current method of regulation locks them in, demeaning their professionalism and casting them as part of the problem rather than as active creators of solutions.”

Burnham’s staff should avoid letting the debate about ownership dominate – ignoring a maxim that says “private bad, public good.”. They should work more closely on how public sector organisations achieve better outcomes. The evidence is available. They don’t need to look very far.

The Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn announced last year if they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor.

The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power.

Last October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further.

“The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department. I know there are areas that we can make savings, and that’s true of every every part of government.”

He added: “There is a moral mission to get our economy growing, give people opportunity, as well as let people keep more of what they earn. It’s pretty simple. We’re Conservative, this is what we stand for.”

A Tory spokesperson acknowledged the party was seeking to make cuts beyond what it had already announced.

“Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, the Conservatives have consistently advocated for a smaller state and a government that does fewer things but better,” the spokesperson said.

“In Birmingham, we will go further, setting out further savings to Labour’s bloated welfare bill and cracking down on wasteful spending as part of our plans to build a stronger economy and a stronger country.”

Kemi Badenoch has previously outlined how the government would cut government spending by £47bn, mainly by cutting welfare spending for all non-British or EU citizens.

The plans would also save £8bn by cutting 132,000 civil service jobs, another £1.6bn by scrapping almost all of Labour’s clean energy scheme and more than £7bn by cutting international aid.

In August she promoted Griffith, who previously worked as chief operating officer for Sky, from his role as shadow business secretary.

In government, Griffith worked in the Treasury under Kwasi Kwarteng and was one of the ministers tasked with defending the mini-budget even as the markets tanked in response.

On Friday Badenoch promised another £4bn of spending reductions, including taking another £2.5bn out of the aid budget – leaving it with just £1bn as year – as well as reducing the budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport by £1bn.

The Tory leader said she would use half of those savings to pay for an additional 50,000 prison places. She has previously promised to use half of any cuts she makes to reduce the deficit.

Griffiths’ leaked comments come as the Tories prepare to gather in Birmingham for their annual conference, with Badenoch seeking to make a virtue of the growing distance between Labour’s plans for government and her own.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised a series of potentially expensive interventions, including a new national care service and public control over utility companies, as he seeks to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”.

However, Badenoch, who has called Margaret Thatcher her hero, is attempting to gain an electoral advantage with her vision of lower taxes and a significantly smaller state.

“[Thatcher] is somebody who brought a lot of wealth and prosperity to this country,” the Tory leader told ITV Meridian on Friday.

“Privatisation was a success … I don’t think that Andy Burnham running the water companies is the answer to those problems.”

The Tories remain in third place in the polls, behind Labour and Reform UK, although Badenoch’s personal ratings have rallied over the last 12 months.

Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marbles

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 14:46:50 GMT

Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’

In a ceremony replete with the sort of fanfare usually reserved for great events, Greece and Bulgaria have formally exchanged “a treasury” of relics and bones, sealing a cultural deal negotiated over decades.

The handover involved priceless religious objects removed from Greece at the height of the first world war, as well as remains thought to belong to Tsar Samuel, Bulgaria’s revered medieval warrior ruler.

Greece hailed the exchange as emblematic of the headway countries could make in similar repatriation disputes, with the prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, saying he hoped the accord would bolster Athens’ campaign to retrieve the Parthenon sculptures and send a clear message to Britain.

“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he told a crowd gathered for the ceremony in Thessaloniki on Saturday. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.”

The Greek-Bulgarian deal, reached after 50 years of intense cultural diplomacy between the two neighbours, was also an example of the “political will” needed to settle the west’s longest running cultural row, Mitsotakis said, referring to the fifth century BC Parthenon marbles. “It took time, and above all, political will and determination to overcome the obstacles of the past,” he added.

Under the agreement, 48 relics, including icons, crosses and ornate ecclesiastical vessels, pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the first world war, will be returned to Athens. In the more than 100 intervening years, they had been safeguarded at the National History Museum in Bulgaria.

Meanwhile, the remains of Tsar Samuel, regarded as a national hero for his role in battling to preserve his country’s independence from the Byzantine empire, were discovered by archaeologists more than 60 years ago in a border area of Greece.

Authorities arranged a homecoming with full state honours, with the tsar’s bones flown to Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, on a military aircraft accompanied by an escort of jet fighters and a 21-gun salute upon arrival. Free transport had been organised for pilgrims to pay their respects.

In his own address at the handover, Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, a former air force officer, said: “These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve, and must have, the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestor. If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger.”

Mitsotakis emphasised that Greece’s campaign to win back the Parthenon marbles was neither “dictated by a vague national claim, nor does it call into question the mission of museums worldwide”.

Athens remained committed to repatriating the sculptures, he said, because it would allow viewers to fully enjoy what has long been seen as the high point of classical art if the masterpieces were reunited.

“It is precisely this same principle – the principle of the integrity of a monument – that underpins our continuous efforts to reunite the Parthenon sculptures. The Parthenon constitutes a unique and singular case,” he said of the building that is the predominant temple on the Acropolis of Athens.

“[The campaign] is about the restoration of a universal monument that remains violently dismembered. My country will not accept arrangements that imply recognition of foreign sovereignty or the supposed borrowing of its own treasures. On the contrary, it now believes that the time has come for truth, for reason, for justice and morality.”

The fifth century BC carvings were sawn from the Parthenon on the order of Lord Elgin, Britain’s then ambassador to the Sublime Porte, in what have since become highly contentious circumstances.

They were acquired by the British Museum in 1816 after the bankrupt peer was forced to sell them and have been on display there ever since.

When is the right time to compare US politics to the Nazi era? This expert on Christian nationalism says: now

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 13:00:02 GMT

Robert P Jones argues that declining white Christian influence has fuelled an alliance with Trump, and warns it is reshaping US democracy

The lawyer Mike Godwin famously came up with the “law” that, as an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler approaches one (or 100%).

Robert P Jones thought long and hard about whether to go there in his latest book. But the more he studied US demographic numbers, considered the rise of Christian nationalism and heard Donald Trump use the language of racial purity, he found the conclusion inescapable. “This is our 1933,” he writes.

So it is that Backslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracy begins with the rise of the Nazi party and the complicity of the German people, including German Christians and churches.

Jones cites Martin Niemöller, a Lutheran pastor imprisoned for opposing Hitler, remembered for the poem First They Came. But for the first four years of Hitler’s reign, he notes, Niemöller did not fully oppose the Nazis. He later regretted that he and the Protestant German church did not speak out sooner.

Backslide returns to the analogy in its epilogue. He writes: “Just as God asked Niemoller where he was between 1933 and 1937, God will ask us where we were between 2025 and 2028. Just as Germans who backed Hitler and the Nazi Party after 1933 were fully aware of what they were joining, so Christians who have backed Trump and the MAGA movement a second time know and bear responsibility for what they are now endorsing.”

Sitting in his downtown Washington office, the president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) contends that US democracy is experiencing a severe “backslide” that is directly aided and abetted by an “apostate” white Christianity, including Trump’s language on the campaign trail.

“This dehumanising language, talking about immigrants as vermin, and this racial purity language, like they’re ‘poisoning the blood of our country’. What does that mean? If they’re poisoning the blood, what’s the pure blood? We know where that story goes,” he said.

Trump has repeatedly used the concept of genetic inheritance. In 2020, addressing a mostly white crowd in Minnesota, he declared: “You have good genes, you know that, right? You have good genes. A lot of it is about the genes, isn’t it, don’t you believe? The racehorse theory, you think we’re so different? You have good genes in Minnesota.”

Normalisation is a perennial danger.

“If don’t want to live in a place where we have a thuggish police force that’s kidnapping people off the street in masks and killing US citizens in the streets, now’s the time to speak up,” Jones said.

Backslide cites historian and philosopher Hannah Arendt’s 1950 The Aftermath of Nazi Rule report for Commentary magazine based on interviews with postwar Berliners: “A great number of Germans, especially among the more educated, apparently are no longer capable of telling the truth even if they want to.”

Jones grew up a Southern Baptist in Jackson, Mississippi, went to church five times a week and earned a master of divinity degree. His previous books include The End of White Christian America in 2016, White Too Long in 2020 and The Hidden Roots of White Supremacy and the Path to a Shared American Future in 2023. He called this one Backslide very deliberately.

In international political science, “democratic backsliding” has become the established academic term for the systematic erosion of democratic norms, judicial independence and voting rights. Yet Jones recognises that the term carries an even older resonance.

“In the evangelical world I grew up in, backslide was a word we heard all the time – a theological word about the fear of falling away from the faith,” he says, tracing the word’s history back through the Oxford English Dictionary to the 16th-century Protestant reformer John Knox.

In Jones’s diagnosis, white American Christianity has committed a profound act of apostasy by trading its spiritual core for political dominance. By endorsing anti-democratic tactics, white Christian institutions have become the primary engine behind the country’s autocratic slide.

To understand how a major religious tradition arrived at this moral impasse, Jones turns to the arithmetic of demographics. When Barack Obama was elected president in 2008, white Christian Americans still constituted 54% of the US population. By 2014, that figure had dropped to 47%. Today, white Christians account for 41% of the country.

The decline among white evangelicals, long considered a bedrock of conservative politics, is even steeper. At the turn of the 21st century, white evangelicals represented a quarter of all Americans; today, they make up barely 13%. The Southern Baptist Convention, the country’s biggest evangelical denomination, has lost more than 3 million members since its 2006 peak.

Faced with shrinking numbers and cultural marginalisation, white evangelicalism embraced not spiritual renewal, but existential panic – creating fertile ground for Trump’s demagoguery.

“Trump loves to talk about the art of the deal and, in many ways, there’s been a massive quid pro quo deal struck between a declining white evangelical population and Trump,” Jones observes. “His big appeal to them was less about policy and more anti-immigrant: I’m going to restore an America that looks like you, and I’m going to restore power to the Christian churches.

“He was literally saying on the campaign trail: this is a quid pro quo deal. Give me your votes and you won’t even have to vote again. I’ll fix it so you don’t have to vote again.’”

This transactional alliance marks a complete departure from the religious right of the late 20th century, which wrapped its political ambitions in the language of morality.

“You don’t hear those words any more,” says Jones, contrasting today’s movement with Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority or the “Values Voters” summits of the George W Bush era. “What we have now is an overtly anti-democratic Christian nationalism flying under the banner of: ‘We believe this country belongs to us, and we’re going to use the power we can to claim it.’”

This Faustian bargain relies purely on power rather than shared theology – a dynamic starkly highlighted by the contrast between Trump and his running mate, JD Vance. While Vance recently discussed the End Times with 22-year-old evangelical podcaster Bryce Crawford, awkwardly reflecting on his evangelical upbringing and subsequent conversion to Catholicism, Trump operates largely without theological pretence.

Jones continues: “He makes straight appeals to self-interest: if you’re for me, I’ll be for you. Evangelicals are willing to forgive a whole host of sins for the idea that he is going to bring them back into power as their numbers are dwindling.”

The real world manifestation of this transaction plays out every Sunday across thousands of congregations. While high-profile megachurches such as First Baptist church in Dallas make their political allegiance explicit, Jones contends that overt political sermonising is rarely needed.

“Once you have churches that are largely segregated by race and increasingly segregated by partisanship, all you really have to do is keep out any critique. It’s reinforced by Fox News, Christian radio and going home to people of like mind. You don’t have to overtly teach Christian nationalism; you just keep it from being critiqued.”

PRRI’s extensive empirical data undermines the widespread belief that religious attendance automatically fosters civic tolerance or democratic values.

Jones says: “Particularly among white evangelicals, on several measures around Christian nationalism, anti-immigrant views, anti-Black views, and anti-Muslim views, going to church actually makes your views more extreme. It’s not the case that more church is the answer to democracy.”

The dangerous potential of this theological radicalisation materialised dramatically during the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol. Christian symbols were displayed prominently throughout the insurrection, including wooden crosses set up on Capitol grounds and rioters holding “Jesus Saves” banners alongside Confederate flags.

Yet official investigations largely overlooked this central element, influenced in part by political figures like Congresswoman Liz Cheney on the House select committee. “I was stunned to see very little of it in the House select committee report,” Jones recalls. “It was a huge loss and a huge skewing of public perception that we didn’t take those Christian symbols at the riot seriously.”

Today, this blend of Christian nationalism and military authority reaches into the upper echelons of the national security apparatus. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, sports tattoos featuring Crusader iconography – including the medieval battle cry Deus Vult (“God wills it”) next to a Jerusalem cross – while renaming the Department of Defense as the “Department of War”. Hegseth has welcomed vocal Christian nationalists such as Pastor Doug Wilson to lead a worship service at the Pentagon.

Jones comments: “I can’t imagine much more dangerous than somebody who thinks, ‘I am the instrument of God, I alone understand how the forces of good and evil are aligned,’ while holding the power to deploy the most powerful military force the world has ever seen. While George W Bush took care after 9/11 to explicitly state that the US was not at war with Islam, today we are making radicalisation propaganda films for extremists by presenting ourselves as a Christian nation at war with Islam.”

Behind the public spectacle of rallies and political theatre, ideologues such as Russell Vought, a key architect of Project 2025 and advocate of the “unitary executive” theory, are laying the groundwork for a government rooted in Christian nationalist principles. “They are building an apparatus designed to institutionalise this worldview across the federal government,” Jones warns. “It is an intentional, long-term project to reshape American democracy in their own image.”

Despite the alarming trajectory detailed in Backslide, Jones resists total pessimism. The central message of his book is that “backsliding is not irreversible” and that national recovery remains possible through honest confrontation with history and sincere repentance.

Across the country, alternative Christian voices are beginning to organise against Christian nationalism. Figures such as James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian running for the US Senate in Texas, and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas are offering a pro-democracy theological vision.

“For a long time, mainline Protestants were taught propriety and politeness, leading to a reticence to speak out,” Jones notes. “If we don’t want the public and future face of Christianity to be only Christian nationalism, we have to present a public version of Christianity that is compatible with democracy – one that leans into care for the orphan, the widow and the immigrant.”

Ultimately, Jones argues, neither sacred texts nor historical precedents will dictate the future of US democracy. He hopes his book will make white Christians realise they face a decision similar to the one that confronted the establishment Christian church in Nazi Germany in 1933.

“It’s a wake-up call to see the bright lines that are being crossed, to be clear-eyed about how dangerous that is, and for those readers who are Christian – particularly white and Christian – to realise we have a particular responsibility to offer a different version of faith. Because it is our faith that’s been hijacked and used to legitimise this illiberal, anti-democratic, authoritarian movement that’s running rampant and taking over in the US.”

Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 13:00:01 GMT

Approval ratings for Tory leader and her party have crept up as she has asserted her style and authority but big challenges lie ahead

A year ago, Tory MPs were braced for the prospect of yet another leadership battle to topple Kemi Badenoch as the party sunk to historic lows of 14-16% in the polls.

At the time, the word “November” was uttered in hushed tones – this being the decisive month when rebels would be able to mount a challenge, Badenoch having served 12 months in office.

But times appear to have changed and – against the odds – the Tories have undergone what has been termed a “Keminisation”, with the leader asserting her style and authority on the party, despite its wider poor performance in the polls.

“Right now, Kemi is the only thing that’s holding them up,” says Luke Tryl, the director of the More in Common thinktank, which conducts focus groups and polling. “If they ditched her, I think they’d be certain for electoral oblivion.”

Badenoch is running a party still discounted as toxic and incompetent by much of the electorate, but polling numbers and focus groups suggest some of them have recently begun to give her more of a hearing.

The party has crept up from the teens to the low 20s – occasionally edging ahead of Reform UK for the first time in almost two years.

“It’s not great for them, but it’s a lot better,” says Tryl. “The problem is the party brand. She is now in our approval ratings net neutral and has been net 1 or net 2. She was in the minus 30s and now only her and Burnham have positive approval.

“Progressives don’t like her, but when you come to those who might conceivably be Tory voters there’s a lot of ‘like her, don’t like the party, she tells it like it is, wish she was in another party’. I do think the Kemi bounce is real. People talk about her having improved and they have seen her PMQs clips.”

Data from the other pollsters backs up the idea that the public is more open to Badenoch than before. James Crouch, the head of policy and public affairs at Opinium, said Badenoch’s approval rating had been rising since May 2025, when she was at -27, to -3 in its latest poll. He said that among 2024 Conservative voters she had the approval of 64%, compared with just 8% who did not approve, while of those who voted Conservative in 2019, 56% approved of her, while 16% did not.

Further research from YouGov this week found four in 10 people used at least one negative term to describe the Tory leader, one of the most common themes being a perceived unpleasantness. But three in 10 included one or more positive terms in their description, strong and intelligent being the main compliments.

Some Tory MPs attribute Badenoch’s improvement over the last year to a willingness to learn and take advice on her performance. This is in spite of her having the preternatural public self-confidence to claim to the FT this weekend that she couldn’t think of any mistakes she had made, saying everyone makes them but “nothing comes to mind”.

But insiders say she has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points, with the party’s conference slogan set as “Stronger economy, stronger country”.

She has also improved her prime minister’s questions appearances, partly with help on preparation from Conservative grandees such as David Cameron.

Tory MPs believe a turning point for Badenoch was the defection of Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman to Reform – because their departure removed a source of destabilisation on the right, and it gave her an opportunity to show decisiveness in pushing Jenrick before he jumped. She has also been aided by the increasing questions over Nigel Farage and Reform UK’s finances, with the party’s dominance in the polls slipping.

However, the arrival of Andy Burnham on the scene for Labour has changed things.

Giles Kenningham, the former Conservative director of communications who now leads the Trafalgar Strategy advisory firm, says Burnham “raises the bar … he’s a great communicator and comfortable in his own skin”.

“It’s a harder ask now. Starmer was not a great orator or someone who electrified voters … Burnham has had a great conference but all eyes are now on the budget, so her conference needs to be on the economy and welfare. John Healey’s speech didn’t say anything, and there is an opportunity for Badenoch to put pressure on them and drive the agenda.”

Badenoch’s star has also risen further with the membership of the party, the most recent ConservativeHome poll showing she has a 87% net satisfaction rating with the party faithful.

Despite this, a number of Conservative aides and insiders believe that Badenoch’s future is still not totally secure if the party does not start to creep above Reform UK on a sustained basis. One pointed to the Tory selection races – excluding some high-profile former MPs from standing – as a sign of perceived weakness that those around Badenoch are worried about her being challenged. “She is not alone among politicians in not liking tall poppies,” said one Conservative strategist.

“Ultimately, she is not immune from a challenge,” said another. “The shelf life of politicians is getting shorter and shorter. Leaders are much more exposed and the job is precarious. The thing most in her favour is that there are currently no other obvious contenders.”

‘Sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment’: the Cornell gang-rape case and the failure of #MeToo

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 13:00:01 GMT

As the university and local police defend their treatment of the alleged perpetrators, women decry a familiar story

Student safety advocates in the US call the start of the fall semester at universities “the red zone”. Fraternities, sororities and off-campus bars throw parties welcoming students back to school. It’s supposed to be fun, but it can also be dangerous: more than 50% of sexual assaults that occur at colleges happen during that six- to 10-week period.

It was mid-October of 2024, during the red zone and just before a deluge of Halloween celebrations, when, a former Cornell University student says, she was gang-raped by a group of fraternity brothers. Recent attention on these allegations sparked widespread outrage this week, reviving a contentious national debate about how authorities respond to allegations of sexual assault on US college campuses.

The anonymous young woman at the center of the story – known as Jane Doe in court documents – filed a civil lawsuit last month, accusing seven men of plying her with drugs and alcohol and assaulting her over the course of seven hours at their fraternity house. The woman originally went to the house to visit a friend; she claims she arrived intoxicated and willingly took the party drug ketamine with the men. Later, she says, she became incapacitated by the drug, which is a dissociative anesthetic, while the men “commanded” her to keep snorting it.

Jane Doe also alleges that the Ivy League university’s ensuing internal investigation was too lenient toward the men. None have ever been charged with a crime. Two were expelled for their misconduct, while five were given lighter punishments: writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a suspension. Some still attend the school. All seven men denied wrongdoing during Cornell’s investigation.

Public outcry over the case reached a breaking point on Thursday, when the New York governor Kathy Hochul stepped in to appoint a new special prosecutor to investigate the incident, which the original district attorney declined to prosecute. Now, state attorney general Leticia James will decide whether or not to take the case to a grand jury, which would decide whether there was enough evidence to charge the men with a crime.

In a statement, Cornell University defended its investigation of the incident. It closed the fraternity chapter involved and barred the group from campus. “We will continue to examine and strengthen our policies to ensure we are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated, those who come forward are supported, and individuals found responsible through our processes are held accountable,” the statement read. (Cornell directed the Guardian to this statement when reached for comment.) After intense public pressure, the university agreed to hire external, independent lawyers to investigate whether its handling of the allegations was appropriate.

Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, has said that he did not pursue the case two years ago because the woman’s first account to police did not say that she was drugged, incapacitated or forced into sex. He later said he did not read her full interview, only a shorter statement written by campus police and signed by Jane Doe. Her full statement included the sentence: “I can say with 100 percent confidence that I was raped,” but this did not make it into the final statement sent to Van Houten.

In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the woman exchanged friendly messages with some of the men, expressing concern about rumors that were spreading on campus about the event. She also maintains that the alleged assault began as a consensual encounter. It is common for sexual assault survivors to downplay their experiences as a coping mechanism. False rape accusations are incredibly rare.

One of the most damning pieces of evidence in the lawsuit involves screenshots of Snapchat messages sent in a fraternity group chat; at one point, an alleged participant named Jonathan Newell referred to Jane Doe as “free pussy”, advertising the alleged assault as it unfolded.

What upsets many women most about this case is how normalized such actions seem. About one in four undergraduate women experience sexual violence during college; 60% of rapes involving university students involve perpetrators who are known to the victims. Last year, a survey of female undergrads at Cornell found that 35% of respondents experienced “nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation”. That figure was up from 23% in 2023.

“There are so many people in America who find this so familiar,” said Lisa Wade, an associate professor at Tulane and author of American Hookup: The New Culture of Sex on Campus. “Not just the incident itself, but also the response by Cornell.”

As the case plays out in the courts, the so-called “Cornell 7” have become the literal faces of the enduring prevalence of sexual assault on campus, and the institutional failure that allows that behavior to flourish. Their names and images are plastered on social media posts calling for accountability. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper that has doggedly covered the lawsuit, led the way with an op-ed column titled “Cornell Won’t, We Will”. The piece began by listing the alleged assailants’ names. “We know who you are and we refuse to let you benefit from this University’s concealment,” wrote the editorial board.

A former South Park writer named Toby Morton launched a website detailing the specifics of what Jane Doe alleges each man did to her. Morton wrote on Instagram that he plans to sponsor billboards about the case. The actor Florence Pugh weighed in, pleading on social media for men to be “as horrified and as sickened as us [women]”. She added that “college/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world [building] men [who] get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and won’t be harmed in return”.

When content creator and commentator Michael Tracey threatened to release the name and personal details of Jane Doe – going against decades of established journalistic norms for reporting on alleged rape victims – women flooded TikTok in her defense. The Spartacus-style rallying cry of “I’m Jane Doe” hit feeds, with users sharing stories of their own experiences with sexual assault. “All of us women are jane doe, and we will all continue to ban [sic] together for her,” reads the caption of one clip liked more than 267,000 times.

College admissions advisers told the New York Post that some of their high school clients pulled their early decision applications to Cornell because they would not feel safe in the community.

This outpouring recalls the early days of #MeToo, a global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse ignited in the wake of initial allegations against convicted rapist and former film producer Harvey Weinstein. But Wade, the Tulane professor, said she sees this case as “metabolizing the failure of #MeToo”, which promised a so-called reckoning in 2017. Ten years later, manosphere influencers teach their followers to see women as sex objects, and Americans re-elected a man who infamously bragged about grabbing women “by the pussy”.

Sexual assault survivors have long faced victim-shaming. Jane Doe’s narrative is complicated, and the New York Times reported that the alleged victim did not realize she had been raped until she read someone else describe the event as such on a social media forum; she had texted one of the accused that: “At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt.” This is not an unusual trauma response: it is common for victims to continue relationships with their abusers, as it provides some semblance of control over the situation.

But the messy timeline emboldens bad actors and conservative commentators who seek to advance an anti-woman agenda. These young men have not been convicted of a crime, and it would be difficult for prosecutors to convict them of rape due to a New York state legal loophole that does not consider a victim to be incapacitated if she willingly contributes to her own intoxication. (Jane Doe stated she arrived at the fraternity house drunk and willingly took substances with the men, though she also says they coerced her into snorting ketamine.)

The Free Press, a vocally “anti-woke” publication run by Bari Weiss, chastised the “court of public opinion” for “already puni[shing]” the Cornell 7. Dasha Nekrasova, one of the edgelord hosts of the Red Scare podcast, spent much of this week trying to shame Jane Doe and calling women who are upset over the lack of accountability in this case “deranged”.

“There’s a sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment that is also driving the response to this,” Wade said. “#MeToo happened, and nobody cared. Here it is again.”

Elizabeth Armstrong, a professor at the University of Michigan who studies gender inequities in universities, says that there have been “big waves of outrage” over sexual assault on campuses since the 1980s, when Mary Koss first coined the term “date rape”. The last national dialogue took place around 2015, when a Columbia University student carried a mattress around campus for a performance art piece based on her sexual assault.

More than a decade later, the issue has only gotten worse. The Trump administration has gutted Title IX protections, which prohibit sex-based discrimination in universities that receive federal funding, and limited the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under it. Just this week, Trump announced that universities no longer have to investigate assaults on students that take place off-campus. (The Cornell case occurred at a frat house.) “We have an administration that is actively rolling back protections for student survivors,” said Amanda Walsh, deputy director for external affairs at the Victim Rights Law Center.

But Walsh, who works closely with survivors, says that gen Z women have much less internalized shame over their assaults than previous generations, who were often taught that women invite sexual assault through their actions. “It feels like the focus has shifted away from talking about what the woman did, and more appropriately to exploring the behavior of the men involved,” she said. “I always admire how much they focus on the behavior of the person who harmed them, rather than asking: ‘What could I have done differently? Why did this happen to me? I see college students really pushing back against that.”

The Cornell case has revived discussions on abolishing Greek life, the student social club system that is behind fraternities and sororities in the US. This week, a Vogue article called for universities to “ban frats once and for all”. It’s not unprecedented: the Pennsylvania liberal arts college Swarthmore did so in 2019, after campus publications leaked racist, sexist and homophobic documents written by fraternities. “That would be a really real change, but I doubt that will happen,” said Armstrong.

Elizabeth Allan, who leads the Hazing Prevention Research Lab at the University of Maine, added: “It’s important for everyone [in Greek life] to think how these groups might reflect larger societal norms and expectations and the ways in which [bad] behavior is reinforced.”

Most of all, Walsh worries how all the attention on this case will affect Jane Doe, and the countless other anonymous victims who are sure to come after her. “I’ve been in this field long enough to know that however much support she receives is exactly how much negativity she’ll get on the other side,” Walsh said. “At this point, with the political moment and online response, it almost feels like supporting a survivor of sexual violence feels political or partisan, which is wild.”
