‘It’s been hard’: families await the return of the USS Abraham Lincoln

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:00:55 GMT

After reports of suicide attempts and food shortages, the aircraft carrier is expected to dock in San Diego this week following a record-breaking 250-plus days at sea

A mother in San Diego is counting down the days until her son comes home.

“I had a big sign made, welcoming him back,” she said. “I can’t wait to see him.”

Her son is one of roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been deployed for nearly a year, and since late February was supporting US military operations against Iran.

What began as a deployment bound for the Pacific, anticipated to return in the spring, became something entirely different after the United States launched its war with Iran. The Lincoln was diverted to the Middle East, and the deployment became what one military official described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era”.

The months that followed were marked by combat operations, deployment extensions, a record-breaking stretch at sea, and reports of shortages of food and basic supplies and deteriorating mental health among some crew members, including reports that several crew members had attempted to jump overboard.

Senior Trump administration officials pushed back against accounts of poor conditions, but some families and veterans warned that the length and intensity of the deployment were taking a toll on both those serving onboard and their loved ones.

As reports of conditions leaked out, the Lincoln soon became a flashpoint in the increasingly contentious debate over the war and, for some, a symbol of the strains and pressures the conflict has placed on the US military and the people serving in it.

Now, after months at sea, the Lincoln is in the final stretch of its journey back to San Diego, where it is expected in the coming days.

But as the carrier heads home, the toll of the deployment has come into sharper focus. In late September, the navy disclosed that during the deployment, eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group had attempted to take their own lives.

When the Lincoln left San Diego last November, its deployment was expected to be relatively routine. The carrier was scheduled to spend several months in the Pacific region before returning home to California in the spring.

Instead, as the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, the carrier was redirected to the Middle East.

The Lincoln and its strike group, carrying approximately 6,000 to 7,000 sailors across roughly a half-dozen ships, were soon pulled into combat operations, which would see them shoot down “more than 200 Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps drones threatening international shipping and US forces”, according to Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command. The group’s guided-missile destroyers, he said, engaged in “arguably the most intense combat at sea the navy has seen” since the second world war while the carrier’s air wing carried out hundreds of “decisive strikes on IRGC targets”.

The crew worked long hours as the carrier remained at sea for months without a port visit. The war disrupted regional resupply routes and traditional hubs, making it harder to replenish the ship and rotate personnel, especially after Iran damaged a US navy base in Bahrain.

By August, the Lincoln had spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea.

Armen Kurdian, a retired US navy captain who served on the Lincoln in 2005, described the carrier as a “giant floating city” where sailors live in close quarters, and “you’ve got aircraft smacking down on decks repeatedly, hundreds of times per day, and that rattles the ship”.

The strain of this deployment was compounded by uncertainty over when the sailors would come home. Some familiessaid they went weeks without hearing from their loved ones, and for stretches of time, they said, those onboard did not receive letters and care packages from home.

Then reports began to emerge about conditions on the ship.

In April, photographs purporting to show poor-quality meals on the Lincoln circulated widely online. The US navy denied reports of food shortages, calling such claims “false”.

But by August, some families began describing a more troubling picture of what their loved ones onboard had told them about the conditions: shortages of food and basic supplies, plumbing problems, and exhaustion and deteriorating mental health among the crew. Two leading military newspapers also reported that there had been two attempts by sailors to jump overboard, causing concern among families and military health experts.

That month, it was reported that more than 200 family members attended a virtual town hall with navy leaders to discuss their concerns. One spouse reportedly said her husband, a sailor onboard, had texted her that day, saying: “He hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow.”

One mother whose 19-year-old son is onboard the carrier said this week that there were periods when she went a month without hearing from him. When they did communicate, she said, he sometimes sent photographs of the food, which she said looked “horrible”.

At one point, he told her about a power outage on the ship, but assured her that he was doing OK. He would tell her how other sailors had begun “to not be themselves” and were “losing themselves”.

“It’s been hard knowing the conditions and the type of food they’re being fed, and just not having any contact for long periods of time, and them being gone so long,” the woman, who requested anonymity, said. “It’s just been difficult.”

The reports of supply shortages and declining morale and mental health prompted outrage from Democrats, and swift pushback from senior officials in the Trump administration.

Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary who has pledged to restore the “warrior ethos” to the US military, said the conditions on the Lincoln had been “completely misrepresented”. Navy officials acknowledged that the war had disrupted traditional supply networks, but maintained that the carrier had adequate food, medical care and supplies.

When reporters asked Donald Trump whether the families were concerned about the reported conditions on the vessel, he claimed, “No, they’re not,” and when asked if he thought the deployment had gone on too long, he responded: “Not nearly long enough.”

For some naval families, that comment was difficult to hear.

One mother whose son was onboard the Lincoln said she became angry when she heard Trump’s comments.

“I thought, you know, this guy has never served a day in his life,” she said. “Neither has his family, none of his children have – how would he feel if it was his kid on that ship?”

She said she understood that the sailors were at war, but what troubled her was how long the deployment had lasted, with no opportunity to leave the ship and little sense of when the crew would return.

“For a long time I didn’t hear from him because he didn’t have internet or whatever,” she said. “So it was hard not knowing what’s going on, and then listening to news reports about all this stuff that’s going on, I was very worried.”

When she was finally spoke with her son after the reports of the suicide attempts and poor living conditions emerged, she asked whether he was eating, and if he was OK. She said he told her he was eating three meals a day, and sounded well. But from thousands of miles away, it was impossible to know for sure.

The picture emerging from the Lincoln was complicated, and worried families scrambled to try to piece together what was happening through brief phone calls and text messages, as well as news reports relaying what other relatives had heard.

Some families weren’t surprised by the reports, saying that their relative onboard had described similar conditions. Others, however, said their relative had described nothing of the sort, which led them to believe that some of the accounts circulating online had been overblown or just the experience of a handful of sailors.

One mother, herself a navy veteran, said she believed some reports about food and plumbing had been “blown out of proportion”. Food on these vessels in general, she said, could be “pretty disgusting”.

Her bigger concern was the length of the deployment, the lack of port visits, and the inability of sailors to receive mail and care packages from home for extended periods.

“I can’t imagine not feeling the ground under my feet for that amount of time,” she said. She also worried about sailors on their first deployment and whether such an experience might influence their decision to re-enlist.

For some families, the feeling of helplessness became overwhelming.

In August, Jefferson Kelley, whose son is onboard the Lincoln, wrote to his senator, Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, offering to take his son’s place on the ship for the remainder of the deployment.

In the letter, shared with the Guardian, Kelley proposed what he called a “parent swap”.

“If there is any lawful way for me to serve in his place so that he may return home, I am asking for that opportunity,” he wrote.

His son had never complained to him or his family about conditions on the ship, Kelley said, adding that he often responded that he was doing fine, but as a father, he said he couldn’t help by worry about his son, especially as the reports continued to emerge.

“I was trying to show that I am someone that is willing to do more than just sit at home and say somebody should do something or complain on social media,” Kelley said, describing his son’s deployment amid the war in Iran as a “very, very difficult experience” for the family.

On 15 August, as headlines about conditions on the Lincoln intensified, and as Democratic lawmakers demanded more information from the Pentagon, Adm Cooper, who heads Central Command, visited the carrier.

Not long afterward, he released a statement, claiming that of the US navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln “currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health”. But, he added, “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect”.

A long deployment at sea, Cooper said, “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways”.

In an opinion piece in the Wall Street Journal that week, Cooper wrote that “the crew is tired, but they continue to fire on all cylinders”.

“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” he said. In the essay, Cooper said that “recent media reporting has portrayed varying perspectives on operational tempo, crew morale and the realities facing our deployed forces”, adding: “What I found aboard the Lincoln is that many elements of those stories are old news.”

That same month, for one sailor, the strain of being away from home was compounded by events happening there. In a post on social media, Joshua Aviles, a sailor onboard the Lincoln, wrote that he had just learned that his father was detained by federal immigration authorities.

Aviles said his father had a driver’s license, social security card and work permit, and that the family “had done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting”.

“I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days ‌knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” he wrote in a Facebook post.

US immigration officials said at the time that Aviles’ father had entered the country illegally, and that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws”.

Several days later, Aviles said his father was released.

In late August, it was finally announced that another US aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, had arrived to relieve the Lincoln, and that the Lincoln would be heading back to San Diego.

On the journey home, the Lincoln docked in Thailand for several days, giving sailors a chance to walk on land and rest before beginning the final passage home.

In Thailand, the Guardian spoke with several sailors, who requested anonymity, who described eating “uncooked beef” and sliced-up, uncooked potatoes during the deployment. One sailor said that in his opinion, the decline in living standards was down to the battle conditions imposed during the combat operation, dubbed Operation Epic Fury, rather than the unprecedented length of deployment.

Another of the sailors said that the hardest part of the deployment was “pushing through, keeping the mentality”, while another serviceman hinted at the toll the long deployment had taken: “Some people adapt to it, but not everyone.”

Shakeria Fairfax, whose daughter, Jada, is onboard the Lincoln, couldn’t pass up the chance to be reunited with her daughter after such an intense deployment. She flew to Thailand, and still, to this day, Fairfax struggles to describe the moment they saw each other.

“The best way I could describe it is just kind of like when I first looked at her it was the overwhelming sense of love after having had so much time apart,” Fairfax said in an interview this week. “There was such a sense of pride, love and pride.”

For two days in Thailand, they played their favorite card game, went shopping and did what Fairfax called “girly things” – manicures, pedicures, facials and massages.

“It felt like we had some normalcy back in our lives after having been apart,” she said.

Like several other families the Guardian has spoken with, Fairfax did not want to disclose details of her daughter’s experience on the vessel, but described her as “extremely resilient”.

The deployment was Jada’s first, her mother said. She had completed basic training in October before she was deployed in November. When Fairfax woke to the news in February that the US and Israel had launched their war against Iran, she “couldn’t believe it”.

“We don’t come from a military family, and now my child is at war and I don’t know what that looks like,” she said.

Not long afterward, Fairfax lost contact with her daughter for several weeks, receiving only a handful of emails saying that she was OK. Then, on Easter weekend, Jada finally FaceTimed her mother. “It was beautiful,” Fairfax said.

Over the months that followed, Fairfax remembers only one occasion when her daughter told her she was feeling discouraged. Fairfax said she felt powerless, and asked her what she could do to help. Jada, who turned 25 onboard the ship in June, asked her mother to tell her stories about when she was growing up, she said.

So she did. “I told her stories. I sent her photographs,” Fairfax said. “Some of them she received, some of them she didn’t.”

Jada told her mother about some sailors onboard the ship who did not have the same kind of support system – people who did not receive care packages or have family members sending them reminders of home. And as the deployment continued, Fairfax said she could only imagine how difficult that must have become for those sailors. She and her daughter have since talked about finding a way to help those who do not have that support, she said.

For Fairfax, there was never much of a question about whether she would go to Thailand to see her daughter when she docked, as to her: “It was really about showing up for my daughter.”

Now she hopes to be able to head to San Diego to welcome her home.

The most serious disclosure about the deployment came after the Lincoln left Thailand.

In a letter responding to questions from the Democratic senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, acknowledged that eight navy personnel in the Lincoln strike group had attempted to take their own lives during the deployment, but said that no sailor had died from the attempts.

Cao said one sailor assigned to the air wing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter”. The sailor was treated by the vessel’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-up care, Cao said, and the sailor’s family was notified.

Another sailor, he said, attempted to go overboard in March, but was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was “also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to home port”, he added.

According to US Department of Defense data, there were 356 attempted suicides recorded in the navy in 2024. There were 287 in 2023, and 282 in 2022. This month, NPR reported that a 21-year-old sailor onboard the USS Fort Lauderdale, which had been deployed in the Caribbean as part of the Trump administration’s operation around Venezuela, died by suicide in June, a month before the vessel returned to Virginia.

Cao said that the navy launched a suicide prevention and response taskforce earlier this year, and also said in the letter that the Lincoln had deployed with five chaplains, an embedded integrated prevention counselor, a psychologist, a clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and a facility dog.

Cao said that the Lincoln “maintains adequate food supplies” but that due to the ship’s “participation in major combat operations with limited opportunities for resupply in a combat ‘environment, the number of main entree options served during regular meal hours was reduced from two to one for a short time”.

“Four meals were served daily, and all meals provided were nutritionally balanced, with adequate calories per day made available to every sailor,” he said.

The navy also acknowledged that earlier in the deployment the ship had experienced “localized piping failures” and temporary issues with its desalination units but that “shipboard engineering teams successfully completed repairs, and the potable water supply remains safe and tested daily”.

The new information prompted further calls from members of Congress for investigations and greater transparency.

In a statement, Gillibrand, who is a member of the Senate armed services committee, criticized the Trump administration’s handling of the reports from the vessel.

“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” she said, adding: “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect.”

In response, a White House spokesperson said that Trump has “rightfully restored a focus on readiness, lethality and supporting our war fighters at the Pentagon”.

“The president cares about our troops more than anyone, and he is ensuring our brave service members have all the resources they need to be successful as the United States military continues to economically strangle the Iranian regime,” they added.

Richard Blumenthal, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, also requested that navy leaders provide an “accounting of the eight suicide attempts”, including when they occurred and when senior navy leaders were informed of the incidents. He has also asked navy leaders to “detail the steps you will take to protect sailors’ mental health and wellbeing during future extended deployments”.

In an interview with the Guardian, Donald Guter, a retired navy judge advocate general, described the eight reported attempts as a “tremendously concerning number” but said that “given the operational tempo and the total lack of opportunity for port calls, in a way, it shouldn’t have surprised people”.

He described the Lincoln’s deployment as “extraordinary”, saying that spending “that long at sea without any breaks, at that operational tempo, is stressing on anyone”.

Carl Schuster, a retired US navy captain, said that during his long deployments, which lasted between six and seven months, it was not unusual to have one or two suicide attempts.

But, he said, “keep in mind, the Lincoln spent over 250 days at sea in a nine-month deployment, which is a much longer deployment and much more time entirely at sea than I ever did, so I’m not surprised at the additional stress and the additional attempts”.

“We’re asking the crews to sacrifice much more than was normal in my day,” Schuster said. “All of us have a breaking point.”

Lory Manning, who served more than 25 years in the navy, said that given the size of the strike group and the unprecedented length of the deployment, she didn’t think it was that “far out of bounds to have that many attempts” across thousands of people who “have been bottled up on ships for 10 months”, particularly amid prolonged uncertainty, deployment extensions and intense combat conditions.

“I’m very glad that nobody succeeded,” Manning said.

John Cordle, who retired from the navy in 2013 after 30 years of service and served in a carrier strike group, said he could remember only one suicide attempt onboard a ship of the two that he was in command of, so to him, “eight seems like a lot”.

Cordle said that his longest deployment had been seven and a half months and his longest period without a port call had been 110 days.

“I never had to deal with conditions this extreme,” he said of the Lincoln’s deployment.

He urged the navy in the future to be more transparent earlier about the conditions onboard, especially with the families, and said that he hoped the leaders learned from the Lincoln’s deployment.

Several veterans also cautioned that the strain of these deployments could potentially affect enlistment in the future.

“Given the history of what does and doesn’t make people re-enlist, it’s certainly quite possible that none of them want to go through that again,” said Manning, “and maybe not the sailors, maybe it’s their families that don’t want to have to go through it again.”

During a town hall in late August, Adm Daryl Caudle, the chief of naval operations, warned that long deployments could become more common. That warning came as, earlier this year, the USS Gerald Ford returned from a record-breaking 326 days at sea, marking the longest deployment by a US warship since the Vietnam war.

“In the short term, until I can grow the navy we need, I hate to admit it, but longer deployments are going to be probably part of that,” Caudle said.

Matthew Brown, a US navy reserve commander and former captain of the USS Scout, said he visited the Lincoln in mid-September.

Brown runs Chimney Trail Health, a behavioral healthcare company that specializes “in creative adaptations of cognitive behavior theory”. He said the Lincoln’s captain had invited him to provide his company’s cognitive readiness training program to the sailors as the carrier headed home.

He said he delivered an in-person seminar, “sort of like a tabletop workshop-type thing”, to those onboard, and that it was “well received”.

At that time, the crew were on their journey home, and Brown said he observed that their “morale was that they were obviously quite tired because it was a very like rigorous deployment” but that “they were resolute”.

The sailors, he added, “were strong, and many of them maintained a very good sense of humor”.

For future deployments, Brown said that having more personnel onboard trained in the basics of cognitive behavior theory and equipped with evidence-based materials could help when it comes to addressing some of the mental health challenges that may arise.

Later in September, the congresswoman Sara Jacobs, a Democrat representing California’s 51st district, which includes San Diego, said she joined a bipartisan delegation for in-person oversight of the Lincoln as it journeyed back to San Diego.

“I raised my concerns directly with the ship’s command and received a briefing on logistics, supply issues and lessons learned for future deployments,” she said. “I also met with sailors and marines onboard who painted a very different picture of this war; they shared stories of the deployment and their struggles to wash clothes, get medicine and healthcare, and eat enough food.”

Jacobs said that she didn’t blame the ship’s leadership, saying they had done the best they could under difficult circumstances. Instead, she said she blamed the president, whom she accused of “knowingly launch[ing] a war without the required planning and strategy needed”.

She said she would push for an investigation into the conditions and a House armed services committee hearing to hear directly from service members once they returned.

Meanwhile, another US carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, was just recently dispatched to the Middle East.

In a video statement in early September, navy leaders said that they were learning from the Lincoln’s deployment, and had loaded the Roosevelt up with additional food, hygiene products and other supplies before it got under way.

“We’re also focused on quality of life,” they said, adding that they will provide additional entertainment and fitness equipment onboard, and said that they were improving communication with families throughout the deployment.

“To the Lincoln team, thank you for what you accomplished, and for what you taught us, and to the Roosevelt team, we’re doing everything we can to make sure you are ready for the mission,” they said. “You and your families.”

The expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world. Burnham needs to block it

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 07:00:53 GMT

A third runway would fly in the face of reason. If we are to prioritise human life over short-term ‘growth’, we need to use planes less, not more

If a third runway is built at Heathrow, what will be the impact on the wealth of the nation? It will cost us somewhere between £23.4bn and £62.5bn. These are not my figures; they weren’t calculated by environmental groups, but by the Department for Transport.

For decades, government ministers have told us that airport expansion is essential for “growth”. As chancellor, Rachel Reeves claimed that a third runway at Heathrow would add 0.43% to GDP, figures we later discovered came from a report commissioned by the airport. The transport department’s own analysis concluded that the real addition to GDP would be between 0.03% and 0.05%: eight to 14 times less. Against this, it weighed the social and environmental costs of the project, to reveal a massive net loss. It found that a third runway would cause major harm to the health and wellbeing of up to 3 million local people.

But even these figures don’t capture it. The climate breakdown caused by the runway affects the entire planet, yet the costs to other countries aren’t counted. So again we must ask, why does the government support it?

Or does it? Though Heathrow expansion remains official policy, when asked at the weekend, Andy Burnham said the runway was “contested” and “principally it’s a matter for London and London MPs”. That sounds hopeful.

We also learned that the project has been delayed yet again. Though Heathrow announced last year that its plans were “shovel-ready”, it now admits the runway would take four years longer to build than it claimed: the estimated completion date is now 2039.

By then, or so we must hope, a government might have decided to take the climate impact seriously. If so, the new runway would need to be shuttered the moment it opened. Otherwise, according to the government’s Climate Change Committee, “almost all CO2 emissions in 2050 will be from aviation”. Heathrow’s expansion alone, the committee says, would cause more carbon emissions by 2054 than “any other sector of the economy”.

And even this is not the end of it. The committee considers only the carbon dioxide planes produce, but the other impacts are even greater. A paper in the journal Atmospheric Environment suggests that, over 100 years, the nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, soot, volatile organic products, water vapour and other compounds released or formed in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere by planes raise the heating caused by flying by 115%. Over 20 years, they raise it by an astonishing 517%.

Given that crucial Earth systems may be approaching their tipping points, and heating today triggers further greenhouse gas releases from forests, wetlands and permafrost, the 20-year horizon is crucial. But these other compounds are considered in neither international treaties nor the UK’s Climate Change Act. The impact of flying is officially and massively underestimated.

While the heating effects of almost all other sectors can be greatly reduced by technology, there are simply no good solutions for aviation. Successive governments have justified airport expansion plans with the promise of “sustainable aviation fuel”. Mostly they mean turning biomass into kerosene, which is even worse than using fossil fuels. If this substitute is to reach any kind of scale, it will either swallow up existing cropland, driving starvation, or it will cause the expansion of cropland into forests, wetlands and other habitats, accelerating the environmental crisis. An analysis by the Royal Society found that meeting existing UK aviation demand (never mind future growth) with energy crops “would require around half of UK agricultural land”. That’s the opposite of sustainable.

“Sustainable aviation fuel” can also mean synthetic fuels made from captured CO2 and green hydrogen. But the Royal Society found that for existing aviation, we’d need to use between five and eight times the UK’s entire renewable electricity capacity. And still, aeroplanes would release a lethal chemical cocktail – not just CO2 but those other compounds – into the high atmosphere, so only a fraction of the problem would be solved. Worldwide, a paper in the journal One Earth found that even with a wildly unrealistic programme of technological change, in which fossil jet fuels were phased out completely by 2040, the global heating caused by aviation would more than double by 2070, thanks to rising demand.

As for hydrogen-, ammonia- or battery-powered commercial aircraft, they all fail on technical or safety grounds, even before we ask where the power comes from. The “prototypes” endlessly showcased by the airlines, which never get beyond the artist’s impression, are nothing but “perceptionware”, designed to solve political problems, not technical ones.

If Heathrow expansion goes ahead, passenger numbers in the UK are forecast to rise from 299 million in 2025 to 491 million in 2050. As other sectors decarbonise, the proportion of climate breakdown caused by flying climbs and climbs, until planes account for almost all of it.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The only effective strategy is to reduce demand. There’s a progressive means of doing so: the frequent flyer levy. Wealth and flights are strongly linked. In 2024, 48% of England’s population did not fly at all. But 5% of the population took five or more flights abroad, and these account for 33% of all journeys. Increasing demand has been almost entirely driven by frequent flyers, who are highly concentrated in the highest income quintile. The levy would not be charged on the first flight someone took in any year, but it would escalate with every additional flight.

This is just, proportionate and – unlike all the techno-bollocks – immediately dispatchable. Otherwise, we continue to subsidise a wealthy, selfish minority with our money, our health, our wellbeing and the degradation of the living planet. How is that fair?

What government support for airport expansion shows is that “growth” is simply an excuse for giving powerful lobby groups what they want. When asked whether growth was more important than net zero, Reeves replied: “Well, if it’s the No 1 mission, it’s obviously the most important thing.” That’s another way of saying money is more important than human life. But, as the figures show, it was never about growth at all. It was always about meeting the demands of the airport lobby and wealthy passengers.

Now we wait on Burnham. Will the flight of reason continue? Or will human and planetary welfare at last outweigh the lobbyists?

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 06:00:51 GMT

Green party debate over the motion ‘Zionism is racism’ comes amid renewed arguments over the meaning and history of a contested term

Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green party, has said he is an anti-Zionist. As his party conference prepares to debate a motion that “Zionism is racism”, what precisely is Zionism and what is the history of the claim that it is racist?

Modern Zionism developed in the late 1800s out of several strands of thinking on the future of Jewish collective and cultural identity, emerging from a millennia-old religious yearning to return to Zion, which runs through Jewish holy texts. The term came, however, to be most associated with Theodor Herzl’s brand of political Zionism, the movement for Jewish self-determination and statehood in the context of rising European antisemitism.

Although Zionism tends to be seen by critics as a monolithic political idea, its history has encompassed multiple, often contradictory, intellectual strands including the notion – proposed by the philosopher Martin Buber before the foundation of Israel – of a binational Arab-Jewish state in Palestine.

Since the foundation of the state of Israel in 1948, the debate over Zionism inside the country has largely centred on liberal and rightwing, or “revisionist”, camps – the latter represented by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party. Issues such as settlement, occupation and whether Israel should be defined as an ethno-nationalist Jewish state moved to the core of political contest.

However, as Dov Waxman, a professor of Israel studies at the University of California, wrote in the Conversation last month, the issue is further complicated by the fact that, despite contested definitions, the idea of Zionism for many Jews represents something more amorphous: “Jewish liberation and sovereignty, a safe haven from persecution, a revival of the Hebrew language, and a renewed sense of collective pride, especially after the Holocaust.”

One critique of Zionism – used as a shorthand for the state of Israel – is that it is a “colonial” project.

Those critics, in parts of the left, in the wider Arab world and among some anti-Zionist Jews such as Polanski, would point to three pieces of evidence. First, the violent displacement of Palestinians during the Nakba, or “catastrophe” for Palestinians, that accompanied the founding of the Jewish state.

Second, they argue Israel has created an apartheid system of unequal rights in the occupied territories that denies Palestinian ambitions to statehood and their own self-determination and, third, that within Israel those of Palestinian origin are discriminated against.

Before the establishment of Israel in 1948, Palestinians had a vibrant society across British Mandatory Palestine, but their connection to historical Palestine has often been dismissed or diminished by significant strands of Zionist thinking.

At the heart of academic debate is how widespread the use by some early Zionists was of the notion of a “land without people” for a “people without land”, which critics have used as evidence that Zionism was a colonial enterprise at its very beginning.

In contrast, Zionists point to the evidence of a historical presence of Jews in the Holy Land, as well as for many a promised biblical patrimony in a homeland from which Jews were displaced and that many hold up as a refuge in a hostile world.

The argument that Zionism is racism, while controversial, is not new. The phrase came to particular prominence during the cold war, when the UN passed resolution 3379 in 1975. The so-called “Zionism as racism” resolution compared “the racist regime in occupied Palestine” to apartheid South Africa. Sponsored’ by the Arab League and promoted by the Soviet Union, it passed with support from countries in the developing world but was later revoked in 1991 under pressure from the then US president, George HW Bush.

Proponents of the argument say Zionism privileges the rights of Jews in Israel over non-Jews via a discriminatory system. Opponents of the framing describe it as antisemitic as it singles out Jews as a group to deny them alone the right to self-determination. They argue that, by delegitimising the basis for Israel’s founding as a Jewish homeland, it acts as a cover for antisemitism.

The war in Gaza has intensified arguments about the nature of Zionism, in part driven by the overtly racist framing of senior Israeli political figures towards Palestinian society after the 7 October deadly Hamas attack on southern Israel in 2023.

An employment tribunal two years ago found that the views of David Miller, a former professor of political sociology who was sacked by the University of Bristol in 2021, that “Zionism is and always has been a racist, violent, imperialist ideology premised on ethnic cleansing” amounted to a protected philosophical belief under the 2010 Equality Act, a case upheld on appeal.

A highly controversial figure, Miller has also argued in social media posts that Zionists have worked as “infiltrators and subversives”, gained access to not just all UK political parties but also “the media, entertainment industries, the law, financial institutions, sports and all sorts of apparently obscure parts of the UK”.

Miller is a key figure in the anti-Zionist Movement and has links to Greens for Palestine, which is proposing the Green party motion on Zionism is racism.

‘People are deserting it’: why are London mansions struggling to sell?

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 06:00:50 GMT

For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areas

An elegant Georgian facade, a full-width balcony and an exclusive address in South Kensington just steps from the Natural History Museum and the V&A. Yet the listing price of this west London flat at Queen’s Gate Gardens has dropped by nearly £1m since last year, to £4.4m.

It is far from an isolated case. A nearby house originally listed at £20m was slashed to £14m this year, says a local estate agent. In neighbouring Notting Hill, a stucco-fronted property that came to market two years ago at £16m is now being offered for less than £14m, they said.

London’s premium property market is stuck in a rut. While borrowing costs and stretched affordability weigh on everyday buyers, the city’s richest residents are also making deep cuts to the prices of their multimillion-pound homes.

This market is a world away from the rest of the UK property market – where the average house price was just under £275,000 in September, according to Nationwide. The well-heeled neighbourhoods also present a stark contrast with much of the capital, where Londoners struggle to get on to the housing ladder, face rising rents and a lack of affordable housing, and estate agents report the market for flats is now “dead”.

But neighbourhoods such as Knightsbridge, bordering Hyde Park and home to Harrods, are also feeling the pinch, said Harry Dawes, a buying agent based in Belgravia.

“There is a flat on Pont Street, a five-minute walk from Harrods, which sold at £4.4m in 2014, then sold at £3.5m. It can now be bought at £2.5m.”

For decades, London’s property prices raced ahead of the national average. But that gap has been slowly narrowing: while the average price of a UK home rose by about 2% in the year ended in June, prices in inner London boroughs fell by 8.3%, according to the Office for National Statistics.

That drop has been particularly pronounced in Westminster – which includes areas such as Marylebone, Belgravia and Mayfair – with prices down 25.4% year on year. In the City, prices slumped by 20.4%, and in Kensington and Chelsea, prices fell 14.7%.

Properties in the capital became overvalued in the mid-2010s after a period of rapid price growth, said Anthony Payne, the chief executive of the data analyst LonRes. London was then hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs.

Now, owners who bought at the peak now face losses of as much as 25% if they choose to sell, according to estimates from the estate agent Savills.

“London benefited dramatically from international investment and buyers wanting property here as a store of wealth and a way of making money,” Payne said. “These are the people that inflated the market, but now more and more of them are deserting it.”

Jeremy Gee, the managing director at the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates – whose portfolio includes a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park – said the decline had also been driven partly by the exit of super-wealthy groups from the UK, especially after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.

“There is a section of society who have left the UK recently for lots of reasons, but mainly because of tax,” he said.

“When there are not that many buyers and lots of properties, the prices are going to be softer. Many of our sellers have decided that enough is enough – let’s just sell the property and move on.”

Tax changes have put sellers on edge, too, he added. Last year, the former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced plans for a “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.

This nervousness has triggered a slowdown across the higher tiers of London’s market. Prime properties spent an average of 186 days on the market in the first half of 2026, up from 178 days in the first half of 2025, according to LonRes. Over the same period, the average discount to asking price widened from 8.3% to 10.4% – sellers have grown more likely to accept lowball offers.

Sellers, who normally own these properties for at least a decade, “don’t like it but have to accept it,” said Dawes.

“If they are older, they have to take a lifetime view on their property and accept that from a profit and loss perspective, this last trade might not look good.

“We bought three flats for a client’s kids last year – two in Chelsea and one in Notting Hill – and every seller was selling at a loss.”

Even with multimillion pound discounts propping up on the market, Stuart Bailey, the head of super-prime London sales at the estate agent Knight Frank, said there were still buyers willing to pay above the asking price for “the very best in class” properties.

“A fabulous address, lovely views, immaculate style and newly refurbished,” he said. “It is a matter of premium or discount, retail or trade, brand new or not, and there is nowhere in between. It’s the discounted properties dragging the market down.

“Sellers are more and more realistic about moving on,” he added. “They do not see material price growth on the horizon.”

“With a Labour government the concern is always that there’s going to be some kind of wealth tax somewhere,” he said.

“But many wealthy people also just accept the cost of taxation and that London is simply an expensive city to live in.”

after newsletter promotion

Camilla Dell, a buying agent, said demand is still strong from a wide base of international buyers, including Americans, Singaporeans and Nigerians. Politics, she said, rarely comes up in conversation.

“Most people accept that the UK does not have the best political stability but they want to live here,” she said. “And actually, it helped that Andy Burnham ruled out an overhaul of property taxes in the next budget.”

Sluggish prices in London are in stark contrast with the likes of San Francisco and Lisbon (a hub for Europe’s digital nomads). Both cities have benefited from booming wealth in the tech sector, with prices rising by 4.8% and 3.3%, respectively, in the first half of this year. Tokyo has been the global standout, with prices up 7% as international buyers have swooped on a weak yen and snapped up luxury properties already in low supply.

Berlin’s prime market, which was the worst performer in Europe, has suffered under the weight of rising borrowing costs and meagre economic growth.

While the multimillionaires’ tier of the property market is being squeezed, the billionaire “super-prime” end of the market is buzzing with activity.

This year, billionaire Reform donor Nick Candy sold his Chelsea home for more than £270m, which is believed to the UK property market’s biggest single house sale in history. Meanwhile, the Holme, the 40-bedroom mansion inside Regent’s Park, is reportedly nearing a £190m sale, less than two years after it was sold for £139m in 2024.

“There have been some very big transactions in super-prime – those are people buying long-term family homes and trophy assets,” Dawes said.

For agents, their cut on these deals – typically about 2% – can run into the millions, and business is thriving. The sale of homes priced at £10m or more climbed 50% in the three months ended in June, compared with the same quarter in 2025, according to the property developer JLL. Meanwhile, Savills found that transactions in the £15m to £20m bracket rose by almost 40%, also in the second quarter of this year compared with last.

The rise of newly minted multimillionaires from the world of tech and social media is driving new renovation trends, too – with more calls for home cinemas, steam rooms, saunas and dedicated yoga and meditation spaces, according to the interior designer Nu Projects.

Still, many of the wealthy are waiting on the sidelines. Beauchamp says that seven out of 10 of its ultra-prime clients are now choosing to rent rather than buy, because they want to save on maintenance, stamp duty, service charges and property taxes – as well as anxiety over whether the government will introduce higher taxes on property, wealth and pensions.

It is pushing prime rental stock into scarce supply. Prices in this market rose 1.6% in the year ended in June, according to Savills. Super-expensive tenancies, where tenants hand over at least £5,000 a week – were up 17% last year, according to Knight Frank.

Such intense competition for “best in class” properties mean that even in a fragile market, the most discerning buyers can still face stiff competition, advisers said.

“There’s still demand from overseas buyers who want to buy best-in-class trophy assets,” Gee says. “American and Middle Eastern buyers are underpinning that market.

“But then there is everything beneath that. Anything secondhand, needing a bit of work, where you might normally find a domestic buyer, that is where it is a bit stickier.”

The outlook for the broader prime market remains less rosy. The estate agent Strutt & Parker has downgraded its forecast for prime central London price growth to 4.4% by 2030, compared with an estimate of 9% to 12% at the start of the year.

For now, the balance of power remains with buyers in London, Payne said.

“I look at some of the stuff that’s coming on the market and you just think to yourself, ‘My God, this is such unbelievably good value’,” he added.

“Hand on my heart, I do not think we are at the bottom of the market yet.”

From Digger to The Strokes: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 05:00:52 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Tom Cruise transforms in Alejandro Iñárritu’s heavyweight satirical comedy, while the NYC indie rockers are in the UK for an arena tour

DiggerOut now Tom Cruise is back, but he’s giving flyboys and secret agents a rest in favour of a transformation into a powerful oil tycoon, in director Alejandro G Iñárritu’s 2027 Oscar bid. But here’s the kicker: it’s not a sober, serious Oscar contender, but a wild and comedic big swing. Dig in.

The WeightOut now As character motivations go, the need to be reunited with your child is a powerful one. That’s what’s driving Ethan Hawke in this Depression-era historical thriller, in which a convict must transport gold illegally through the wilderness if he’s to be allowed to see his young daughter again. Also starring Julia Jones and Russell Crowe.

VerityOut now Anne Hathaway’s golden era of psychological thrillers (see also: Eileen, Mothers’ Instinct, Mother Mary) keeps on trucking. In this Colleen Hoover adaptation she plays an unstable novelist who may or may not be a murderer. Josh Hartnett plays her husband, and Dakota Johnson the ghostwriter caught up in a nightmare.

Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman RushdieOut now Prolific film-maker Alex Gibney directs a documentary about the aftermath of 24-year-old Hadi Matar’s 2022 attack on Salman Rushdie. Based on the literary titan’s own bestselling memoir, it contains footage filmed by his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths. Catherine Bray

Beyond the Music MediaCity, Salford, 7 to 9 October As well as offering an industry talks programme, the annual Beyond the Music conference showcases new talent over three days. This year’s lineup includes Jamaican-Irish rapper JayaHadADream and noisy sister duo Alt Blk Era. Michael Cragg

The Strokes6 to 28 October; tour starts London Having galvanised gen Z via 2020’s The New Abnormal, New York’s premiere indie rockers arrive in arenas in support of their new album Reality Awaits. Single Going Shopping should slot nicely next to Reptilia, Last Nite and Someday. MC

Leonkoro Quartet Wigmore Hall, London, 6 October Impressive new quartets appear constantly in classical music, but this group are the real deal. Their first recital as Wigmore Hall associate artists combines Beethoven and Schubert with the UK premiere of a new work by Finnish composer Sauli Zinovjev. Flora Willson

Arbenz, Neame, Osby, Churchill Watermill Jazz, Dorking, 6 OctoberDorking is the last UK stopover for Swiss drums original Florian Arbenz’s European tour with US sax star Greg Osby, UK piano virtuoso Ivo Neame and resourceful UK singer Immy Churchill. Neame also plays 1000 Trades in Birmingham on Friday with his own trio. John Fordham

Painting the French Riviera Royal Academy of Art, London, to 31 January Timed perfectly to coincide with the weather turning miserable, the Royal Academy is taking a warm, summery look at the Côte d’Azur and what made it such a destination for the artists who shaped modernism, such as Picasso, Matisse, Renoir and Raoul Dufy. It might make you very, very jealous.

The 90s: Art and Fashion Tate Britain, London, 8 October to 14 February Tate Britain’s big autumn show is a dizzying exploration of life in the UK during the hedonistic, hectic, drug-addled, rave-filled, Britpoptastic party decade that was the 1990s, with art by the likes of Juergen Teller and Sarah Lucas, all curated by former Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful.

Living Labyrinths: Art and Fungi Royal Albert Memorial Museum, Exeter, 3 October to 21 February Uncover all sorts of mycological marvels in this exhibition about the “culture of mushrooms”, featuring fungi-focused watercolours by Beatrix Potter, collages by Cy Twombly and mycelial art by a whole host of contemporary artists.

Mike Nelson Modern Art Oxford, 3 October to 11 April The master of large-scale, terrifying, atmospheric installation art returns to this Oxford institution 22 years after his last show here, this time tackling themes of belief, freedom, protest and memory. Eddy Frankel

Rent Tom Stoppard theatre, London, to 27 March A high-voltage new take on Jonathan Larson’s powerful musical, starring Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo. Set in 80s New York in the midst of the Aids/HIV crisis, the show focuses on a group of young artists forging a living and falling in love. Miriam Gillinson

London City Ballet Arts theatre, Cambridge, ouring to 24 OctoberIt is only two years since artistic director Christopher Marney revived this ballet company, and he’s taken it swiftly from 0 to 60. It lands in Cambridge with a programme including Glen Tetley’s Firebird and a rarely seen work by Jerome Robbins. Lyndsey Winship

King Lear Royal Exchange theatre, Manchester, to 15 November David Threlfall tackles the mighty theatrical challenge that is King Lear – and stars alongside a rich ensemble cast, including musician Nadine Shah and Shakespearean pro Jonathan Slinger. MG

Finlay Christie Guildford, 3 October; Peterborough; Sun; Chelmsford, Wed; Maidenhead, Fri; touring to 9 January It sounds counterintuitive, but leaning into poshness can be a very effective way for comedians to connect with the public. I’m not buying into the ‘Keminaissance’. If the Tories lowered the bar any further, they’d be Reform UK

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 05:00:52 GMT

Rather than ridding the Conservatives of their ‘nasty party’ status, Badenoch has a plan – to cut benefits for young people and demonise the unemployed

Kemi Badenoch is considering doing her job. With her second Conservative party conference as leader looming on Sunday, and her rival Nigel Farage finally losing some ground, the provocateur with a reputation for dodging media rounds and being ill-prepared for briefs has seemingly cured her camera shyness.

In recent days, Badenoch has touted a policy to give the unemployed a “subsistence allowance” that would prevent them from buying booze or cigarettes, sought to bar benefits from young people who are straight out of school, accused Andy Burnham of wanting to take Britain “back to the 1970s” with public control of utilities, and enjoyed some mixed polling.

That the rightwing press has greeted this with a relief bordering on delusion (the Telegraph went as far to suggest the Conservatives could win a snap election) gives a hint of how dismally low the bar is in parts of the Tory camp.

More than two years since the Conservative’s crushing general election defeat, it is not simply that the most successful electoral force in the democratic world has collapsed into irrelevance – but that it has happened with barely a whimper. The juggernaut success of Reform UK, mixed with Badenoch’s unwillingness to fully engage, has given large sections of the media licence to treat Farage as unofficial leader of the opposition, with the Conservatives getting most column inches when another one of them defects to Reform.

The so-called natural party of government is essentially now an afterthought in the national conversation, throwing out an anti-migrant comment here and an ableist speech there in the hope of just getting some attention.

Meanwhile, the country quietly gets on with the day-to-day consequences of the last time it let the Tories govern: fundraising to patch up the roof at their children’s school, waiting a year to get a hospital scan, or walking past their now closed local library.

There has been an audible sigh of relief from Badenoch’s team as her personal poll ratings markedly improved over the past year, even as the Conservative’s image has tanked (as of last month, only 19% of Britons feel the party is ready for a return to government). But talk of a “Keminaissance” misses the point: it means little that the electorate are slightly less put off by the captain if they still wouldn’t get on the ship for fear of drowning.

That, as of last week, Badenoch – nostalgic for the days the Tories were a main player in a two-party system – is still ruling out an electoral pact with Reform is only further weakening her chances of ever seeing No 10.

It’s not as if the Conservatives have made any substantive efforts for reputation rehabilitation. Are they regretful of Brexit? What about Partygate? If re-elected, would they repeat Liz Truss’s deep tax cuts or George Osborne’s austerity? As the public faces mounting crises, from gutted living standards to long NHS waiting lists, Badenoch has largely kept stumm rather than offer any meaningful solutions. Indeed, on a rare occasion she has spoken out on a pressing issue – namely social care – it was to refuse to engage with Burnham’s reforms if paying for it involved tax rises.

You could argue that it would have made sense to regroup after such a large-scale loss – not least when Keir Starmer was expected to fulfil a five-year term – or that it is rather difficult to propose solutions for problems that your party has largely caused. There is truth in both. And yet it is telling what Badenoch chooses to spend her energy on. While the former minister has told her MPs not to expect big policy plans until 2027, she has found time to wade into culture wars including, but not limited to: why she hates critical race theory; a U-turn on the Conservative commitment to meet net zero by 2050; and why she wants the UK to withdraw from the European convention on human rights.

It’s not a coincidence that Badenoch’s main policy intervention ahead of gathering in Birmingham for conference is a universal credit cut that would shame unemployed people not trusted to spend cash to have to use a special debit card while saving a paltry £538m a year for the taxpayer (As context, the state pension bill is now £154bn annually.) It is less a substantive socioeconomic policy and more a wink to the audience, a casual cruelty that would make already hard lives even harder for the vague promise of a point in the polls. That Badenoch presumably genuinely believes in this stuff is a grim added bonus.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The Conservatives will clearly be hoping that Reform’s downward spiral continues and in the meantime, the benefits bill – much like immigration – seems easy pickings. The proposed universal credit cut is the latest in their package of welfare cuts worth £23bn. But that Reform recently announced a plan to slice a staggering £50bn from the social security budget shows that as extreme as Badenoch continues to go in the coming months, Reform will go further. That Farage is now being clipped by Rupert Lowe’s Restore shows neatly enough that no matter what depths you are willing to sink to, someone out there will dig their way lower still. Britain’s hard right in 2026 is effectively a Russian doll: each party pushes the previous one inside, only to reveal an even worse version underneath.

In another timeline, Badenoch would be pivoting to the centre, or at least the centre right, picking up traditional Conservative voters who fear Burnham’s threat of higher taxes and squirm at Reform’s race-baiting. But Badenoch is not the candidate for that fight. For all her inaction, she has been clear about her direction: centrist ideas are no longer wanted in the Conservative party, she has said, and if one-nation Tories have qualms about her rightward push, they “need to get out of the way”.

This is not the opposition era of David Cameron with huskies, or William Hague on a log flume wearing a baseball cap. Badenoch has no interest in ridding the Conservatives of their “nasty party” image. She is rejuvenating it. This is the party of the Windrush scandal, mass disability benefit cuts, and “go home” vans repackaged for an even more toxic climate. The only question is: will it actually work? It is hard to say what’s worse: selling your soul for power or selling it and still losing.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Decline and fall: who will believe in Raheem Sterling now?

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 05:00:51 GMT

Former England winger could face a prison term next month and his career collapse raises many questions

In another world, where careers broke in different directions, Raheem Sterling would be in this England squad now, playing for the manager, Thomas Tuchel, who made him the No 1 target of the new Chelsea era after the Todd Boehly-Clearlake Capital takeover.

He is 16 months younger than Harry Kane, who continues to break records as England’s captain and hit a personal high of 73 goals last season. Sterling, meanwhile, is without a club and awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty at Basingstoke magistrates court to dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after an incident that witnesses feared might kill someone.

How have their careers diverged so starkly? Why is Kane thriving while Sterling lives through such a sad and public decline?

Multiple sources, who asked not to be named to protect relationships, paint a complicated picture of Sterling. One describes him as a “lost soul”. Another believes he has been “hopelessly misguided” in his life and career. To understand his fall, it is pertinent to remember the magnitude of his rise.

Those who saw Sterling’s ascent – from the boy helping his mum on cleaning jobs in Stonebridge to the outrageously gifted footballer in Queens Park Rangers’ academy, to Liverpool’s first team at 17 – recall a player who seemed perfectly calibrated for success.

“Raheem was confident,” says Mark Anderson, the Liverpool youth scout who convinced the club to make him one of the most expensive 15-year-olds. “He played with passion and desire. From the first time I saw him, I thought he had the ingredients to become an international prospect.”

Sterling was quickly training with Liverpool’s first team, where players were stunned that this slight teen possessed a natural strength beyond many adults. He was rarely seen in the gym, yet held his own against Martin Skrtel, Mamadou Sakho and Kolo Touré, who towered over him.

“Raheem was much tougher mentally than some people might have imagined,” Steven Gerrard wrote in his book, My Story, admitting that he and Jamie Carragher did not go easy on him in training.

Sterling’s resilience was tested when he rejected a £100,000-a-week contract and became engulfed in a public storm. It marked a turning point in how he was perceived: from England’s brightest prospect to arrogant young footballer – fair or not.

Sterling gave an interview to the BBC insisting he was not a “money-grabbing 20-year-old”. Liverpool-supporting pundits turned on him. Matters worsened when his then-agent, Aidy Ward, told the Evening Standard that Sterling wouldn’t sign a new deal even if they offered close to £1m per week. Liverpool sold him to Manchester City for an initial £44m that summer.

Public sentiment had begun to shift – from England’s fifth-youngest debutant to the player who told Roy Hodgson he was too tired for a game against Estonia – and the first images of Sterling inhaling from a balloon allegedly filled with nitrous oxide emerged in 2015. Leaving Liverpool darkened the mood, and the reputation has since haunted him. Particularly with England, where he became the scapegoat for the Euro 2016 last-16 exit to Iceland, the abuse so toxic that Sterling branded himself #TheHatedOne on Instagram. He was 21.

Within two years he was the victim of a racially motivated attack outside Manchester City’s training ground and was racially abused by Chelsea supporters during a match at Stamford Bridge.

At his peak, he was spectacular. In 2019, he won a domestic treble with City, scored two goals in the FA Cup final and the winning penalty in the League Cup final shootout and secured the Football Writers’ Association’s footballer of the year award. A year later, Xavi Hernández claimed Sterling was “winning [the] race” to replace Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. The street footballer tamed by Pep Guardiola’s brilliantly rigid systems. By 2021, he had twice finished in the top 15 of Ballon d’Or voting.

This was a player who kept producing when it mattered as England reached the Euro 2020 final: two winners the only goals of England’s group stage, the opener against Germany in the last 16 and winning the penalty that led to the decisive goal against Denmark in the semi-final. But even his attempts to do good seemed to turn some against him.

He became a central figure calling out racism in society, particularly his own depictions in the media after criticism for buying his mother a house. In 2020, he recorded an anti-racism video declaring “I will never tire of being black”, texting the contributors including Kevin De Bruyne, David Alaba and Jordan Henderson, to ask them to take part. He received an MBE a year later. If anything, it made some who did not know Sterling personally more fervently opposed to him.

One source who worked closely with Sterling describes him as “polite and charming”, saying: “He doesn’t come across as arrogant or having an attitude. He’s a nice guy, shy – quite bashful.”

In some quarters, there has been a degree of glee in the way Sterling’s career declined sharply after he joined Chelsea. He had won almost everything and, at 27, was entering the years when many players peak.

Sterling was the player Tuchel told Boehly to prioritise – the American billionaire captivated by the prospect of making a forward fresh from winning his fourth Premier League title in five years their marquee signing. Sterling signed a five-year contract on £325,000 a week.

Tuchel was sacked seven weeks later. In the years that followed, Sterling played under Graham Potter, Frank Lampard, Mauricio Pochettino and Enzo Maresca. One source questioned whether leaving the rigid structures of Brendan Rodgers at Liverpool and Guardiola at Manchester City for the chaos at Chelsea was damaging. From posting extraordinary numbers at City – 23 goals and 14 assists in 2017-18, 25 and 16 in 2018-19, 31 and 10 in 2019-20 – his output dwindled.

A collective decision at Chelsea in summer 2024 to sell him was made based on his personal life and ability to play in the team. In a particularly brutal week, two days before the start of the 2024-25 season, Maresca told Sterling he was not part of his plans and left him out of the squad for the game against Manchester City and a Conference League tie with Servette in which Pedro Neto wore his No 7 shirt. Sterling was forced to train away from the first team.

It seems he was not entirely innocent here. The Guardian was told he was known to turn up late for training when he was supposed to set an example, though sources close to Sterling say he never faced a recorded disciplinary at Chelsea. His treatment ultimately was harsh, though it is understood Maresca assessed his wingers during friendlies until a final call was made.

Sterling made clear he wanted to stay in London for his family, and Chelsea reluctantly sanctioned a loan to Arsenal. He scored once, in a Carabao Cup game against League One club Bolton on 25 September 2024, his most recent professional goal.

When he returned, sources say he was told to stay away from the main facilities at Cobham, though a Chelsea source denied this was the case. Sterling declined loan interest from Juventus, but by January, after six months without playing, needed to move for the sake of his career.

The club agreed to buy him out of the remaining 18 months of his contract at a reduced fee. Their statement announcing his departure was 23 words long.

Sterling chose to rebuild under Robin van Persie at Feyenoord. It was disastrous: ruthlessly mocked on social media by the club’s fans, laughed at in the stadium.

One source who worked with Sterling compared his career trajectory with Michael Owen’s – two teen prodigies whose speed was their greatest asset, and whose careers faded as that diminished. Owen played his final season at Stoke, making eight Premier League appearances from the bench, and retired at 33. Sterling will be 32 in December. Another source questioned whether winning so much and earning vast sums had dulled the desire required to stay at the top.

Sterling returned home from the Netherlands and, 11 days later, drove his Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide from balloons, it seemed like a cry for help. He admitted to officers, when arrested in May, that he had a “problem” with nitrous oxide – a stark admission from an athlete with hopes of playing again.

“It’s sad to see that someone struggles, because he was a devoted father for his children and he was a family guy, a nice guy to be around,” Tuchel said on Friday. “It just seems that he goes through a difficult period. I’m not sure how much is his fault; sometimes you just enter a strange spiral in your life, a downward spiral. Thoughts are with him of course. The belief is always that he can turn it around.”

Standing in the dock in court dressed in black last month, while Liverpool were preparing for a League Cup game against Tottenham, Sterling learned he faces the real prospect of prison when the court reconvenes in November.

“Before he was Raheem Sterling the international footballer, the Premier League player and the name everybody knew, he was simply a young boy with a football who somebody had to believe in,” Anderson says.

Will anyone still believe in him now?

Manchester City’s guilty verdict brings football’s great sell-off crashing to earth

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 05:00:51 GMT

On the day Andy Burnham spoke of the wrong turn Britain took under Thatcher, football was facing a day of reckoning over its own story of corporate acquisition

It was somehow fitting that Tuesday’s damning ruling against Manchester City landed in the heart of the Labour party conference, in the afterglow of Andy Burnham’s rapturously received prime minister’s speech.

I was there, and read the astonishing 40 pages of findings – that City created “sham” contracts to boost income artificially by £900m – on my phone during a long meeting of the Socialist Campaign Group, where people were celebrating Keir Starmer’s ousting and Burnham’s more leftwing direction.

At the core of Burnham’s speech was the wrong turn he says Britain took under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, selling off and privatising council housing, water, energy, transport and care. “We built the common good,” he said, but “the common wealth … created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few.”

He could have been talking about football, too. Where Manchester City have ended up, having been bought by Sheikh Mansour of the Abu Dhabi ruling family in 2008, is a culmination of decades in which “the people’s game” has been carved up for profits. Clubs like City, formed in the Victorian smog of industry by churches, schools and workplaces, then built by generations of supporters into powerful homes of belonging, were sold off just when football finally had enough wealth to go round.

I investigated and reported on that financial carve up in my early years of journalism, and Burnham worked on it too, at the start of his political career, as the administrator of New Labour’s football taskforce.

My 1997 book, The Football Business, in which I likened football’s commercialisation to Thatcher’s privatisations, chimed with many supporters’ groups campaigning against rocketing ticket prices, exclusive pay-TV deals, and the drawbridge the newly mega-rich Premier League had pulled up behind it.

My moment of clarity had come at Manchester City, reporting on an earlier takeover, in 1994 by a beloved former player, Francis “Franny” Lee. I grew up in Manchester and from as early as I could answer the challenge – “which club do you support?” – it was always City for me. My dad took me, fast-walking, hand-in-hand, to big matches in the 1970s, floodlit glory nights of my boyhood. I have always loved the colour blue, especially sky blue, and have never really worn anything red in my life.

For supporters of my generation, the only trophy City won was the 1976 League Cup, claimed with a wondrous overhead “bicycle” kick goal by our winger, Dennis Tueart. I like art as much as the next ignoramus, but the photograph of Tueart’s goal must be the picture I have gazed at more than any other: the perfection of it, Tueart’s straight back in mid-air, arcing the ball behind him into the Wembley net, Newcastle’s opposition defenders frozen in time for ever.

But unlike Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, City never had a period of sustained success. They compressed a golden age into two years, 1968-70, and soon after that League Cup triumph, they were relegated, in 1983. For years, while City fans became celebrated for their loyalty and sod-it humour – taking bananas and other inflatables to matches – there always remained a mournful yearning for success to return.

When Lee finally took City over, acclaimed by all supporters, it seemed like deliverance. As a fan in the old Maine Road stadium, I cheered him on Saturday, then as a journalist on Monday I pestered for an interview. They agreed, and I was escorted behind the scenes, along some threadbare corridors into the chairman’s office, where Franny sat glowing behind the desk.

Everybody involved was so delighted to have pulled it off that they shared details quite gleefully. And that was when I first understood that Manchester City wasn’t a club at all. It was a company, with “owners”, and this had been a corporate acquisition. Franny was one of many other business people, a consortium, who had bought the shares.

Later, one of the lawyers proudly showed me some corporate engineering they had done. They had formed a holding company, Manchester City plc, that would own the old football club company.

The new millions from Rupert Murdoch’s Sky TV had poured into the Premier League, a breakaway in 1992 by the top clubs from sharing TV money with the clubs in the other three divisions of the Football League. This boosted the value of the top club-companies, and the new consortium planned to float City on the stock exchange, like Manchester United and others, where ultimately their shares could then be sold at a profit.

I learned that holding companies were formed to bypass the longstanding rules of the Football Association – the game’s governing body – that restricted shareholders being paid dividends, and directors a salary. The FA imposed those at the dawn of professional football in 1892, allowing clubs to form limited liability companies, but limiting the personal money shareholders could make.

This was to retain the collective, service ethos of a club. A century on, the rules were still in the FA’s handbook, at No 34. To the relatively small but formidable core of people who really care about these principles, “rule 34” became totemic of football’s sell-off, surrendered to enable vast personal gains by investors. That was now deemed antiquated, blazers’ bureaucracy that must not restrain football’s new business dynamism. To me, it was all a gut punch.

This critique was put forcefully to Labour’s football taskforce, with calls by the Football Supporters’ Association for strong regulation to harness the benefits of the new era. Fans understood that German football’s response to the pay TV transformation was to permit corporate reorganisations, but require clubs to be controlled “50% plus one” by mutual supporters associations.

New Labour was never going to introduce a football regulator or major reforms, but Burnham worked hard for concrete improvements.

The Premier League agreed to distribute 5% of its TV deal to improving desolate grassroots playing facilities via a new grant-giving body, the Football Foundation, which has been transformative. Burnham also championed mutual fan ownership of clubs, helping to establish an organisation, Supporters Direct, to promote it.

But the impossible cost for fans of buying and sustaining their clubs has meant over the years that few are mutually owned. The Premier League roared on, and the sell-offs became more corporate. Some original shareholders made fortunes selling, mostly to US investors: about £90m by Martin Edwards at Manchester United; £90m by the Littlewoods pools heir David Moores for selling his Liverpool shares.

Lee and his consortium never managed it, though, and City were relegated to football’s third tier in 1998. Famously he said City would have won a room full of trophies “if cups were awarded for cock-ups”.

Mansour’s acquisition of Manchester City 10 years later can be seen as the pure essence of “Manchesterism” – spending public money on cultural assets and infrastructure to attract business investors – long before Burnham became mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017 and coined that word this year. The splendid new stadium was built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games with £127m from Manchester city council and the national lottery, the council spending £22m on removing the athletics track and conversion for City to move in. The plan was part of the regeneration of east Manchester, where industry had cranked and smoked, then died in the 1980s.

The council leaders could hardly have imagined that cups-for-cock-ups Manchester City would then attract one of the world’s richest buyers, and the oil wealth of the Gulf. But the Premier League’s global ubiquity, the new stadium and the loyal City crowd all added up for Abu Dhabi.

If you set aside the glaring concerns about the ruler of a country taking over a local heritage football club, the human rights and geopolitical complications that introduces, and the central dissonance of clubs being owned by investors at all, Mansour has been a dream for Manchester. He has poured billions into the club, to attract, buy and pay the world’s best players and the best manager, Pep Guardiola.

His new corporate regime expanded the stadium – named Etihad under a sponsorship deal with the Abu Dhabi state airline, which has now complained that the Premier League’s communication of the commission’s findings has created “damaging implications” for it.

As Burnham acknowledged this week when he described the Abu Dhabi ownership as “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”, and gave thanks for the money put in, they have also invested in property development, converting long-derelict mills into apartments for young professionals Manchester was seeking to attract.

The dizzying findings of financial cheating were finally delivered this week from a Premier League investigation process that took eight years, which City repeatedly tried to block. City will appeal, and claim, as they have throughout, that they have “irrefutable evidence” disproving the findings of the three-person commission, which took almost two years.

At the core of Mansour’s ownership has been a ruthless determination not just to make his Premier League acquisition competitive, but to attain total domination. Before 2008, in 116 years of professional football, City only won the old First Division championship twice.

Mansour’s regime has secured the Premier League eight times so far, four FA Cup victories, and the pinnacle, the Champions League, in 2023. The League Cup, so rare and special to my generation, has been brought back from Wembley seven times.

Burnham has boldly broken with accepting Thatcher’s great sell-offs, saying they produced today’s fractures.

As he left the stage to applause and acclaim, football’s great sell-off was crashing to earth.
