‘Elon is my prophet’: how Musk’s Doge team took a wrecking ball to Washington

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 05:00:50 GMT

When the new ‘department of government efficiency’ sent young techies to disrupt federal agencies, not everyone complied. Here’s what happened when one worker fought to protect immigrant data

In the early hours of Saturday 22 February 2025 the following email landed in the inboxes of the entire US federal workforce:

From: HR hr@opm. gov

Sent: Saturday, February 22, 2025

Subject: What did you do last week?

Importance: High

Please reply to this email with approx. 5 bullets of what you accomplished last week and cc your manager.

Please do not send any classified information, links, or attachments.

Deadline is this Monday at 11:59 p. m. EST.

When she noticed the email that Saturday night, Kathleen Walters already had far too much going on in her life. Number one was figuring out if the lump in her breast that her doctor had just detected was a tumour. Half of her known blood relatives had died of cancer, and she was now 52: the lump needed understanding.

Her work life was harder to dramatise with a list. For a start, the specifics of her job at any given moment, as she would have been the first to point out, couldn’t legally be described to others. She was the chief privacy officer at the Internal Revenue Service. She ran a staff of 650 people tasked with preventing any of the 100,000 IRS employees from losing or leaking or even so much as peeking at, unless they had the authority to peek, any of the 266m tax returns they were just then processing from the previous year. “One hundred thousand people is a big-sized town,” said Kathleen. “In any big-sized town, you have some crazy people. I could easily see someone writing, ‘This weekend I audited Beyoncé.’”

Whoever had sent this email asking her to list five things she’d done at work was now demanding that all these people inside the IRS share information that, in many cases, should never be shared. She thought it was nuts.

She responded quickly, and vaguely, with five things she had done the previous week, all the while feeling sure no one would ever read what she wrote. Her phone was already exploding with questions from her subordinates – a few of whom were saying that their replies were bouncing back with a “mailbox is full” notice. Now she had to sit and think about how to minimise the damage that might be caused by 100,000 IRS employees thinking that they’d lose their jobs if they didn’t supply some detailed answer about what they’d done during their work week. A meaningful percentage risked being tossed in jail if they described what they did in an email. It was a crime for an IRS employee even to acknowledge that some specific person had or had not filed a tax return. “People don’t understand what the IRS does,” said Kathleen.

The email came as a surprise, but then the IRS was suddenly full of surprises. Nine days earlier, on 13 February, a Thursday, the first Doge person turned up in the lobby, unannounced, and security called Traci DiMartini, who ran the IRS’s human capital department. There’s a kid down here who said he needs to get into the building, he said. The kid’s name was Gavin Kliger.

Traci called her counterpart at the Treasury department, as the IRS sits inside Treasury, and Treasury always cleared any new political appointees; Treasury had no record of anyone named Gavin Kliger. Traci then called Tim Curry at the Office of Personnel Management – but he had no idea what was going on. Finally, she called security and asked them to escort the young man to her office.

Gavin Kliger came with a chip on his shoulder, it seemed to Traci. He offered not even the faintest smile or the most glancing eye contact. Dressed in black from hoodie to sneaker, he was brusque to the point of rudeness. He looked, and was, just a few years out of college. Eyes on the floor, he explained to Traci that he’d come to sort out the problems inside the IRS and to root out the fraud. “That’s a big job!” she said.

Anyone who worked at the IRS knew that it had its problems; fraud wasn’t likely one of them. Its technology infrastructure was a case study in government dysfunction, but its ethical infrastructure was sound. Like all federal employees, its staff wasn’t allowed to accept more than a free cup of coffee from anyone who might want something from their agency.

Gavin Kliger, in contrast, struck Traci as problematic. He’d somehow laid his hands on badges granting him access to some crazy number of government buildings. His backpack was stuffed with government-issue phones and at least four laptops – and he was now insisting that Traci supply him with an IRS phone and laptop. He also demanded his own IRS email address, access to computer systems with all the taxpayer information, and a meeting with the acting IRS commissioner, Doug O’Donnell. As Gavin sat there, Traci called Treasury again. That guy you said didn’t exist is now here sitting in my office. What do y’all want me to do with him?

The Treasury guy went away, then came back and said that Gavin Kliger had been hired three weeks earlier by the Office of Personnel Management and was attached to Doge – whatever that meant.

In her nine years running human capital departments at various federal agencies, Traci had never seen a new political appointee just turn up in the lobby and demand access to the computer systems. “None of this is normal,” she said, “but we’re still trying to be nice.” She explained to Gavin the IRS rules: before anyone was allowed to work inside the building, he needed to pass a tax audit.

I don’t need to do that, he said.

Yes, you do, she replied.

No, I don’t, he said.

Yes, you do, she replied.

They went back and forth like that a bit until finally Gavin relented. Traci then explained that after he passed the audit, he’d need to be given the mandatory presentations about ethics and taxpayer information. Gavin thought that the IRS should just let him in. “He wanted access to our systems immediately,” said Traci.

Traci’s next call, at 6.30pm that Thursday evening, was to Kathleen, to arrange for her to brief Gavin on data privacy laws and to warn her that the experience might not be entirely pleasant. If I had a kid who behaved the way he does, I’d slap the shit out of him, Traci said – but then Traci was from Philadelphia. Traci was always telling Kathleen that she should try a bit less hard to see the best in others.

By then word of Doge’s arrival at the IRS had spread, and Kathleen had read about them. Anyone who Googled Gavin’s name found a bit more than usually popped up about any given young Doge person. He’d grown up in southern California, where he was into Asian martial arts and the high-school marching band, then had gone on to the University of California at Berkeley. Graduating in 2020 with a degree in electrical engineering and computer science, he’d taken a job as a programmer at Databricks. He’d also been active on X, where he’d retweeted with apparent approval posts from the white nationalists Steve Laws and Nick Fuentes. “One of Musk’s few Doge lieutenants who has embraced the spotlight,” Forbes wrote of him. Most of the other Muskrats scrubbed the internet of their presence. Gavin had written Substack pieces defending two Trump nominees, Matt Gaetz and Pete Hegseth. He’d deleted his X posts, but the Forbes writer John Hyatt had found a research tool, Web. archive, to revive and analyse them. “What emerges is a portrait of an internet edgelord and Musk and Trump superfan who has disdain for government spending, illegal immigrants, and who enjoys the odd racist and ableist joke,” he wrote.

By the time Traci called her, Kathleen was gone for the weekend and 50 miles away from the IRS building: she needed to find someone else to do Gavin’s briefing. Kathleen was white; the two women immediately below her were Black. “They’d both already read about him and were both already uncomfortable,” said Kathleen. Phyllis Grimes, her deputy, agreed to fall on the hand grenade.

Phyllis, who loved working for Kathleen and saw falling on hand grenades as part of her job, never told her how this one had felt. She knew Gavin had expressed enthusiasm for white nationalists, and he likely knew that she knew. She tried to break the ice by walking in with her hand extended; Gavin stared at it and declined to shake it, though he had shaken the hands of the white men who had offered them. “He was kind of cool towards me,” said Phyllis. Before she could even start the briefing, he said, You know, I’ve heard these rules before at other agencies. Yes, she said, but these rules are different, because no other agency is governed by this privacy law, and this law can get you thrown in jail very quickly. As she walked him through the basics – how you can’t use your personal phone for business, how if you happen to so much as glimpse a form 1040 with someone’s name on it you must avert your eyes – Gavin played on his phone. “He’s multitasking right in front of me, typing and texting,” said Phyllis. “It was, here’s a routine that I must endure.”

It fell to Kathleen to draft the five-page agreement required by law for Gavin Kliger to be let inside the IRS building on Monday morning, 17 February. The memo that she wrote over the weekend, and that he signed, gave him access to some of the systems but, explicitly, none that contained taxpayer information.

Traci set him up in a conference room with an assistant at the beginning of the week. “People started getting these calls,” said Kathleen. “It was like getting the call from the principal’s office. ‘Gavin wants to see you.’ ”

Doge had its own private structure in addition to its official one. Officially, President Trump created Doge with an executive order on his first day in office. The president doesn’t have the authority to create or to fund an executive agency, however. Congress does. The Trump administration dodged that problem by taking an office inside the White House created during the second Obama term, the US Digital Service, kicking out the people inside and renaming it the Department of Government Efficiency. The US Digital Service had been given the power to hire talent from the tech sector without going through the usual slow federal hiring process. This now ensured that Doge could hire whomever it wanted without any questions being asked, and make it sound official. In effect, all that Doge had done was create a corpse for itself to occupy.

The zombie killed off the spirit of the original life form. Real Doge had nothing to do with Official Doge or the former US Digital Service or any other government body. Real Doge was more like Elon Musk’s pop-up restaurant. “None of us ever signed a piece of paper saying that we were in Doge,” said one Doge insider. The people who joined either worked for one of Musk’s companies, or knew someone who did, or knew someone who knew someone who did. To be truly a member of Doge was to be included in the group Signal chat and granted access to the sleeping quarters on the sixth floor of the General Services Administration (GSA).

Official Doge employed maybe 10 guys in their 40s and 50s who wore suits and could sort of pass as ordinary political appointees, but none had access to the sixth floor at GSA. “The older guys in the suits were not there to take risks or blow things up,” said one Doge insider. It was hard to say what any of the older Doge suits did except to make way for the young guys when they showed up with explosives.

Most of Doge’s inner circle just wanted to exist in the presence of Elon Musk. “It was, Elon is my prophet, and I worship the ground he walks on,” said one of the older Doge insiders.

As a Doge member, you could get away with saying – or having said – almost anything. What you couldn’t say is that the government actually sort of worked. Or, if it didn’t work, why it didn’t work. This new game rewarded not understanding but speed. The plan was the same plan Musk had executed two years earlier at Twitter: Make sweeping statements about the incompetence and dishonesty of the people working inside the place before you know much about them. Once you’ve terrified the employees, fire them in huge numbers. If it turns out you screwed up and fired the wrong people, hire some of them back.

The people who rallied to the cause and felt qualified to execute Elon Musk’s vision for the federal government shared certain qualities. They were mostly young white males. They were mostly from upper-middle-class or rich families. Most knew or pretended to know how to program a computer. Not all of them, but enough of them for there to be a pattern, had been rejected from the most selective colleges and universities and ended up feeling they’d been screwed by the admissions process. They landed at Penn instead of Princeton, or the University of Nebraska instead of Harvard, with a grievance that added to the foundation of their politics. They thought of themselves as the smartest people in the room and couldn’t understand why the rest of the room didn’t simply stand up and cheer. In Washington they borrowed from Elon Musk their status and sense of superiority. They also seemed to share his pleasure in the idea of people being afraid of them.

Even among the young men sleeping inside the GSA, Gavin was regarded as a force. “Wherever he went, entropy went through the roof,” said one. Just weeks into their new jobs as destroyers of government institutions, the Muskrats had given Gavin Kliger a nickname: the Chaos Agent.

Another surprising email landed in Kathleen’s inbox on 28 February. It was Friday night. “I don’t know why everything always happened on a Friday night,” she said. She’d taken her daughter for pizza and wasn’t meant to be checking her phone when she spotted the emails. The first one that she read had been sent at 6.34pm by a colleague in the IRS legal department. “Melanie requested a data pull,” it read. “It feels not quite kosher.”

Exactly 64 minutes earlier, at 5.30pm, Doug O’Donnell, the acting IRS commissioner, had left his post. O’Donnell’s successor was to be Melanie Krause, until then chief operating officer, who had been installed as acting IRS commissioner by Treasury secretary Scott Bessent. Like Kathleen, Melanie was a career civil servant, though 13 years younger. Kathleen had considered her a friend. “She was really smart, and I thought she meant well,” said Kathleen. “She wasn’t a mean person.” They were both working moms, and Melanie liked to share, and share in, the details of the difficulties. Now she’d apparently told the IRS research department to share taxpayer data. With whom, and for what purpose, became clear in the second email, which came from the IRS director of data management:

Kathleen,

DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] has requested if we could find addresses for 700,000 names of likely undocumented immigrants.

1. Do we have legal authority to use the tax return filing data for this purpose?

2. If the answer to Question 1 is yes, then my second question is related to a file we receive from the Social Security Administration (SSA) that contains Date of Birth (DOB), Date of Death (DOD), Gender, Citizenship, and Name Control Information for all issued Social Security Numbers (SSN). Would our MOU allow us to use this perhaps in conjunction to tax return data for this purpose?

While it is likely that use of SSA data is also needed. The technical feasibility of being able to produce reliable outcome is unknown but likely very low.

Thanks

Kathleen read the first numbered paragraph and stopped reading. The request was plainly illegal. The IRS couldn’t just hand over great gobs of taxpayer information to the Department of Homeland Security or any other agency without a change in federal privacy law. Changing the law was not trivial. She knew that because she’d just done it – to allow the IRS to share taxpayer data with state child support enforcement agencies. The states wanted to know if former spouses who were failing to pay child support in fact did not have the income to do so – and the IRS alone could answer the question. What Kathleen had asked for in that case could not have been less controversial. Basically no one in American politics was willing to come out against child support enforcement, and the change to the federal law had passed Congress in December 2024 with almost no dissent. Yet it had taken 18 months to get it done, with endless meetings on Capitol Hill and the close involvement of the IRS commissioner and the secretary of health and human services. “Doge couldn’t imagine 18 months,” she said. “Doge didn’t have 18 months. Their whole thing was, If you can’t do it legally, we’ll find some way to do it illegally.”

This, Kathleen realised, is how they could grab taxpayer data illegally. By doing it on a Friday night. Using a woman, Melanie Krause, about to take over as acting commissioner, after a 10-minute meeting between her and Scott Bessent. Without informing the executive charged with protecting the information. “She went around me because she knew what my answer is,” said Kathleen.

The violation ran deeper than the law. The specific dataset sought by DHS was in a silo reserved for the tax returns filed by people without social security numbers. The IRS had created the so-called Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (Itin) back in 1996 as a mechanism for undocumented workers and other non-citizens who lacked social security numbers to file a return and pay taxes.

The programme had been a huge success. The IRS had collected hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes through it. Undocumented workers had been able to demonstrate their commitment to the country, and ease their path to citizenship, by paying more than their fair share. (They were still excluded from most federal benefits.) Now DHS wanted their private data, and it wasn’t hard for Kathleen or anyone else at the IRS to see why. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) had gone hunting undocumented workers but lacked reliable home addresses for many of them. The tax returns told you where roughly 7 million of them might be found.

The second Trump administration had a gift for creating such moments. It was as if all at once all these characters in a grand masked ball were forced to remove their disguises and reveal their identities. In the Great Unmasking, the nation’s leading law firms, led by Paul, Weiss, would cave to what amounted to Trump’s blackmail demands to avoid being shut out of federal business. The nation’s research universities, led by Columbia, would change their internal policies and even pay fines to avoid losing federal dollars.

The revealing moments in the civil service were lonelier. They occurred inside people’s hearts and minds, and seldom leaked to the press. After his arrival at the IRS, one of Gavin Kliger’s first acts had been to demand that the agency fire its 6,700 probationary workers, who had yet to be granted civil service protection. By law they could be fired only for poor performance. Gavin had asked Traci DiMartini, in her capacity as head of human resources, to agree to put her name on an email to the mostly young employees telling them that they had failed at their jobs. The Doge people played this trick often. They’d use or try to use civil servants as a kind of ventriloquist dummy so that they, the Doge workers, could keep their names off official documents. But Traci took one look at the email, saw it was plainly a lie, and refused to have anything to do with it. The price of that single act of resistance was her job. Gavin didn’t have the authority to fire Traci, but his new acting commissioner did. “He asked Melanie to fire Traci, and Melanie did it,” said Kathleen.

Melanie Krause’s predecessor, Doug O’Donnell, had been pushed out by Doge after he, too, refused to send the dishonest email to the IRS’s 6,700 probationary workers. When a Doge guy at Treasury called with the order, O’Donnell, who had worked for the agency for 38 years, said he wanted to sleep on it – then had trouble sleeping. “He was struggling with this notion of sending the termination emails with this false justification for the termination,” said a person in whom O’Donnell confided. The next day, he refused to send the email, and the Doge guy said something like, “Well, let me be the first to congratulate you on your retirement.” Melanie had been installed precisely because she was proving to Doge that she was more pliable.

Standing outside the pizza place with her daughter in late February, Kathleen called Melanie. Ever since Melanie had arrived, in the fall of 2021, she had sought Kathleen’s advice. There had been stretches when they met daily. Kathleen just sort of assumed that, faced with a difficult choice, Melanie would do what Kathleen herself would do. “I don’t really get outraged,” said Kathleen. “But I think people need to be confronted when they have done something inappropriate.”

Melanie, what are you doing? she asked. We already have legal opinions about this, and it is obviously against the law.

I didn’t tell them to do it, said Melanie. I told them to think about how to do it – if it was legal.

But she hadn’t asked anyone to find out if it was legal to send Ice the home addresses of 700,000 undocumented workers – culled, somehow, from the 7 million who had paid taxes. She’d told them to send the data over, on a Friday night. In such a way that Kathleen might never have heard about it – or heard too late.

It’s not going to be any more legal on Saturday, said Kathleen.

Let’s meet on Monday to clear things up, said Melanie.

They didn’t meet. Instead, on Monday – 3 March – Kathleen and several other top IRS leaders were called into a meeting with Gavin Kliger.

I’ve figured out something important about the IRS, Gavin said. He paused for effect.

Oh no, thought Kathleen.

Every agency has a superpower, said Gavin. The IRS’s superpower is data.

Everyone in the agency knew that its data was valuable. That was the reason for the strict laws that prevented it from being exploited for profit or political gain. “He said this in a way that he expected everyone to clap when he was done,” said Kathleen.

“No one said a word.” The people around the table – a group that included a woman who had worked at the IRS for 54 years, or 53 years and 50 weeks longer than Gavin Kliger – looked down, or away. Kathleen felt embarrassed for Gavin Kliger. But now it was clear what the meeting was about. Gavin wanted, in his words, “to explore how we can share our data with other agencies”.

Interestingly, he never once mentioned Ice or DHS. Instead, that week, he sought to share data with himself, by trying to access files detailing IRS contracts with outside consultants that also contained taxpayer information. Kathleen denied him access.

The following Monday, she received a cryptic text from a senior IRS official. I’m going to call your cell, but don’t answer, it read. Her phone rang and she dutifully stared at it. Then came the second text: Gavin is asking where your office is and is now trying to find you to fire you because he says you’re the blocker.

The Blocker! It was one of Elon’s favourite terms. The blocker was the person who didn’t understand progress. The person without vision. The person who could not see beyond the way things were to the way they ought to be. The person who didn’t want to live on Mars or possibly even care if anyone ever got there. The inferior person. Traci had been a blocker. Find the blockers between us and what we want, Elon told his young followers. Find the blockers and eliminate them. Maybe more than anything else, Doge wanted the data. Kathleen was the person blocking them from getting it.

She wasn’t sure what she’d done to anger Gavin. It could have been limiting his access to the procurement contracts. It could also have been pushing back on his request to grant Palantir, Doge’s favourite federal contractor, the right to work with taxpayer data. What Gavin’s issue likely was not was her resistance to handing over to the Department of Homeland Security the addresses of taxpayers who lacked social security numbers. Gavin had never brought that up; this particular attempt to break the law wasn’t his idea. It was coming from somewhere else. As she thought she had stopped it, she ceased to worry about it.

And so, roughly two weeks later, on Thursday, 27 March, she was caught completely off guard by an email chain that popped up on her screen. At the bottom was its origin: a note from Melanie, forwarding some document from the IRS legal department, along with what sounded like an innocuous request. “Kathleen, could you help facilitate I won’t be able to join today?” it read, without explaining what she was meant to facilitate or why Melanie wouldn’t be able to join. Scrolling through, Kathleen couldn’t find the document but did see lots of bewildered replies from others who had been included – What is this about? Happy to help but can you tell us what this is? She called the two young lawyers in the IRS legal office who had authored the document referred to in the chain that had somehow gone missing. They explained that the thing Melanie wanted Kathleen to facilitate was a memorandum of understanding for the IRS to share taxpayer data with DHS. Kathleen was knocked sideways. “I thought that it had been stopped,” she said. “I thought Melanie had been caught with her pants down.” The young lawyers now told her that not only had it not been stopped: they’d been working on it since the end of February. “They told me that they were sorry but Melanie had told them to do it and not to tell me or their boss,” said Kathleen.

The situation was obviously bizarre. Kathleen had never heard of an IRS director asking young IRS lawyers to work on something on the side without telling their boss. And if Melanie didn’t want Kathleen to know that she was handing IRS data to DHS, why had she suddenly included her in the conversation? “I think she got scared and dumped it on me to sign off on,” said Kathleen. Melanie was doing to Kathleen what Gavin Kliger had done to Traci DiMartini. She was presenting her with her own unmasking moment and forcing her to make a choice.

Instead of signing off, Kathleen arranged a Zoom call that day, with the people at the Department of Homeland Security who were requesting the data. The “ICE Innovation Lab”, they called themselves. She’d never heard of it. When she Googled it, nothing came up.

A few others joined the call – lawyers from DHS and a privacy lawyer at the IRS named Julie Schwartz. On the call, Kathleen explained that there were some very narrow circumstances that would allow the IRS to lend a hand. If, for example, an undocumented worker had murdered someone and the police had issued a warrant for his arrest. The Ice Innovators explained that they were looking for more than wanted criminals. “Just how many people do you want information on?” asked Kathleen. The Ice Innovators went back and forth between themselves before agreeing that the number was 7 million. They wanted the current addresses of 7 million undocumented workers who had paid their taxes. The most law-abiding, it turned out, might be the easiest to catch.

After the call, Julie, the IRS privacy lawyer, came straight to her office. Julie was usually ice-calm – someone who kept her wits about her. She hadn’t a trace of drama in her. But now Julie was not calm. Kathleen, after that call I’m not working on this thing, she said. I’m not coming in tomorrow. I might not come in Monday. I might not come in ever again.

“I don’t usually deal with life or death stuff,” said Kathleen. “But this was life or death stuff. At that moment I knew I had to quit. Either that or I’m going to get fired, because I can’t facilitate something that will break the law and is going to hurt people. We all have boundaries. That was my boundary.”

That weekend, Kathleen sent Melanie a note saying she’d be resigning. “I didn’t need to tell her why,” said Kathleen. “She knew why.” She’d be leaving just weeks before her 20th anniversary with the agency. If she’d waited until mid-May, she would have been able to retire and receive benefits for the rest of her life. But she didn’t want to retire. Federal law made it hard for a retired civil servant to return, and if the day ever came when the IRS was rebuilt, she wanted to be able to return. She’d just learned that the lump in her breast was benign.

Days later, Melanie beat Kathleen to it and resigned. Kathleen never figured out how much her note to Melanie – and with it the increased likelihood that the attempted data heist would wind up in the press – led Melanie to quit. On her way out the door, Melanie asked the IRS’s head of communications to plant a story in the Washington Post that she was leaving as a matter of principle. The story cast Melanie as a martyr who had quit rather than divulge IRS data to DHS, when Kathleen knew that she had been caught red-handed trying to do precisely that. “I completely misjudged her character,” said Kathleen.

The Ice agents came for the “illegals” long after the property managers had gone home. The only evidence left behind were grainy videos on security cameras and accounts of terrified residents. “They’re coming in the nights, unannounced,” said Antonio Marquez, who ran a company that owned and managed apartment buildings scattered across the south and south-western United States occupied mostly by lower-middle-income Latinos. “We don’t know how they are targeting the units. It’s wreaking complete havoc.”

Antonio’s apartment complex outside Austin houses a thousand people, mostly young families, at least half of whom are undocumented. It had been visited in the spring late at night by teams of Ice agents. They came in unmarked cars, reported the tenants who remained after the raid. They had no warrants and read no rights. They knew, or thought they knew, exactly which doors to jimmy and which locks to pick and which people to take. The next morning a bunch of tenants were simply gone. All that remained was a pile of discarded possessions.

After the first Austin raid, Antonio had erected a tall metal fence around the property. Occasionally, the Ice agents had taken fully documented tenants – including an older woman who always paid on time, and who returned from Ice custody in an ankle bracelet. The great mystery to Antonio was how Ice knew where people lived. “These are fully targeted,” he said. “They already had these people in mind. They have their addresses. And we don’t know how they’re getting them.”

He was too busy doing his job to notice when, on 11 February 2026, the Washington Post reported that the IRS had shared with the Department of Homeland Security the tax data of 47,000 undocumented workers. On the heels of the Post’s scoop, a federal judge hearing a case on the subject summoned the IRS lawyers who had previously sworn that the agency had rebuffed the DHS demands. Under questioning, the lawyers confessed that the agency had lied to the court and that it had in fact shared the data. “The IRS violated the [Internal Revenue Code] approximately 42,695 times by disclosing last known taxpayer addresses to Ice,” the judge wrote in her opinion.

On a hot, sunny afternoon in early March in north-east Austin, it is a lot quieter than it was a year ago, back when Kathleen Walters was still a blocker. Two small children play in a pool, and a worn middle-aged man squats warily in a corner, smoking a cigarette. The wall of the office where the remaining residents come for their mail is decorated with posters advertising the services that Antonio’s company offers. One is more official-looking than the others. Free File del IRS, it reads across the top – and just below, in finer print, it explains how easy and painless it is for a non-citizen to file their taxes.

This is an edited extract from Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis, published by Allen Lane (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Both Gavin Kliger and Melanie Krause declined to be interviewed for the book. Gavin Kliger declined an invitation to comment for this extract. Melanie Krause says that as a non-partisan public servant, “I did my job with integrity, honesty, and transparency”. She denies instructing anyone to send taxpayer information to the DHS or telling lawyers to work on a data-sharing agreement with the agency. She says that refusing to put her name on an email was not the reason for terminating IRS head of human resources Tracy DiMartini. She adds: “I never agreed or wanted to divulge IRS data to DHS. I resigned for personal reasons after I learned that the Department of Treasury had signed such an agreement.”

Five Great Reads: ICE 2.0, millennial motherhood, and skinny-dipping with Christine Baranski

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 22:08:31 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

The Guardian’s range was on display this week across these five very different stories. Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.

Enjoy.

At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets. After officers killed two US citizens during the raids in Minneapolis, public backlash prompted Trump to try a new approach. Now, ICE arrests have hit record levels. In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.

Notable quote: “Before, they were storming around, making a lot of noise Now, they are moving more quietly.”

The violence continues: People are arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home. Recently, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Texas. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents. ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before, despite the new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, promising to avoid negative headlines by cutting the flash and fanfare.

How long will it take to read: Under four minutes.

Further reading: All the stories from the series ICE 2.0: inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet.

Women today are more educated, more employed and more engaged in childcare arrangements than ever before. But research shows that the expectations facing modern mothers continue to grow. In Australia, the statistics illuminate a global phenomenon. New research shows that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has grown by only 102% in the same period.

Between juggling rising costs and managing careers, is there any way out of the total overwhelm?

A problem with no solution: In this personal piece, Kate Lyons writes that millennial women no longer feel trapped in their homes like generations before, but rather, by the impossible juggle of managing their career, relationships and children. Lyons recounts a friend reaching out for advice late one night after their five-year-old had a meltdown before bed. Another woman Lyons spoke to got so desperate she turned towards ChatGPT, asking the AI chatbot how to make her life work. But solutions are not easy to come by. After Lyons assessed the state of her living room, which, “looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them”, all she could offer was solidarity.

Notable quote: “It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.”

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: Why birthrates are plummeting, and why workplaces were built for men.

Polls show that Donald Trump is losing support with the bros that got him elected. As the midterms approach, the cost of living and the war on Iran have left male voters increasingly disillusioned. So how does one win them back? The health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, seem to think the hormone testosterone, often known simply as “T”, is the answer. Or as Sam Wolfson explains, Trump is hoping that “the male populace will vote not with their heads or their hearts, but with their hogs”.

The testosterone dog-whistle: Testosterone is found in the bodies of men and women, with a low amount all that is needed for normal function. But the hormone has emerged on the frontlines of the Trump administration’s many culture wars. While the war in Iran causes problems for Trump back home, Hegseth has shifted the military message to one of machismo. On the campaign trail, he said, “We’re reminding our warriors that their sole purpose is to be the most lethal fighting force on the planet. Full stop. We’re not here to do social engineering, or social justice, or gender-bending, or DEI, or dudes and dresses.” But Wolfson writes that Hegseth’s testosterone push is a “sciencey” way to dog-whistle his sexist message.

Notable quote: “Everything has been politicized in the United States. Vaccines are liberal and TRT is Maga. The needle is apolitical but the content of the syringe is decided by who you vote for.”

How long will it take to read: eight minutes.

after newsletter promotion

Further reading: The Pentagon and “incel” slang, plus RFK Jr’s “peptide wild west”.

Patricia Nilsson was determined to bring porn industry leaders out of the shadows. For five years, she subjected the adult industry to forensic analysis in an effort to reveal who was getting rich through porn and how they were doing it. For decades, the owners of these companies have escaped scrutiny, and they have often enjoyed relative anonymity. But porn is everywhere, and for many young men and women, adult content can be their default sex education. Nilsson argues the owners of businesses that are recalibrating our sexual culture deserve further investigation.

Notable quote: “My argument is not that we should be neutral towards porn, but that we need to accept and understand it as a real industry, and ask what its growth and popularity says about the state of our economy and the world of work.”

The story of porn is the story of the internet: Nilsson argues that even if you do not consume explicit content online, the industry has shaped the way you interact with the digital world. We have porn to thank, she says, for high-quality video streaming and the way influencers sell their online personas. “Staring at content that is algorithmically engineered to arouse you is a perfect metaphor for our relationship with our devices and the internet and social media,” Nilsson says.

How long will it take to read: About five minutes.

Further reading: The malignant rise of OnlyFans managers and the rise of deepfake pornography in schools.

Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant have stories to tell. The actors have joined forces for the first time in a London production of Noël Coward’s comedic play Hay Fever. The Guardian sat down with the actors to get a glimpse of the tall tales told backstage.

Notable quote: When asked if she has ever worked with Grant before, Baranski wryly says: “Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans.”

Skinny dipping in the dark: Recalling her “marvellous house” on a lake in Connecticut, Baranski recounts an evening spent with Mark Rylance when the pair went skinny-dipping and ended up howling at the moon till four in the morning. Pressed on whether taking your clothes off is a prerequisite for visiting, Baranski says: “I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark.”

How long will it take to read: five minutes of gossipy joy.

Further reading: How Richard E Grant ended up on Celebrity Traitors.

The Guardian view on the Conservative conference: a party still searching for a purpose

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:51:19 GMT

Kemi Badenoch has a lot to say about Labour and Reform UK but none of it amounts to a coherent alternative programme for government

The Conservative party is far from the margin of British politics, but it has yet to recover the relevance to which it feels historically entitled. The Tories are flattered by their status as the official opposition in parliament. In the wider country, Reform UK has set the agenda on the right, overtaking Kemi Badenoch’s party in opinion polls and poaching MPs from her benches.

But Nigel Farage’s progress has stalled. Scrutiny of Reform’s finances has made its leader look shifty. Competition from Restore Britain, an extreme nationalist party, has denied Mr Farage the luxury of taking far-right votes for granted. Pandering to a hardcore audience makes it difficult for Reform to affect the moderation required to capture more Tory and Labour votes.

This creates an opportunity for Conservatives to reassert themselves as the mainstream opposition to Labour. Many Tories believe the available space has grown since Andy Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.

Mr Burnham has a bolder agenda than his predecessor, and he communicates it well – qualities that have been rewarded with a poll-ratings recovery. It is also a programme with unapologetic left-liberal ambition – universal social care, free at the point of use; opening the door to public ownership of utilities; dissolving red lines in relations with the EU; electoral reform. Under new leadership, the party has risen out of the defensive crouch from which it fought the election, fearful of offending Conservative sensibilities. Conservatives are duly offended. The vision that Mr Burnham outlined at his party conference last week was a repudiation of Margaret Thatcher’s legacy, and there is no greater heresy in Tory doctrine.

Mrs Badenoch will not struggle to articulate a rebuttal at her party’s conference in Birmingham over the next few days. She is a devotee of the Conservative cult of the Iron Lady, committed to low taxes and a smaller state as axioms of political virtue. She believes there are voters who share that conviction, who will be repelled by Labour, and who are deeply wary of Mr Farage. This is the electoral audience she is targeting.

It isn’t an irrational strategy, but nor is it a well-developed one. Mrs Badenoch likes to debate the opponent she wants rather than the one she has. She accuses Mr Burnham of taking Britain back to the 1970s, without engaging with his analysis of what went wrong in the 1980s or considering that her own nostalgic ideology might need revision with reference to subsequent decades.

Her approach to Reform is even more blinkered. The Tories want voters to take a dim view of Mr Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister, but they are selective in their criticism. Mrs Badenoch joins the fray over opaque donations, but has less to say about Reform’s toxic rhetoric around immigration, largely because Conservative policy fits the Faragist mould. The traffic in defections has slowed, but the boundary between the two parties is porous.

To make her party competitive in British politics, Mrs Badenoch needs more serious arguments. She needs an answer to Mr Burnham that doesn’t retreat into lazy 20th-century political cliche. And she needs to reject Mr Farage’s brand of national populism in terms that give voters reasons to distinguish between their two parties on points of principle, when at the moment there are none.

The Guardian view on Barack Obama’s new podcast: all the president’s books

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:50:35 GMT

From Oprah Winfrey to Dua Lipa, there is no shortage of celebrity literary champions. But the former US leader is in a class of his own

At the Labour party conference Andy Burnham revealed that Hamlet, Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness and Tony Harrison’s poem V are his favourite works of literature. The UK’s first prime minister with an English literature degree was not the only political figure sharing his book choices last week. Barack Obama, the US’s most literary president since Abraham Lincoln, launched a new podcast in which he discusses six books that shaped him with writer friends.

First up was the actor – and recently turned short story writer – Tom Hanks on Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, a meditation on faith, fatherhood and forgiveness in the form of a letter written by a 76-year-old pastor to his son. It was an unabashedly highbrow start. With the exception of John le Carré’s cold war classic Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, Mr Obama’s selections are American: Toni Morrison’s Song of Solomon, Cormac McCarthy’s All the Pretty Horses, James Baldwin’s essays The Fire Next Time and Robert Penn Warren’s All the King’s Men. Questions of democracy, race, power and violence are all here.

The former president’s summer and end-of-year reading lists are known for having an “Obama effect” on sales. This season’s picks include the Booker-shortlisted The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, of whom he has long been a fan. His podcast, A Great Book with Barack Obama, joins a crowded arena. Established celebrity book clubs include those run by Oprah Winfrey and Reese Witherspoon in the US and Richard and Judy in the UK. These are now competing with starry newcomers, such as Dua Lipa’s Service95, appealing to gen Z readers. The British singer’s conversations with bookish heavyweights have seen her hailed as “the best literary interviewer” of our time. Audiences can decide for themselves this month when she is curator and host of the London literature Festival at the Southbank Centre, with guests including Zadie Smith.

With reading for pleasure among young people at its lowest level in two decades, high-profile champions have an important role to play – even if celebrity endorsements are sometimes accompanied by a whiff of elitism. Back in 2001, Jonathan Franzen caused a furore by snubbing an invitation for The Corrections to be featured on Oprah’s Book Club, deriding her choices as “schmaltzy” and “one-dimensional”. The announcement that Lipa would give the Booker prize ceremony speech in 2022 raised eyebrows in the industry. Yet a recommendation from Winfrey or Lipa can catapult a novel on to the bestseller lists.

You don’t need to be a pop star or president to become a literary tastemaker. Online communities such as BookTok and Bookstagram have democratised the book world. Everyone can be a critic today. As the rise of romantasy novels shows, bookfluencers are a powerful new force in publishing.

But in a speeded-up world, books podcasts are a balm for the soul. They can boost debuts, resurface old classics and rescue forgotten treasures. The path from politics to podcasting is now a well-trodden one. But an in-depth literary podcast from a former US president is a first, and not likely to be seconded anytime soon. “There are jokes about the Trump library,” Robinson quipped in 2018. “Because there won’t be any books in there.” For Mr Obama, reading helps to create “a moral framework” and is “a way of understanding the challenges of the moment”. Rarely have literary-minded leaders been so urgently needed.

The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:40:45 GMT

The resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism works

Tomorrow I will be in synagogue to say Kaddish, the traditional mourner’s prayer, in memory of my father who died eight years ago this week. If I were a member of the Green party, I would have reason to believe that that simple act could soon see me expelled as a racist.

It sounds hyperbolic, but the warning comes from Green party activists opposed to a resolution declaring that Zionism is racism, which will be debated at the party conference this weekend. The motion, which if passed would instantly become party policy, holds that Zionism should be “treated as any other form of racism”. On that logic, given that the Greens do not admit members of self-described racist organisations, they could not tolerate members of self-described Zionist organisations – a category that includes almost every synagogue, or synagogue movement, in Britain and indeed the world. Which is why saying Kaddish could lead to expulsion.

All this sounds arcane, but the Greens are no longer a fringe party. They beat Labour in a byelection in February, one of the events that catalysed the eventual removal of Keir Starmer. The Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, hopes to win Starmer’s former seat of Holborn and St Pancras in next Thursday’s byelection. But the row over Zionism has cast a cloud over his campaign. If he loses the seat, many will conclude that the Green surge is over – which would relieve a significant electoral headache for Labour and Andy Burnham. So the stakes are high.

The charitable reading is that this move originates in genuine, and widespread, horror at Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, followed by a series of unfortunate misunderstandings of what Zionism is, who Jews are and how antisemitism works.

That, I repeat, is the charitable reading, but let’s go with it. It’s worth saying that if the proposers of this motion had simply wanted to express their revulsion at the catastrophic devastation of Gaza and those who executed it, they could have denounced Israel and the Israeli government. But their admitted purpose is to go much further – to attack Israel’s very existence and the movement that led to it: Zionism.

As Polanski, who has been twisting in all directions on this subject, has tried to argue, Zionism means different things to different people. The great Israeli writer and peacenik Amos Oz used to describe it as a family name, an umbrella for a wide range of radically different worldviews. Before Israel’s founding in 1948, you’d have cultural Zionists slugging it out with religious Zionists, Marxist Zionists raging against rightwing militaristic Zionists, all of them wholly at odds with the dominant group: socialist Zionists. What they had in common was the simple belief that Jews had the right of self-determination in their ancestral homeland, the land they had for millennia called Eretz Yisrael, the Land of Israel, and which the rest of the world called Palestine.

To this day, that’s essentially what it means to be a Zionist – that you believe in a Jewish national home in some portion of historic Palestine. There are rightwing Zionists who think it should be in all of that land; there are leftwing Zionists who think it should be broadly within the much smaller boundaries that existed before the 1967 war and alongside a Palestinian state. But both groups are Zionists. The racist minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is a Zionist, but so are many of the Jewish and Israeli anti-occupation activists who volunteer to act as a “protective presence”, putting their own bodies between settler extremists and Palestinian villagers in the West Bank. To brand everyone under that one umbrella as a racist shows a deep ignorance of what the word Zionism means and the sheer range of people who identify with it.

It also reveals a wilful misunderstanding of Jews and Judaism. Social media has been full in recent days of supposedly progressive non-Jews telling Jews what Judaism is and what it is not – with an arrogance that, I suspect, they would find unacceptable iin a majority group addressing any other minority – and the same error recurs. Breezily, we are told that Zionism is merely a political ideology, wholly separate from Judaism, which means, happily, that one can denounce the former without expressing any animus towards the latter. If only it were so simple.

Take that Kaddish prayer I’ll be saying. It refers to “Israel” three times. The Jews were called Am Yisrael, the people of Israel, centuries before we were called Jews. What’s more, when I say the prayer, I will, following tradition, be facing east – towards Jerusalem. The prayer book in my hand will be full of references to Jerusalem and indeed to Zion, expressing in a hundred poetic ways a yearning to return. This is not some new, political thing. It’s what Jews have been saying and doing for millennia. Many, many centuries before Zionism was a political movement, it was a longing – the need to end a painful exile from the Land of Israel – enshrined in the very heart of Judaism.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Which is one reason why, incidentally, the language of “settler colonialism”, repeated in the Green motion, fits Zionism so badly. When, say, the French settled in Algeria, they were not returning to the land where the French people were born, where French had been spoken two millennia earlier, and to which the dispersed and lethally persecuted French people had longed to return for 2,000 years. It’s also why, though of course there are plenty of anti-Zionist Jews, you will struggle to find a synagogue beyond the fringes of ultra-orthodoxy that does not identify in some way with Zionism – not, I stress, with this or that Israeli government or policy, but with the idea, the dream, of the Jews’ return to their ancient home. That dream became a matter of basic human survival after a history of bloody persecution reached its climax eight decades ago, in the murder of 6 million Jews by the Nazis and their collaborators across Europe. It’s that need for a refuge from antisemitism – a racism that claimed so many lives, for so long – that the advocates of Sunday’s motion would declare to be racism.

A group of Jewish Greens tried to alert their comrades to these dangers, asking for an amendment that might allow Jews to go to synagogue, but they were rejected. When one committedly anti-Zionist Jew rose to speak at a party workshop last week, he was shouted down with cries of “Zionist”. Polanski, who is himself Jewish and has called for the motion to be amended, says there’s a simple solution: if Jews denounce Israel in the terms demanded, agreeing to condemn “the occupation … the apartheid … the genocide”, they should be left alone. But the resolution itself insists on more. For Jews to comply, they would have to deny all connection with their historic homeland. This has so often been a feature of antisemitism: century after century, Jews are told that if they only disavow this belief or that practice, if they only say these words, they will be admitted into polite society. Where once Jews were told to embrace Christ, now they are told to disavow the world’s only Jewish country. The specific demand has changed; but the impulse is the same.

In each generation, those making such demands of Jews believe they are acting in a righteous cause. The Christian persecutors of the Inquisition were sure that they were honouring Jesus; today’s Greens are certain they are advancing the cause of anti-racism, even as they would hound and defame and shame a tiny minority. Any Green party member voting for this motion should reflect on that history and consider the company they are joining. It will be full of people they despise – but they will fit right in.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Englishness is not defined by ethnicity

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:33 GMT

Maariyah Seedat wonders at what point does her family become ‘English’ enough, Mark James Slater has always regarded himself as British and not English. Plus letters from Dr Richard Seabrook and Alan Baker

Jason Okundaye’s piece on defining Englishness mirrored my own experiences as a member of an ethnic minority (Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone?, 26 September).

As a child, growing up in multicultural Leicester in the 1990s and 2000s, I was “corrected” by adults in positions of authority – the vast majority of whom were white – for wanting to call myself English. It was a descriptor that I could not claim and, implicitly, was not my right because of my skin colour. I learned very quickly that referring to myself as British was the better, less objectionable option.

It always rubbed me up the wrong way. At what point does my family become “English” enough? How many generations later? I love my country of birth, and when I am abroad my Englishness is never brought into question, so why can my country not accept me as I am?

I believe that lived experiences like mine indicate why ethnic-minority adults “prefer an identification with Britishness”: a potent mix of historically being put in one’s place, and a desire to avoid exhausting circular arguments with those who cannot see beyond the colour of one’s skin. Maariyah SeedatToronto, Canada

Given that my grandparents’ family names are a mixture of Norman French, Dutch and Huguenot French, and we have probably lived within the borders of England from arrival to today, and that I was born in London, is it strange that I have always regarded myself as British and not English?

My understanding of being English is either the staid and stuffy upper classes residing in rural isolation or having some background role in an embassy or assurance office or living in a working-class community of very similar people in the terraced streets around a (former) factory.

That isn’t me. I am as invested in the other British cultures of Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Cornwall, the West Indies, Pakistan, Australia, India, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Africa and the US, not to mention western Europe and more recently eastern Europe.

Simply being English is such a restrictive definition, and I am proud to be counted as British as any of my neighbours. Mark James SlaterHelston, Cornwall

Jason Okundaye asks “Can you be English and non-white?” The answer is no, according to the government’s own system of coding ethnicities for the 2021 census. English appears as a subcategory of white, and not elsewhere. Thus it is not possible using this coding scheme to describe oneself as, for example, Black English, whereas you can choose to declare yourself Black British.

So the racist implications of “Englishness” are baked into the coding scheme until such time as “English” is moved out of its colour category and treated as a cultural identity (whatever that is) rather than as a consequence of DNA. Dr Richard SeabrookBeckenham, London

While Jason Okundaye claims as a simple truth that “there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s ‘English’ have descended”, he misses a more important general point.

While I am able to claim to be a personally responsible agent as a grandfather, father, husband, researcher and writer, I am unable to claim responsibility for the fundamental structure within which I have acted and continue to act. I was born in Canterbury, Kent and thus I am English. My birth certificate, dated 20 October 1938, records my “sex” as “boy”. I am simply not responsible for my nationality or gender.

I am accordingly neither proud nor ashamed to be an Englishman: that is just a matter of fact. And this in turn means that I cannot either adulate or castigate others of different nationality or gender on the grounds of those characteristics alone. The right’s fixation based on bloodlines and biological inheritance has no foundation: it is baseless and crass. Alan BakerCambridge

Utilities are public services – and should not be run as businesses

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:22 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane advocate “turning [utilities] into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim” (Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it, 25 September). So still companies, but with a public interest rather than a profit motive. This is still the wrong approach.

Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage.

The present government appears to be edging sideways, through metro mayors and joint working, towards governance for city regions. This should be formalised and given a full portfolio of responsibilities, powers and resources for strategic planning, economic development, education, health, transportation, infrastructure and the environment. Infrastructure should include water and sewerage.

As an example, urban rainwater needs to be collected and recycled for cooling, which was normal practice for thousands of years in southern Europe. Such practice should be moving north to include water reserves for wildfire control. How could such provisions, urban cooling and wildfire control ever be met through the profit motive?

If the present water companies in England have liabilities that exceed the value of their assets, and cannot meet their legal responsibilities, then it is difficult to see why they should be rescued and maintained through public expenditure. Roger Read Former secretary general, Metrex

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane put forward a poor argument for maintaining private ownership of utilities. Instead of comparing the present situation with how things were when the water utilities were publicly owned – surely the fairest comparison – they cite spurious examples of the alleged failings of other nationalised industries.

We are alone in the world (apart from Chile) in having a wholly privatised water industry; is everyone else out of step?Sally ThompsonCardiff

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane give some interesting thoughts on the public control of utilities. These could also apply across the complete essential services sector, from water companies to dental practices. Few who experienced the performance of the old postwar nationalised industries would wish a return to this failed model. However, why not just keep it simple and legislate to force all essential-services operators to list as companies on the London Stock Exchange?

For each sector, further legislation could set maximums for yields and permitted borrowing: two key indicators of company activity. The public would then be more inclined to invest in the companies, just as they do at present with National Grid. Ian Graham Port Carlisle, Cumbria

Other countries learn from their elders’ wisdom – so could Britain

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:17 GMT

A German service matches retired professionals to firms that use their experience, writes Alan Coppin, responding to an article about a 90-year-old Japanese competitive bodybuilder

Your feature on the 90-year-old bodybuilder Toshisuke Kanazawa was a joy (‘I’m 100% natural’: how Japan’s 90-year-old bodybuilder is still winning titles, 25 September), but it’s also a useful provocation. Almost 30% of Japan’s 123.7 million people are over 64 yet, rather than being written off, people like Kanazawa are still contributing well into their 90s.

Britain does the opposite. Between 670,000 and 860,000 people drop out of the UK workforce annually, and by their 60s more than a third of people are economically inactive. The loss is a stock of judgment and knowhow that simply walks out of the door.

Germany offers one model. Founded in 1983, its Senior Expert Service has a pool of more than 14,000 retired professionals and has arranged more than 60,000 placements by matching engineers, accountants, former military and skilled tradespeople with the small firms, charities and schools that could use their experience. Nothing like it exists here. There’s a second potential beneficiary: the almost 1 million young people not in employment, education or training. It is hard to think of a better use of an elder’s time than helping one of them get a foothold.

Modest pilot schemes in one or two sectors, modelled on the German system, would quickly show whether it is worth scaling up.

Kanazawa’s story shouldn’t just prompt admiration for one exceptional man. It should trigger a serious look at whether Britain is wasting a resource it already has: the thousands of experienced people it puts out to pasture every year. Alan CoppinAuthor, The Human Capital Imperative: Valuing Your Talent

Andy Burnham’s ultimate test will be whether people’s lives improve

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:03 GMT

Measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services, says Sarah Davidson

Re your editorial on Andy Burnham’s conference speech (29 September), the outcome that all governments should seek is a real improvement to people’s lives, particularly for those with the least, and without storing up problems for future generations. But that requires ministers to measure what matters and use that evidence to guide decisions.

The good news for the prime minister and his colleagues is that the Office for National Statistics already collects robust evidence about our lives through its UK Measures of National Well-being Dashboard. Yet there is little suggestion that this sort of data has been driving policy, including tax and spending plans.

If improving lives is the goal, measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services. Sarah DavidsonChief executive, Carnegie UK

USA v Mexico, Nations League, F1 in Malaysia and NFL – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:50:06 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

David Tindall and John Brewin have all the breaking news and more for your essential launchpad to the weekend’s football. There’s bound to be more fallout from the Manchester City furore, but they’ll be fully attuned to the tantalising Nations League feast on offer. First up is England’s next stop in their busy schedule: a meeting in Rijeka with familiar foes Croatia at 5pm. Later, Scotland journey to Skopje for their League B Group 1 clash with North Macedonia, and they won’t be ignoring the other game in England’s group as Spain lock horns with Czechia in Oviedo. Plus Leagues One and Two fixtures. If the National League is your passion and you are travelling to a match, they would love to hear from you. Send your thoughts and observations to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

F1 fans will be rising early to follow qualifying, with Billy Munday at the wheel of our live blog. The championship battle takes an intriguing twist as Mercedes teammates Kimi Antonelli and George Russell renew their rivalry at an unlikely venue⁠. Although Sepang remains a permanent fixture on the MotoGP calendar, it has not hosted a grand prix since 2017 after the Malaysian government said it could no longer justify the ⁠hosting costs given the declining ⁠returns. But the Mercedes duo will now be fighting for supremacy there after the original Bahrain race was relocated from Sakhir due to the Iran war and ⁠tensions elsewhere in the Middle East.

England travel to Rijeka to take on Croatia before rounding off their four-match international splurge against Czechia at Wembley next Tuesday. So far, a defeat by Spain, a 2-0 win over Czechia, and Harry Kane and Anthony Gordon the Three Lions’ standout players. That victory was England’s eighth straight away win in all competitions, so there’s the tantalising prospect of setting a national record. The last time England won nine away games in a row was back in the 1960s when the Beatles, the Bee Gees and Engelbert Humperdinck were topping the singles charts – between December 1965 and October 1967, under World Cup-winning manager Sir Alf Ramsey. There’s a landmark beckoning for England’s No 1 goalscorer too: Kane could become just the fourth England player to score in six consecutive away games. The others? James Windridge (six from March to June 1908), Tom Finney (seven from September 1946 to May 1948) and Stan Mortensen (six from May 1947 to October 1948). Scott Murray helms the blog.

Anyone seeking a sporting fairy tale this weekend can look to events unfurling at Old Trafford. Sporting immortality awaits Trinity’s players if they can complete a transformation from top-flight also-rans to Super League champions. The club’s glory days were back in the 1960s, when the likes of the Fox brothers, Don and Neil, and half-back Ken Rollin were among league’s biggest names. Those times appeared long gone until last week’s seismic semi-final win over Wigan lifted the club’s modern counterparts to within 80 minutes of erasing well over half a century of hurt. Daryl Powell’s Wakefield team have been built around experienced former finalists such as Tom Johnstone and Mike McMeeken, but also bolstered by overseas players like Caius Faatili, Caleb Hamlin Uele and Jazz Tevaga, who arrived as relative unknowns but have helped form a thrilling and free-scoring spirit. It’s been quite a hiatus for title glory too for Warrington, with Sam Burgess’s Wire seeking to end their 71-year wait for a league title. Lee Calvert hosts our Grand Final blog.

Luke McLaughlin is on clockwatch duty as Scotland fans search for some uplift after the 3-0 defeat by Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday when an early red card for Jack Hendry effectively rendered Sebastien Pocognoli’s home debut a write-off. The Scots have now gone four matches without a goal for the first time in 55 years but have an ideal opportunity to put that right in their third Nations League B1 encounter. North Macedonia have conceded five goals without reply in their opening two games and have also failed to score in their six matches since a 7-1 defeat to Wales last November. With just one point and no goals from their opening two Nations League fixtures after a 0-0 draw in Slovenia, this match in North Macedonia takes on an added weight for the new manager and his squad.

There’s little love lost between these North American sporting rivals and this international friendly at State Farm Stadium in Glendale sees Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT measure their progress against Concacaf’s leading nation. The USA are on a hot streak coming out of the World Cup, where they fizzled in the group stage but came to a shuddering halt against Belgium. A 4–1 win over Peru and a 4–2 victory against Chile in St Louis sees Poch’s collective in fine fettle, with teenagers Julian Hall and Mathis Albert making an impact. Rafael Márquez’s El Tri venture to Arizona following a pair of 1–1 draws against Colombia and Peru. We’ll be live-blogging the match, with Jeff Rueter reporting.

With Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton trailing Kimi Antonelli by 103 points in third, the title fight has effectively become a straight duel at the top and George Russell arrives in Malaysia brimming with the momentum. Baku was the Briton’s weekend as he became only the seventh driver on the grid to achieve a grand slam – pole position, leading in every lap, clocking the fastest lap and taking the victory, his third of the season. A championship fight that once seemed to be slipping away from the Mercedes driver has suddenly become a realistic proposition. The question remains, however, whether Russell can turn one extraordinary weekend into a sustained challenge or if Antonelli will respond immediately with eight rounds remaining in the 23-race season. With Red Bull’s four-time world champion Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc charging hard in practice, a crackling race beckons. Join Yara El-Shaboury for lap-by-lap updates.

John Brewin and Rob Smyth share the blogging duties in the buildup to more Nations League fixtures, with the Republic of Ireland, Wales, Germany, Netherlands, Portugal and Norway all engaged in compelling fixtures. Breaking news, fun facts, wildly divergent opinions – join the footballing fray by emailing your notes and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Renée Slegers’s Gunners already trail WSL leaders City by seven points and a defeat would leave last season’s runners-up 10 points off the top after only five games following a 1-0 defeat at Chelsea last weekend. Arsenal let slip a two-goal lead in their midweek Champions League match against Paris FC, the 2-2 draw memorable for a bizarre mistake by Leah Williamson, who gave away a late penalty by putting her hand on the ball from a goal-kick. Slegers’ side did at least score twice for the first time in six fixtures, but they have only registered two wins this season. A win then is vital for Slegers and her side at the Etihad, where the furore around the club’s devastating guilty verdict on more than Premier League 100 charges has cast a pall over the hosts’ season. The women’s team is not implicated in the systemic breaking of financial monitoring rules and impressed on Thursday in their 1-1 Champions League draw with Real Madrid. Rob Smyth keeps the updates flowing.

Daniel Gallan has his hands full for an evening of Nations League games, and the clash of Republic of Ireland against Israel behind-closed-doors match in Serbia is certain to be dogged by political fallout between the two nations over the conflict in Gaza. The 2-2 draw with Austria leaves the Republic third in their group at the halfway point, three points behind leaders Austria and level on four with second-placed Kosovo after beating Israeli 3-0 in the reverse fixture in Debrecen, Hungary. Wales upset the World Cup finalists Norway 2-1 in Nations League A on Thursday night and next face Denmark in Cardiff, seeking to avenge last weekend’s 2-0 defeat in Copenhagen.

After covering Indianapolis Colts v Washington Commanders at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (the first of nine games being played outside the United States this season), Graham Searles resumes his blog post for Sunday evening’s clutch of NFL clashes. Winless Miami Dolphins face unbeaten Minnesota Vikings while elsewhere Denver Broncos meet San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs take on Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers meet Super Bowl champions Seattle Seahawks.
