D. A. in Cornell Rape Inquiry Declined to Review Additional Evidence

The New York Times October 03, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Records show that campus police officers informed Tompkins County prosecutors that they had conducted additional interviews beyond taking a statement from the woman who said she was raped.

By Michael Rothfeld and Hurubie Meko

The Tompkins County district attorney said recently that the evidence he reviewed in 2024 made it impossible for him to bring charges in the Cornell University rape inquiry.

But records obtained by The New York Times show that the same district attorney’s office declined to review any additional evidence gathered by the campus police department beyond a six-page statement signed by the former student, now known as Jane Doe.

The decision not to review the additional evidence has not been previously reported.

On Nov. 25, 2024, a Cornell police investigator, Jeffrey Northrop, spoke to a member of the district attorney’s staff, Jeff Huddle, about additional interviews the police had done, the records show.

Prosecutors did not express interest, saying they agreed that based on the woman’s statement, “criminal charges would not be pursued in this case,” Mr. Northrop wrote in a note documenting their call.

By that point, the police had conducted numerous interviews, reviewed chat messages, logged anonymous tips, reached out to lawyers for some of the accused men and spoken to at least two others, the records show.

On Friday, Gov. Kathy Hochul harshly criticized the district attorney and the Cornell police for the way they handled the investigation and appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor, giving her power to bring criminal charges.

All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied any wrongdoing, and none has been charged with a crime.

Reached on Thursday, the Tompkins County district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, said by email that any additional records gathered by the Cornell police were “not pertinent to our analysis because we had Jane Doe’s comprehensive account of the events.”

Mr. Huddle referred questions to the district attorney.

The interaction between Mr. Northrop and Mr. Van Houten’s office was one example of what experts said appeared to be numerous law enforcement shortcomings in the investigation of Jane Doe’s account.

Mr. Van Houten has said that based on Jane Doe’s lawsuit he would reopen the investigation.

But his office’s decision at the time not to examine additional evidence that had been gathered, or to seek any additional inquiry beyond a single — and as it turns out, incomplete — campus police statement, was a stark departure from how complicated sex crimes investigations should be handled, said former prosecutors and other experts.

Mr. Van Houten has defended his original decision not to prosecute, saying Jane Doe’s account in her police statement “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual.”

He said the facts in her initial statement did not constitute a crime under New York law, and that he had never been contacted by Jane Doe or her lawyers before her lawsuit.

The former prosecutors, however, said the district attorney’s approach fell short in multiple ways, including his failure to bring Jane Doe in to be interviewed by his office and his apparent total reliance on a statement recorded — and, more broadly, an investigation conducted — by the university police.

“We would never rely on a campus police investigation,” said Rick Trunfio, a former sex crimes prosecutor in upstate New York and now an adjunct law professor at Syracuse University. “There’s too many problems with that.”

Mr. Trunfio and other experts said the investigation should have been handed off to a specialized police or prosecution team like the special victims bureau he founded at the Onondaga County District Attorney’s Office. Also problematic, he added, is that the Cornell University Police Department was “beholden” to the school, which would have had to report under federal law if a gang rape on campus was prosecuted by civilian authorities.

“You think Cornell University wants to report something like that?” Mr. Trunfio said.

A Cornell representative who speaks on behalf of the campus police declined to comment, citing the pending litigation.

In the police statement reviewed by Mr. Van Houten, Jane Doe said she had been drinking before she went to a party at the Chi Phi fraternity house on the evening of Oct. 19, 2024, and before agreeing to a threesome with two of the men, and snorting ketamine, which she said she had never done before.

She then described being in a bedroom as the evening escalated, with up to seven men entering and leaving as the night wore on — some having sexual contact with her and some snorting ketamine off her body, she said. She described feeling coerced, being “pretty incapacitated” and “numb” and feeling trapped.

“I felt like hiding under the covers of the bed was the only option for me at that point, because the individuals who had just entered the room were standing between me and the only exit from the room,” her statement said.

The transcript of a Nov. 14 interview she gave also contained more definitive language that the police omitted from her statement: “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.”

The language in her recent lawsuit was stronger still: It said she was “incapable of consenting” when she arrived at the party, was “forced” to have vaginal and oral sex, and that one of the men “commanded” her to snort ketamine off his penis. (Her police statement said he was “implying” she should snort it.)

Deborah Tuerkheimer, a Northwestern University law professor who has written about sexual violence cases, said the complexities of such cases require taking enough time to build trust with the person reporting a sexual trauma to ultimately bring out the fullest account possible — while simultaneously interviewing other witnesses and gathering any electronic evidence.

“You would really want to spend some time doing all of that before you arrive at any conclusions about whether this was a case that you could move forward on,” she said.

Ms. Tuerkheimer said there is a pattern of law enforcement “short-circuiting” sexual violence investigations by the police prematurely compiling a statement that did not capture important parts of an interview, and the prosecutor then using that statement to conclude a criminal case was not viable.

“I wouldn’t call what the police did in this case, or what the prosecutor did, an investigation,” Ms. Tuerkheimer said. “It wasn’t.”

The campus police investigation, which continued until January 2025, included interviews with other students who belonged to or had socialized at the fraternity, and people who had called in with information. The police also sought and collected records for some social media and phone records of the accused men.

But the experts questioned why the Cornell police had not obtained warrants to search and seize the men’s phones in the days after the woman reported being assaulted.

The police also made relatively light-handed attempts to arrange interviews with the men, who dodged those efforts until most retained lawyers who advised them not to cooperate, records from the investigation show. More seasoned investigators might have been better able to elicit statements from a group of male college students, one ex-prosecutor said.

The men received varying punishments after a civil rights investigation by Cornell’s Title IX office.

On Jan. 31, 2025, the Cornell police investigator, Mr. Northrop, informed Jane Doe at the campus police headquarters that the district attorney had declined to pursue criminal charges. She “was upset, but she stated that she understood,” Mr. Northrop wrote in notes about their meeting.

He gave her his business card. The case was closed “pending any further developments,” he wrote. Mr. Northrop did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Van Houten has subsequently acknowledged also reviewing Snapchat messages from the night of the encounter in which one of the fraternity members seemed to invite others to come into the room with Jane Doe.

Mr. Van Houten has also said that his office does not do its own investigation and relied entirely on the police. But as he readied to re-examine the case, he said he had assigned a senior female prosecutor who has experience with sex crimes to prepare the case for a grand jury.

His office may not get the chance given Ms. Hochul’s decision to appoint Ms. James as special prosecutor.

Jane Doe’s attorney, Thomas Giuffra, applauded that move.

“My client has been failed by government and educational institutions throughout her efforts to obtain accountability,” he said.

William K. Rashbaum contributed reporting.

Michael Rothfeld is an investigative reporter in New York, writing in-depth stories focused on the city’s government, business and personalities.

Hurubie Meko is a Times reporter covering criminal justice in New York, with a focus on the Manhattan district attorney's office and state courts.

Omani Co-Pilot on FlyDubai Flight Is Said to Have Extremist Views

The New York Times October 03, 2026

FlyDubai Attack

Advertisement

Supported by

It was unclear what background checks had been carried out before he was allowed to fly to Israel.

By Julian E. BarnesAaron Boxerman and Jane Bradley

The co-pilot who violently attacked the captain of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and then tried to crash the airliner had embraced extreme Islamist views, prompting security officials in Oman to scrutinize him earlier, according to two people briefed on the matter.

The co-pilot was identified as an Omani man named Hamam al-Hamami, who was the first officer on FlyDubai Flight 1073, the two people said, as did an Arab official.

The investigation so far indicated that he had acted alone and had no known ties with Iran, which has long sought to target Israelis abroad, the Arab official and two U. S. officials said. The three officials and the two people briefed on the Omani scrutiny of Mr. al-Hamami spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation into the attack.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Lone wolves can be hard for counterterrorism officials to detect. A recent social media post attributed to Mr. al-Hamami showed a photo of a former Qaeda leader, CNN reported. Concerns about his radicalization raise questions about what background checks had been carried out before allowing him to fly. It is unclear whether the Omanis had shared their concerns with security officials in Israel, the United Arab Emirates — where the flight originated — or with the airline.

Mr. al-Hamami’s identity was first reported by Al Arabiya, a Saudi Arabian broadcaster, and The Wall Street Journal first reported Oman’s concerns about his radical ideological views.

More than 170 passengers, mostly Israelis, were on the FlyDubai flight on Wednesday when the co-pilot began stabbing the captain less than an hour before it was supposed to land. The plane plunged more than 17,000 feet in less than two minutes, flight tracking websites showed, as its pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, fought off the attack. Captain Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, and passengers intervened, averting a crash.

The attack is the subject of an international investigation. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel told Fox News on Thursday that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” but he did not elaborate. The plane’s passengers were mostly Israeli, some of whom said the crisis evoked the feelings of dread they had last felt on Oct. 7, 2023, during the Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

A LinkedIn profile bearing Mr. al-Hamami’s name said he lived in Muscat and had worked at Oman Air for seven years, leaving in 2025. The profile said he had studied engineering at RMIT University in Australia, and, more recently, aviation at Buckinghamshire New University in Britain. The page made no mention of FlyDubai. The LinkedIn profile has been deleted.

After the failed attack on the plane, two posts appeared on the profile, CNN reported. One depicted a photo of Ayman al-Zawahri, who led Al Qaeda after Osama bin Laden’s death and was killed by the United States in 2022. It was not clear who made the posts or whether they had been scheduled in advance to be published.

The U. A. E. said on Thursday that it would take the lead in investigating whether the attack was linked to terrorism. Both Captain Machchhar, who was wounded in the attack but is in stable condition, and Mr. al-Hamami have been transferred to the Emirates from Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing.

A group of passengers is credited with saving the aircraft by rushing into the cockpit and subduing the co-pilot after being alerted by a mother’s screams, before treating the wounded Captain Machchhar.

Adam Goldman and Vivian Nereim contributed reporting.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Jane Bradley is an investigative reporter for The Times. She is based in Toronto, where she focuses on security, organized crime, money and power.

Chris Rock Has Been Thinking About Forgiveness

The New York Times October 03, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

Chris Rock is inarguably one of the greatest stand-up comedians of all time. From specials like his 1996 breakout, “Bring the Pain,” to his most recent, “Selective Outrage” in 2023, he has established himself as not only scabrously funny but also fearless and insightful when tackling race, politics, relationships — you name it. Rock’s movie career, though, has been more variable. He’s been in plenty of hits, often alongside his friend Adam Sandler (two “Grown Ups” films; 2005’s “The Longest Yard”). And I’d point to the cult-classic hip-hop satire “CB4” (1993) as well as “Top Five” (2014), about a superstar comedian at a career crossroads, as film work that ably translated Rock’s intelligence and wit to the big screen. But there hasn’t quite been a cinematic statement on par with his stand-up. Until now. “Misty Green,” which opens Oct. 9, is an indisputable leap forward.

The film, the fourth that Rock has written, directed and acted in, is about a midcareer Hollywood actress named Misty, played in a riveting performance by Rosalind Eleazar (best known for the Apple TV show “Slow Horses”). Misty is at a moment of peak personal and professional crisis, and her story allows Rock to examine serious questions about social inequality, getting older in show business and compromise. I wanted to ask him about those subjects as well as his thoughts on comedy today, forgiveness and what his future holds.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

One of the themes of “Misty Green” is status: who has it and who loses it when it comes to success, money, relationships. I want to know: When do you feel insecure about your status? I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the last few years, post-Covid, and a lot of it is about not feeling insecure. A lot of it is about “you’re enough.” But I don’t ever really feel insecure about my “status,” per se. Occasionally I’ll meet people that are obviously working harder than me and that’ll make me feel insecure. Adam Sandler, Rick Rubin. You’re like, “How many things are you doing right now?” And some people are better with their kids than me. I think I’m a good dad.

You kept them off the pole. I kept them off the pole, but they’re on OnlyFans!

The movie makes Hollywood very appealing, because of the talent there and the love that people have for doing what they do, but it also makes Hollywood seem awful: racist, sexist, chipping away at your soul. Has that been your experience? You’re not going to get a “how bad Hollywood is” soliloquy from me. I always say every generation laughs at their children’s racism. So my kids are like, “This is racist,” and I’m like [Rolls eyes]. And what I would call racist, my mother would laugh at. Are there bad parts about Hollywood? Yes. But it’s still better than a normal job by a ton. I used to work at Red Lobster. I used to work at a home for severely autistic adults. I had the night shift, and sometimes you had to change the diaper of a grown man. So what if I can’t get a sketch on? So what if somebody doesn’t respond to my script? I used to wipe people’s asses!

But the question of compromises comes up throughout the film. There’s compromises in everything, man.

So what are the compromises that you’ve had to make in your career? I came up in cable television. I could say what I wanted. Honestly I don’t know if I could do “Bring the Pain” today. I’d have to compromise. But in ’96, I did pretty much whatever I wanted. Dude, I made “Pootie Tang.” I did a documentary about hair. So I’m the last guy to complain.

A second ago you said you didn’t know if you’d be able to make “Bring the Pain” today. That’s a sentiment I see a lot: comedians saying, “I don’t know if I’d be able to make that today.” But do you really think that’s true? You’re right. I’d be able to make it. As a matter of fact, I’ll go even further, “Bring the Pain” would be bigger today. You know why? Because you wouldn’t be able to report on it. The New York Times wouldn’t be able to say it was great. It wouldn’t be on Netflix. It would be like the Shane Gillis thing, which would actually elevate it. You know, The New York Times has got a weird thing with comedy.

What’s the weird thing? The Times, The Journal — they ignore the nuance. So it’s like, This is the manosphere-conservative thing, or, This is the wokey-woke thing. And all the people in the middle they kind of ignore. I remember five, 10 years ago, Bill Burr sold out Madison Square Garden. At that point, maybe eight comedians had sold out Madison Square Garden. I wake up the next day and I want to read the review. There’s no review, because Bill Burr is this guy that walks a crazy line. Is he conservative? Maybe. Wait a minute, he’s got a Black wife. Oh, he’s sexist. Wait a minute, there’s a lot of women here. You guys are not [expletive] with that middle. So anyway, “Bring the Pain” would be bigger today because it would be less lauded.

I think something has happened in comedy since Trump was first elected, where it seems like comedians feel as if they have to subtly or overtly signal their politics. Audiences are looking for that, and comedians are giving it to them. Maybe. I mean, I’m trying to decide if I’m gonna go back out now. Do I want to?

Why wouldn’t you? Do I want to jump in this bed? I don’t know. I am loving directing. Maybe I should do a run of pictures.

I have a question about Rosalind Eleazar and “Misty Green.” What did she bring to the part that wasn’t in the script initially? When I’m directing, I say, “It’s my movie, it’s your part.” And it was hers, man. Put it this way: I only met Rosalind about a month ago. For the months we were shooting, there was only Misty. She was Misty in the audition. She was Misty through the whole filming process. She never asked me one question that didn’t have to do with the character.

There’s a scene in the film where her character performs at a nightclub, and we see that she’s also an incredible singer. When I saw that, I was thinking about the amount of talent that’s out there — even people who are not household names. It’s staggering. Do you understand who makes it and who doesn’t? Talent must have so little to do with it. There’s a lot that goes into it. Right place, right time. What kind of friend are you? That goes a long, long way. Even now if I look over my career, probably half of my gigs are just somebody going, “Oh, he’s cool.” You have to be considerate. You have to ask people how they’re doing. A lot of artists, we’re so self-centered. So to answer your question, yes, there’s a lot of talent out there, and a lot is just right time, right place. Sometimes you’re on the subway and you see a guy playing the violin, and you’re like, They should be at the Met. Like, what the [expletive]?

Who’s someone you’ve worked with that you thought was incredibly talented, but they were self-destructive or they just never got a break? Ooh, I can’t say that. I wish I could. I’d say that off-camera. There’s a bunch of people. That self-destructive thing is a really sad thing. A self-destructive person is basically a person that makes six bad decisions a year. That’s 359 days of being fine. But those six bad decisions a year will [expletive] up your whole life.

How many bad decisions a year do you make? I don’t know. Show business is like the Olympics. And in the Olympics, the difference between first and last can be less than a second sometimes.

I want to ask another question about the movie. Were there ideas that you’d had about men and women that you then had to examine in order to credibly create the character of Misty? Because in a lot of your comedy, you make distinctions between men and women, but the distinctions are coming from the male point of view, and “Misty Green” is so much about a woman’s story. Did it take any excavation to be able to do what you wanted to do with her character? Saying there are stark differences between men and women is a perfect device for comedy. It doesn’t work in a drama. I’ll say this: Part of all this therapy is developing empathy and really being able to get inside of another character. So the last four or five years, I’m a way more empathetic person. It also helps that my daughters are like grown-ups, so I really watch women around my house. My daughters don’t forgive my sins, but they give me an education that I wouldn’t normally have.

I want to go back to directing. It was 12 years between you directing “Top Five” and “Misty Green.” What took so long? Life, Covid, I got divorced, which meant I had to make real money. Maybe I had some other scripts that the market didn’t respond to. It’s not like I was sitting around. But Covid was a time to be like, OK, what am I doing with my life? And other [expletive] I don’t feel like talking about. I had a lot of stuff going on the last 12 years.

Did you come up with answers to “What should I be doing with my life?” I should be directing small movies, character-driven pieces. Maybe I’m not in the movie as much as I used to be. So I’ve been writing a lot more. I’m actually working on a book of essays. We’ll see where that goes.

Could we talk about those things you don’t feel like talking about? I mean, I’m a big boy. I can answer stuff coolly, or not answer. Whatever. What do you want to know?

Is there more to say about the slap than what you said in your last special? I’m good, man. That was so long ago.

Not that long ago. I wish everyone well. I’ve moved on with my life.

Do you forgive what happened? I’m not going to get into clickbait things. I don’t think I’m in a beef. I’m done, dude. I’m done.

Let’s return to the movie. I was slightly surprised to hear that you don’t have anything that bad to say about Hollywood, given the content of the film, which to me was about how hard and hurtful to an artist’s soul Hollywood can be. So what were the themes that you were interested in exploring in “Misty Green?” I’m really into expiration dates. Everybody tells you that you can do art forever, and that’s just not true. In show business, you’ve got to reach certain plateaus by a certain time or else you’re going to be in trouble. So Misty is turning 40, and it’s a little bit of an expiration date happening. But, yeah, I wanted to do a movie about Hollywood. I wanted to do a movie about L. A. It’s this tale of two cities. Sunshine and palm trees, but we’re constantly walking over homeless people — the most liberal people in the world. Rodeo Drive and Skid Row are in the same city, probably eight, 10 miles apart. In a lot of ways, America’s like that: very rich, very poor. We live in a world where either you order [expletive] or you deliver [expletive], and you really don’t want to deliver [expletive], you know?

What should your response to that disparity be? So, the running title of the book that I’m writing right now is “When the Homeless Know Your Name.” Because when the homeless know your name, you feel that. Somebody asks you for money on the street, they just ask you for the money. When they ask me, they say, “Yo, Chris!” I don’t know what I should do. First of all, who the hell carries cash anymore? You give what you can.

I want to dig into that feeling a bit more. When the homeless know your name, what do you feel? Put it this way: I get up around 7. I get coffee by about 7:15. I go to my supermarket, get some fruit, and inevitably there’s always a bunch of guys setting up for the day. Did you ever see “12 Years a Slave” or any slave movie with a free slave? The slaves look at Chiwetel [Ejiofor]. He’s dressed all cool and he got his hat and they’re just looking at him like: “How the [expletive] did this happen? We’re the same.” That’s me at the supermarket in the morning. They’re looking at me, not even as a famous person, just like, “Who’s this brother buying mango at 7:25 in the morning?” Because there are no Black dudes living in SoHo. Am I answering your question?

Yeah. You’ve seen behind the veil. Yeah, and it’s like, they’re looking at me, and I’m looking at them, because I know I could be that. I know if I don’t walk into a comedy club in ’84 or ’83, I’d probably have a normal job. I’d have a lovely life, by the way. I’m not one of these guys who thinks that if I didn’t find comedy, I’d be in jail. No, I’d work for Amazon and I’d have a wife and some kids and I’d be OK. I’d be the funny guy on the Amazon route.

It’s interesting that you’re writing a book because I remember, before the pandemic, there was an announcement that you were working on a book about interracial relationships. What happened there? The book never showed up. I’m not trying to be like a gangster or anything. When you’re writing something about race, especially in this era of everybody taking everything out of context — I just didn’t feel like everything I was saying to the publisher, they were listening. I was like, I don’t trust these people. So I gave the money back.

How much was it that you gave back? It was a significant sum. More than I’m making today.

I’ll make a check out to you later. Do you think that taking things out of context is an ongoing problem for artists and comedians? There’s so much discussion about whether somebody said something offensive or who’s allowed to say what, and I never know how real that is. I hate to say, it’s just B. S. It’s just nerd bullies. Do you know how easy it is to go, “What did you mean by that?” before you elect to be angry at something? It is so easy to ask somebody: “Hey, man, could you not say that thing? I just felt a certain way when you said that.” Then if you’re ignored, yes, reply with anger. But it is so easy to pause and just go, “Hey, what did you mean?” I don’t know who I was having this argument with, but they said, “People are so sensitive.” I’m like: “No, they’re not sensitive. They’re mean. And they can’t stop being mean.”

You think it’s all about meanness? I’m just saying, meanness is the new kale. It’s on the platter, OK? It’s like, “Oh, do you got any mean here?”

When is offense justified? People are entitled to their feelings. Don’t get me wrong. We’re all entitled to be offended. Don’t take me out of context. Context does matter, though. A lot of people are ignoring context because it prevents them from being mean.

This morning when you came in, you said, “I don’t think I’ve been here since I filmed ‘Top Five’ with the canceled all-stars, Scott Rudin and Charlie Rose.” And I listened to a podcast interview you did with David Spade and Dana Carvey earlier this year, and you also used the phrase “the canceled all-stars” to talk about Louis C. K. and Kanye. How do you think about questions of forgiveness and who gets forgiven and why? Hey, man, I’m Black. When you’re Black, white people believe every accusation is a conviction. I grew up at 619 Decatur Street, between Howard and Saratoga. A guy named Roger Logan, who I grew up with and was one of my best friends’ brothers, went to jail for years for a murder he didn’t commit. And here’s the weird thing: His brother used to plead with me to pay for a lawyer for Roger, and I never did it. I always had a no-lawyer thing. I’ll pay your mortgage; there’s a bunch I’ve paid for — education and all sorts of [expletive]. I always stay out of lawyers because it’s so open-ended. And it still [expletives] with me. I had the means to help him and I didn’t. I don’t know if we could’ve got him out or not, but still. So all that to say, Black men get accused of [expletive] they didn’t do all the time, every day. We let Black men out of jail and go: “Whoops! That Black guy just did 30 years — too bad.” So to answer your question, hopefully I don’t get accused of anything, but it’s real when people get accused of things, and you better be real sure they did it. Am I making sense?

You’re making sense. I think you’re describing a kind of lived empathy that —— I’ll go even further. My grandfather, Allen Rock, killed a man. Legend has it, he thought the guy was sleeping with my grandmother. The guy lived next door. He told the guy, “If you take another step in my yard, I’m going to shoot you.” The guy took one step and my grandfather blew him away. My grandfather went to jail. He was a preacher. He gets out of jail on a Wednesday, and by Friday he was picking us up from school. Within a year or two, he was the reverend of that church again. My brother Charles shot a guy. I say all that to say, my grandfather went to jail. He did his time. So a) if you’re going to accuse somebody, make sure they did it. And b) when people do things, there’s a time limit in the real world. In your world, you just shun people. But in the real world, we have to live with each other. It’s up to the victims to forgive, and two things can be true: My brother shot a guy. I love my brother. Because I love my brother, does that mean I think the person should have gotten shot? No. The last thing I’ll say: When I was a kid, I was in police lineups two, three times. Stay away from Howard Avenue. Howard and Decatur.

In Bed-Stuy? In Bed-Stuy, and you’re minding your business and you get swooped up. And now you’re in a police lineup. And you’ve seen enough cop movies to know that behind that window is a person — could be a man, but probably a woman — and if she points at you, your whole life’s over. If she points at me, she’s wrong, but she’s not lying. She’s traumatized, and when you’re traumatized you try to wrap [expletive] up. My dad drove a newspaper truck, and I’ve been reading the paper since I was a kid. The news has taken all the nuance out of it. Everything’s black and white.

I want to go back to what you said about becoming a more empathetic person. How does one consciously learn to be more empathetic? And is being more empathetic good for a comedian? It better be, or I’m in trouble. I don’t know if I’ve learned to be empathetic. A friend of mine told me I had Asperger’s a few years back, and I got it checked out. It wasn’t Asperger’s, but it was a thing called NVLD, nonverbal learning disorder. It requires its own level of therapy.

What are the effects of that? The effects are that I’m really bad at reading nonverbal signals. I catastrophize, I have black-and-white thinking — both things that are great for being a comedian but bad in personal life and real relationships. So I’ve been learning. I have to see a woman once a week. “Misty Green” would be the first piece of art that I’ve done since my diagnosis.

You said earlier that part of what you were talking about in therapy is feeling like you’re “enough.” When do you have self-esteem questions? All artists have self-esteem questions, especially the good ones. An artist is an egomaniac with an inferiority complex. I would absolutely fall into that. “I am great. I hope they notice.” So, yeah, I can feel that way. Eddie Murphy makes me feel like that. In the presence of Eddie Murphy, I can get a little insecure.

Of course. Also, not to name-drop, but one of my biggest regrets in life is I could never relax around Prince. He wanted to be friends. Hanging out, I couldn’t not be like, “Oh [expletive], Prince is drinking ice tea!”

Did you and he ever get to a place where he was normal? I mean, a normal rock star. Those degrees of normal are so different than yours. I remember, I was at Prince’s house. I’m in Minneapolis. I’d just done some shows, and he had a party for me at Paisley Park. I am literally in the vault, and he’s playing me new music, and there’s lots of people there, and his wife called. I think he was married to Mayte at the time. And he was like: “Everybody be quiet! Be quiet!” It’s like 200 people. Mayte called, he’s picking up the phone, and he goes: “Hey. Nothing. Nah, I’m just chillin’. Yeah, I’ll probably go to bed in a couple of hours. Love you, too.” And then the party started again. [Sings] “Gett Off”! Right away!

Even Prince has to take that call. Even Prince had the check-in.

You said that you want to direct more films, but you also talked about the idea of an expiration date, and it can be hard for comedians to get older. It can definitely be hard for comedians to get older.

It’s hard to stay edgy. Well, nobody stays edgy. You become the establishment. Early in your career, it’s your performance, but it’s also the promise of who you are. So the public is investing in this thing, this stock. But later on you’re like LeBron. It’s all results and we’ll give you a one-year deal — as long as you play like LeBron. I mean, I’ve seen careers and people change. Steve Martin’s the king of reinvention.

If you listen to a Steve Martin album, because of the style of comedy he’s doing — absurdist and whimsical — you’re never asking yourself, Does he really believe that? But now audiences are asking, Does the comedian believe what they’re saying? So when you’re telling jokes about real-life things, are we supposed to understand that you believe what you’re saying, or that you’re just saying what you need to say to make the bit work? Jokes tend to work better when there’s some truth in them, when you’re not just making up stuff. I think the audience can tell who’s fake. They can tell if you’re married, they can tell if you’ve got kids, they can tell if you worked. You can’t fake anything. The thing about comedians is, there’s no mystique. There’s no Ziggy Stardust of comedians. You are who you are, and they’re rolling with you or not.

Do you think you are who you are in your film work? I think “Misty” is a good barometer of me right now. I’m like every character in the movie on some level.

Hopefully not the Adam Driver character, a guy who procures prostitutes for Saudi princes. There is nothing different between the Adam Driver character in my movie and the Jack Lemmon character in “The Apartment.” It’s just an outfit and some hairstyle.

And the drugs. Alcohol is the biggest drug in the world. What are you talking about? See, you are leaving out your nuance. You literally are making my point in front of me. You conveniently made yourself stupid to make a point.

I never conveniently make myself stupid. You’re so much smarter than that!

If people are like, David left out the nuance of what drug Jack Lemmon was using in “The Apartment”! — I’ll die on that hill. It hurt you that Jack Lemmon was basically the same character. And you have this love for “The Apartment,” which is deserved. It’s one of the best movies ever. But that’s what he was. He was a pimp.

I guess you’re right. I don’t know where to go from that. Jack Lemmon is a pimp. In “The Apartment” he’s a lovable pimp, but a pimp nonetheless.

In so many ways, we all are. Or hoes! Mostly hoes.

You know, before we spoke initially, I had asked if you could send over the names of some films that were influential on “Misty Green.” You sent a list that included Bob Fosse’s “Cabaret,” “Bad Lieutenant,” “Klute.” Can you tell me how they helped shape your vision for your movie? There’s a great line in “Husbands and Wives,” the Woody Allen film. He’s playing a professor, and the line is something to do with, You can’t teach people to write; all you can do is expose them to great writing and hope they pick up on it. It’s kind of the same thing with film. You can’t teach a person really to make a good movie. You just gotta show them some good movies and hope that they run with it. All of those movies, especially the Fosse stuff — there’s a lot of “Lenny” in “Misty Green.” I love those movies. My mother would always say, “If you feed a kid long enough, he starts to look like you.” If you love movies hard enough, you’ll eventually make that kind of movie.

Wait, did Fosse also direct “Star 80”? Yeah! “Star 80” is my go-to. How could I forget “Star 80”? “Misty Green” is so “Star 80.” The Fosse stuff more than anything has been an influence.

There’s a line in your movie that I wanted to ask about. The character that you play in the film says to Misty, “True love starts at forgiveness.” Is that your experience of forgiveness? Yeah. You don’t really realize if you love somebody until you have to forgive them. I can enjoy myself with just about anybody. It’s when somebody tests you, when somebody betrays you, when somebody lets you down and you still want to be around them — that’s love. I have a friend that’s going to be nameless that might have gotten canceled. Another friend of mine was like, “How can you be friends with that person?” I was like, “If you’re only friends with your friends when they’re good, they’re not your friends.” If you’ve got a bunch of people that are only going to be there when you’re good, you have no friends. That doesn’t mean condoning abusive behavior; you can reprimand your friends. That’s also part of friendship.

But we all have a line, right? You and I live in different worlds. I’ve got friends that are in jail. I’ve got friends that are drugged out. I don’t live like you.

You don’t know that. I can tell.

I mean, you happen to be right. And by the way, I’m not being dismissive of you. I’m just saying that my friends have tested me more than yours, and maybe I’ve tested them. I’m not religious, but I’m a Christian, and God forgives. That’s what it’s all about. The problem with quote, unquote, wokeness — and don’t get me wrong, it is great that marginalized people have a voice; it is great to advocate for anybody that feels marginalized — but the problem is we’re in the Old Testament right now, and the Old Testament has no forgiveness. The Old Testament didn’t work, so they had to write a remix called the New Testament.

There’s been discussion lately about how the Woke 1.0 era, which refers to the immediate post-George Floyd era, was “crazy.” Do you see that moment in time as just “crazy?” Was there anything redeeming about it? I think I just answered. Again, it’s great to help those that need help. We need more of that. The problem is when you institutionalize it. My half a joke: The Salem witch hunts — I’m sure the first three witches they caught were actually witches. But then you open up a witch office, and now you gotta start lying because you got overhead. You gotta justify the witch hunters’ pensions and [expletive]. I’m glad that all of this stuff happened, it needed to happen, and because it happened, maybe I’ve heard some voices that I probably wouldn’t have heard otherwise.

Let me switch gears and ask a comedy question. Sure — but before you do, because I keep saying how bad my friends are: I have some genius friends who are unproblematic, the most progressive. Some of the greatest artists that have ever lived, some that you know of and some that you don’t, are my friends.

All right, so on the record: Chris Rock’s friends are perfectly fine people. One thing I always wanted to ask a great comedian is, Do you understand what the purpose of laughter is? Why do we laugh? I never thought about it that hard. Here’s what I do know: The greatest feelings in life are sex and laughter. We break up with people that we have great sex with all the time. We don’t break up with anybody that makes us laugh. And the ability to laugh at oneself is probably the highest form of intelligence. The inability to laugh at oneself is a sure sign you’re dealing with an idiot.

Chris, professionally or personally, what keeps you up at night? I don’t worry about anything.

Everyone worries about something. I’m not worried about nothing, dude. I’m worried about my kids, but the world? The world is the world. The world is exactly what it wants to be. It’s sad where it’s sad, it’s happy where it’s happy. But this is what people want.

What do you mean “this is what people want”? People have the America they want. If they want to change it, we’ll see.

Is it the America you want? I’ve been here a while. I have a long sample size. Martin Luther King was shot in 1968. Black people pretty much live where Black people lived in 1968, especially in New York City. Maybe a neighborhood or two is gentrified that wasn’t. Maybe Beyoncé has more points on her deal than Aretha Franklin did. People are nicer. Blatant disrespect in the streets doesn’t happen like it did in 1968. But the distribution of wealth, the access to education, the access to health care is pretty much where it was when Dr. King got shot. And I could say that about other places in the world, too. Somehow I got out of it. But Louis Armstrong was the most famous singer in the world in the ’30s and ’40s, so Black entertainers have always gotten off the Titanic before everybody else.

Let me try to end with something more hopeful. Hey, “Misty Green!” Oct. 9! Sexy movie! A24! Those guys are great. No oppression there.

I asked what keeps you up at night. But what gets you up in the morning? You know what’s weird? I’m excited every morning. It’s my favorite time to get up and take my walk and get my fruit, listen to the news a little bit. ’Cause every day can be great. Even when you know what’s going to happen, you don’t know what’s going to happen. So I wake up pretty happy, man. And I’m very fortunate. I’m not going to sit here and act like my experience is everybody’s.

I appreciate you taking the time to speak with me. I especially enjoyed it when you pushed back. Oh, man, that’s always where the good stuff is. I’ll leave you with this: A friend of mine called me up, she was working on her special, and she said, “I’ve had a hard time writing material.” I said: “Well, you have this podcast. What I need you to do is go to your podcast, and every hard episode, that is where the material is. Every one you thought was a hard time, that’s where the good [expletive] is.” So if I’ve given you a hard time, this is the good [expletive].

As David’s admiring editor, I really loved that Chris Rock gave him a bit of a hard time in this interview, and David loved it too. Rock was open, thoughtful, engaged — and also happy to push back when David asked about something he didn’t want to get into (the slap) or didn’t agree with (that Adam Driver’s character in Rock’s new movie is any different from Jack Lemmon in “The Apartment”).

Their conversation covered so much ground — Rock’s sense of America today, friendship, comedy, Hollywood, income inequality, Prince! — and the result is something I hope readers, listeners and viewers will find fascinating and entertaining. I know I did.

This interview has been edited and condensed from two conversations. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Cal Christie

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

Trump, Putin, Ukraine and an Oil Deal: 5 Takeaways

The New York Times October 03, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

A proposal to bolster relations with the Kremlin through the purchase of Russian energy assets is striking even for an administration that regularly mixes personal business interests with foreign policy.

By Eric Lipton and Anton Troianovski

Reporting from Washington

It is one of the most alluring opportunities in global energy.

The foreign assets of Lukoil, the Russian energy giant, are being sold off at fire sale prices because U. S. sanctions have made them nearly worthless for investors in Russia. Gas stations in the United States, refineries in Eastern Europe and oil fields around the world are up for grabs.

Now, the process of selling off those assets has become intertwined with White House efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine. And some of the key figures poised to benefit from the Lukoil sale have ties to President Trump’s family and his associates — including the administration’s envoys to Russia. The revelation raises new questions about conflicts of interest in an administration that has regularly mixed personal interests with national interests.

Here are five takeaways from The New York Times’s investigation of the proposed transaction.

The Trump administration has long argued that discussing business deals with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could help convince him to mend ties with the West and end his war on Ukraine. The administration signaled recently that some deals could move forward before the war ends. But the specifics have been murky until now.

When Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Mr. Putin at the Kremlin last month, the Russian president asked them to get the Lukoil deal done. The Americans said they would work on it, reasoning that doing so could build good will with the Kremlin while also lowering global energy prices.

The leader of the investor group is Todd Boehly, a billionaire asset manager and co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, among other holdings. He is also a major donor to Mr. Trump’s political causes. He contributed $1 million to Mr. Trump’s affiliated MAGA Inc. political committee last December, just as negotiations on the Lukoil deal were heating up.

Mr. Trump; his three sons; Mr. Kushner; Ivanka Trump, one of the president’s daughters; and the Witkoff family all have financial ties to partners in the deal, which requires sign off from the Trump administration and the Kremlin. The Trump family and the president’s advisers do not have a direct financial stake in the transaction. But their business partners would benefit financially if the multibillion-dollar deal is completed.

The investors who have teamed up with Mr. Boehly include one of the richest investment funds in the Middle East, International Holding Company, which is overseen by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family.

Sheikh Tahnoon separately runs outfits that own nearly half of World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded by Mr. Witkoff and still run by Zach Witkoff, one of Steve Witkoff’s sons. Donald Trump Jr. and Barron Trump, two of the president’s sons, also are stakeholders and co-founders of the company, and so they too are effectively business partners with Sheikh Tahnoon.

Sheikh Tahnoon, one of the most powerful players in Abu Dhabi and the United Arab Emirates, controls companies that oversee Lunate, an investment fund that took a major stake in the private equity firm Affinity Partners, which was set up by Mr. Kushner after he left the White House at the end of Mr. Trump’s first term.

Another investor in Mr. Boehly’s group is a pair of Syrian-born Qatari billionaires, Moutaz Al-Khayyat and his brother Ramez Al-Khayyat, who have partnered with Mr. Kushner and Ms. Trump to build a multibillion-dollar resort complex planned for the Mediterranean coast of Albania.

Trump administration officials are celebrating how the Boehly-backed deal would help U. S. energy security, as the package includes everything from oil production sites to refineries and gas stations. The U. S. government would also take a direct stake in the new enterprise via the U. S. International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that helps finance projects overseas. But given the makeup of the investment group, a large share of the resulting company — and the profits it creates — would be foreign owned, according to participants in the negotiations.

Approving the Boehly deal now being negotiated with the help of the White House would mean rejecting a competing offer from Carlyle, a Washington-based global investment management firm that already has investments in refineries in Europe. Carlyle’s bid, by comparison, would mean an all-American owner. But Carlyle does not have similar financial ties to Mr. Trump’s family and political advisers.

Eric Lipton is a Times investigative reporter, who digs into a broad range of topics from Pentagon spending to toxic chemicals.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Cornell Case Revives Anger About Handling of Campus Sexual Assault Cases

The New York Times October 03, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

A lawsuit alleging rape at Cornell has led to an outpouring of women sharing stories about sexual violence on college campuses.

By Stephanie Saul and Emma Goldberg

A lawsuit alleging rape at a Cornell fraternity house has set off a wave of anger among women on college campuses and beyond.

Campus sexual assault survivors and their supporters have published essays in school newspapers and inundated social media in solidarity with the complainant, known in court records only as Jane Doe.

Some are using the familiar #MeToo hashtag of an earlier movement to combat sexual abuse and harassment. Others have adopted a new one: #IAmJaneDoe.

In one opinion article in the University of Pennsylvania campus newspaper, students wrote that “sexual violence happens far too often on college campuses everywhere.”

“It’s time to face the fact that the ‘Cornell incident’ isn’t just born of Cornell problems, or limited to a Cornell issue,” the students wrote.

The outrage flooding social media and rising up on campuses follows similar waves of disgust about campus sexual violence that emerged more than a decade ago and then reignited after the broader #MeToo reckoning that began with Hollywood sexual assault revelations. Driving the campaign in support of Ms. Doe is a feeling that not enough changed after similar movements.

The Penn students wrote, for example, that past responses have been bureaucratic, and that universities “prioritize bolstering their own image” instead of making deeper changes that protect women from assault.

Celebrities have also joined the outcry. Mariska Hargitay and her Joyful Heart Foundation, which supports domestic violence survivors, posted: “Survivors deserve to be believed and kept informed. Silence protects no one. To her: we support you.”

During an appearance in Ithaca, N. Y., Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called the 2024 episode at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house part of a “culture of rape” on college campuses.

In the lawsuit, the young woman says she was assaulted at the Chi Phi house on Cornell’s campus, names seven men who were involved and says the university and law enforcement agencies did not do enough to punish or pursue prosecution of the men.

The men involved have denied the allegations, while the university, the fraternity and prosecutors have said they responded appropriately given the information they had at the time.

Lawyers point out the difficulty of prosecuting such cases in court, particularly when many complainants, including Ms. Doe, change their accounts over time. Records obtained by The New York Times present a murky picture of what took place. The woman indicated in one text message to one of the men that “nothing illegal” had happened. But she also told police investigators that “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.”

The widespread condemnation of accused men could create an unfair dynamic, according to Andrew T. Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the Cornell men, Gillio Lopes. He said the “danger in a case like this is that an accusation, amplified often enough, can harden into a verdict before the evidence is ever tested.”

Mr. Miltenberg, known for representing students against sexual misconduct claims, said the attention was compounded by statements of public officials that seemed to side with Ms. Doe.

On Sept. 28, Attorney General Letitia James posted on X: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and prayers.”

Several days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Ms. James to take over investigating the case.

Mr. Lopes has unequivocally denied the allegations, Mr. Miltenberg said.

The online outpouring in support of Ms. Doe has also led to a backlash, with some right-wing commentators condemning her and others trying to reveal her identity.

Federal data shows that nationally, there were 6,000 to 6,200 reports of rapes on campus a year from 2014 to 2019, or about eight to 11 per 10,000 on-campus students. But reports declined drastically during the pandemic years, when many students took classes remotely. Since then, they have begun to rise again.

The data does not show how many reports resulted in action or were substantiated.

But the available data suggests the problem has been widespread. Over a quarter of undergraduate women reported some form of nonconsensual sexual contact by physical force, or because they were unable to consent, according to a large survey of students conducted by the Association of American Universities in 2019.

That survey also found evidence of a growing awareness about rules and resources, as universities built out new policies and training.

At Cornell, a survey conducted by the university found that roughly one-third of undergraduate women said they had unwanted sexual experiences.

For some current Cornell students and recent graduates, reading Ms. Doe’s claims of assault has prompted them to share memories of their own experiences of sexual misconduct. Many said that the allegations weren’t entirely surprising because of how often they had heard about friends who said they had been assaulted at parties.

“To be honest, there are so many during my time there that it almost feels like it all blurs into one,” said Claire Ting, who graduated from Cornell last year and served in student government, referring to conversations with friends about upsetting sexual experiences.

“We would see posts and discussions talking about the sexual assaults that happened,” she added. “The buzz would die down and then it would happen again.”

The response, she said, was “hurdle after hurdle of bureaucracy.”

There have been other moments in recent decades when campus sexual assault has dominated the national conversation. When the documentary “The Hunting Ground” was released in 2015, for example, it galvanized a movement.

Lady Gaga sang the film’s theme song at the Oscars, where she was introduced by Joseph R. Biden Jr., then the vice president. At the time, statistics showed that one in four women on campus reported being sexual assault victims. Just months before the film’s release, the launch of a White House campaign to end campus sexual assault — “It’s On Us” — seemed to signal a changing tide.

More than a decade later, though, the allegations at Cornell prompted questions among survivors about whether anything has changed.

Kacey Lee, who graduated from Cornell in 2025, said she was both “shocked and not shocked” in the fall of 2024 when she heard about Ms. Doe’s reported assault.

“Being around frat culture and knowing how people can be there was a level of — not that I was expecting it, but I was not the most surprised,” Ms. Lee said.

While federal data shows that Cornell has reported as many as 28 campus rapes in some recent years, its on-campus undergraduate population is the largest of any Ivy League school. When adjusted for its size, Cornell mirrors many of its peer institutions.

Cornell officials have said they disciplined the men after investigating Ms. Doe’s allegations, but didn’t provide details. They have defended their response and cautioned against a “false narrative,” which they said could depress reports of sexual assault.

In a message on its website, the university said it had strengthened its policies around sexual assault in recent years. “Our goal is not simply to respond appropriately when sexual misconduct is reported,” the school said, “but to build a community in which sexual violence is prevented, people feel safe coming forward, those who do are supported, and individuals found responsible are held accountable.”

Elise Siemering, who has said she was raped 14 years ago by a fellow student at High Point University in North Carolina, said she found comfort in the social media outpouring.

“The women and men who say, ‘I am Jane Doe,’ it gives you a glimmer of hope that there are people in our nation who try to shield her as much as they can,” said Ms. Siemering, who was among more than 30 people who told their stories in the 2016 book “We Believe You.”

Annie E. Clark, whose allegations of sexual assault at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill served as the basis for “The Hunting Ground,” said this week that the growth of social media had, in some ways, helped women.

“With the advent of social media, more people are sharing their stories and know that they are not alone,” said Ms. Clark, co-founder of the organization End Rape on Campus.

Indeed, social media platforms are where the original #MeToo movement gained steam, a little less than a decade ago, spurred by disturbing disclosures about the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

Researchers at the University of Chicago documented the role of #MeToo on social media as a catalyst for social change, noting that the hashtag was used on Twitter, now X, 19 million times between 2017 and 2018, the first year of the movement, and in dozens of different languages.

The hashtag became “a sign of empowerment for victims who may have feared they were alone,” the researchers found.

But since then, a series of federal regulatory changes has created instability in the handling of campus sexual assault cases, according to Kenyora Johnson, chief executive of End Rape on Campus.

Referring to the release of “The Hunting Ground,” she said, “Eleven years later, we’re still talking about survivors struggling to be heard.”

The film was released shortly after a highly publicized incident at Florida State University, and featured a freshman who brought sexual assault claims against Jameis Winston, a Heisman Trophy winner who is now the starting quarterback of the New York Giants.

Before that accusation became public, a second woman had sought counseling after reporting a sexual encounter with Mr. Winston, saying that she felt violated by the incident.

Mr. Winston, who denied misconduct, was not prosecuted in the case, although a story in The New York Times raised questions about law enforcement handling of the inquiry. In 2016, both Florida State and Mr. Winston settled lawsuits filed by his accuser, according to reports at the time.

Although many of Cornell’s current students and recent graduates are too young to remember the #MeToo movement, they expressed frustration about the pervasiveness of sexual violence around them.

At a Cornell student government forum on Thursday afternoon, a junior, Jane Wang, came forward and said that she saw herself reflected in Ms. Doe’s experiences.

“I cannot speak on behalf of all survivors because the pain, hurts and trauma that each of us carries is our own,” Ms. Wang told the student government representatives.

Students warn one another about the risks of fraternity parties immediately when they get to Cornell, said Hannah Shvets, a senior who also serves on the Ithaca Common Council. Young women, she suggested, are largely left to fend for themselves.

“From the day we get to campus there’s awareness — be cautious, go in groups,” she said. “Students feel like often fraternities can partake in behavior that other clubs or organizations would get shut down if they did.”

Stephanie Saul reports on colleges and universities, with a recent focus on the dramatic changes in college admissions and the debate around diversity, equity and inclusion in higher education.

Emma Goldberg is a Times reporter who writes about New York City and the Mamdani administration.

‘How Does That Happen?’: America’s Execution System Is Long Flawed

The New York Times October 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The failed execution of Christa Pike, which left her clinging to life in Tennessee, was the latest grisly error to take place in an American execution chamber.

By Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs

The failed effort to kill Christa Pike has placed a harsh spotlight on the practice of capital punishment in America, one of 17 countries to carry out an execution last year, as well as the regularity with which those executions go awry.

Ms. Pike was given two doses of lethal pentobarbital but then rushed for medical care when it was clear she was still alive. She was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator in a hospital as of Thursday night.

“It is hard to see how this can be allowed to continue — not only in Tennessee, but nationwide,” said Maya Foa, the chief executive of Reprieve, an anti-death penalty group. She called the failed attempt to kill Ms. Pike “one of the most catastrophic executions” in U. S. history.

In 2025, 47 people were executed in the United States, more than in any year since 2009, though still below the peak of 98 executed in 1999. Yet even as technology has evolved and new tactics have been tried on death row prisoners, officials continue to botch executions.

Prisoners have suffered for long periods as doctors fail to find a suitable vein. Some have died in gruesome, unintended situations involving blood or flames. But Ms. Pike, who was convicted of murder in the 1995 killing of her classmate, survived, and is now part of a minuscule cohort of prisoners to have done so.

On Thursday, President Trump expressed disbelief at Tennessee’s error. “How does that happen?” he said. “It shouldn’t be very difficult.”

Mr. Trump, an outspoken advocate of capital punishment, began his second term by ordering prosecutors to pursue the death penalty in more cases. And in April, he said the Justice Department would allow additional methods of execution such as firing squads.

A majority of Americans continue to support capital punishment, but that backing has declined in recent decades, according to public opinion polls.

Ms. Pike’s botched killing was the second time this year that Tennessee officials failed to administer a lethal injection. In May, the state called off the execution of Tony Carruthers because staff members couldn’t find a suitable vein.

On Thursday, Gov. Bill Lee paused executions in Tennessee and called for a review of the state’s policies. Mr. Lee, a Republican, had ordered a similar review in 2022 after officials failed to properly test the drugs before an execution.

Many expressed frustration that a process meant to kill Ms. Pike ended with her being rushed for lifesaving care. The mother of Colleen Slemmer, the 19-year-old woman killed by Ms. Pike, said she’d been deprived of justice for her daughter’s killing.

While 27 states have the death penalty on the books, fewer than half of those have carried out an execution in the last five years. And several states have issued brief moratoriums, like Tennessee did, in recent years after errors in the death chamber.

Virginia, which over its history executed more people than any other state, became the first Southern state to abolish the death penalty in 2021, and Ohio’s governor said in June that he wanted his state to abolish it, too.

By far, the most common execution practice in America is lethal injection.

Lawsuits and pressure on drug suppliers have made these injections more difficult to carry out, forcing some states to explore alternate methods. South Carolina executed three men by firing squad last year, doubling the number of firing squad executions in modern times, and several other states have authorized the method.

One of the lawmakers who proposed the firing squad in South Carolina said he believed it was more instantaneous and caused less suffering than the electric chair.

The Death Penalty Information Center, a research group, says that lethal injection, introduced in 1982 as a more humane alternative to the electric chair, has had the highest failure rate in executions.

These failed attempts include the 2021 case of John Grant, who vomited and shook for several minutes during Oklahoma’s first execution since 2015, when it had mistakenly used the wrong drug to stop another prisoner’s heart.

In Alabama, executioners tried for hours to find the veins of Joe Nathan James in 2022 as he lay in the death chamber. They eventually sliced into one of his arms in what is known as a “cutdown” in order to give him the fatal drugs, according to a private autopsy.

And in 2024, Idaho executioners tried for nearly an hour to insert an intravenous line into the arms, then hands, and then legs of Thomas Creech, who was then 73. He remains one of eight people on Idaho’s death row.

Alabama pioneered another tactic in 2024, when it began killing prisoners with a nitrogen gas that deprives them of oxygen. State officials heralded the first nitrogen execution, of Kenneth Smith, as a new frontier.

“Alabama has done it, and now so can you,” said the state’s attorney general, Steve Marshall, encouraging other states to adopt Alabama’s protocol. One did: Louisiana carried out its first execution in 15 years last year, using nitrogen gas for the first time.

Several witnesses to Alabama’s execution, though, told The New York Times that they were disturbed by what they saw in the death chamber.

Mike Sennett, a son of Mr. Smith’s murder victim, Elizabeth Dorlene Sennett, said he was advised by officials that the prisoner would take a few breaths and succumb. “That ain’t what happened,” he said. “After about two or three breaths, that’s when the struggling started.”

“With all that struggling and jerking and trying to get off that table, more or less, it’s just something I don’t ever want to see again,” Mr. Sennett said.

That description is not dissimilar to those offered after the United States’ first execution by electric chair, in New York State in 1890.

A front-page headline in The Buffalo Evening News said the death of William Kemmler in Auburn “was an awful sight” and declared “the process a failure.”

In that execution, a doctor had announced Mr. Kemmler’s death only to realize, in a panic moments later, that he was still alive.

“This man is not dead,” the doctor cried, according to the Evening News account, and asked for the current to be turned back on.

Mr. Kemmler’s lips dripped, his chest moved, and he made a loud wheezing and groaning sound. Finally, he was again pronounced dead.

“FAR WORSE THAN HANGING,” The New York Times wrote on its front page on Aug. 7, 1890.

One doctor involved predicted there would never be another electrocution.

Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs reports on stories across the United States, including natural disasters, protests, unsolved mysteries, high-profile criminal cases and more.

Senate Races in Republican States Tilt Toward Democrats, Polls Find

The New York Times October 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democrats are performing strongly in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats to win control of the chamber, new New York Times/Siena polls found.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. Surveys

Among likely voters. Shaded areas represent the margin of error.

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 504 voters in Alaska conducted Sept. 24 to Oct. 1, 606 voters in Iowa conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1, 605 voters in Kansas conducted Sept. 22 to 30, 616 voters in Ohio conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1 and 615 voters in Texas conducted Sept. 21 to 30.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

By Patricia MazzeiRuth Igielnik and Sophia June

A month before the midterm elections, Democrats have opened leads or battled their way to ties or near-ties in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats to win control of the chamber, according to new New York Times/Siena University polls.

Democrats lead among likely voters in the Senate races in Texas and Alaska, two states that consistently vote Republican, the polls found. They have an edge in Ohio, which has been tilting rightward for years. Republicans have a slim edge in Iowa, and Democrats are neck-and-neck with Republicans in Kansas, which has not voted for a Democratic senator since 1932.

President Trump’s deep unpopularity, disapproval of the Iran war and frustration over high gas prices and the cost of living are reshaping the electoral landscape, the polls found.

Taken together, the new polls suggest that the Democrats have multiple paths to retake the Senate majority, despite a challenging map that had favored Republicans going into the midterms. To win Senate control, Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats while holding on to their current seats in three battleground states, a difficult task.

But there are signs that it is increasingly possible. On Friday, a top Republican super PAC pulled its money out of the Senate race in North Carolina, signaling that the party is not optimistic about being able to defend its seat there. The super PAC, called the Senate Leadership Fund, plans to redirect resources to Kansas, where Republicans have growing concerns about holding their seat.

The polling suggests Democrats are increasingly competitive in these Republican states.

Likely voters

Registered voters

Registered voters (Ohio), likely voters (Texas, Iowa)

Likely voters

Likely voters

Note: Margins are calculated using unrounded vote shares when available. Polls are not available for every state from all pollsters.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

[Follow all of the latest polls heading into November’s elections.]

In Texas, James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, has opened up a six-percentage-point lead in the race against Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued attorney general and Republican nominee who has been strongly supported by Mr. Trump.

Austin Vaughn, 30, an independent voter who works for a nonprofit and lives in the Houston area, said he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but plans to support Mr. Talarico this fall.

“He’s the one actually listening and hearing that those are problems,” said Mr. Vaughn, referring to rising costs. “And the Republicans on the other side are gaslighting everyone and saying they aren’t real problems.”

In Alaska, former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, is ahead of Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by seven percentage points. The polling aligns with the results of the state’s nonpartisan primary in August, when Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan appeared on the same ballot, and she won by eight points. A majority of voters there said that they viewed Ms. Peltola favorably; the poll was conducted after allegations of poor treatment toward her staff came to light.

In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, holds a narrow three-point edge in his comeback bid against Senator Jon Husted, the Republican incumbent, with voters saying they prefer the well-known Mr. Brown over Mr. Husted on nearly every issue in the poll. Mr. Brown has an 11-point advantage over Mr. Husted on the question of who would better handle the increasingly potent political issue of data centers, the poll found.

And in Iowa and Kansas, two Midwestern states that have been hit hard by the economic effects of Mr. Trump’s policies, the races are neck-and-neck. In Iowa, Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, has a one-point edge over State Representative Josh Turek, the Democrat. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, and Senator Roger Marshall are locked in a dead heat.

The polls suggest Democrats are performing well with independent voters, who often decide elections. Across the five states, Democrats hold a 24-point advantage with the group. On issue after issue, independent voters say they trust Democrats over Republicans — including a 30-point advantage on which party does what’s best for ordinary people in their state.

In all but one of the states, Democratic candidates are seen as less ideological than their Republican counterparts. In Ohio, voters were about equally concerned that the candidates were too ideological; 37 percent said they thought Mr. Brown was too far to the left, and 36 percent said Mr. Husted was too far to the right.

It is a striking transformation in five states Mr. Trump won every time he was on the ballot. In Ohio, which he carried with 55 percent of the vote in 2024, only 38 percent now approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance, down from 44 percent in June.

Soaring gas prices, which were driven above $4 a gallon by the Iran war, have continued to hurt the president’s popularity, particularly in the Midwest. About half of Republicans in Iowa and Ohio said that they disapproved of Mr. Trump’s handling of gas prices. Across all five states, Democrats are now more trusted than Republicans to handle the cost of living — reversing the advantage Mr. Trump had on the issue in those states just two years ago.

The New York Times/Siena Poll

Sept. Surveys

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 504 voters in Alaska conducted Sept. 24 to Oct. 1, 606 voters in Iowa conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1, 605 voters in Kansas conducted Sept. 22 to 30, 616 voters in Ohio conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1 and 615 voters in Texas conducted Sept. 21 to 30.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

“You used to be able to get a house — a pretty good house — for under $200,000,” said Bethany Deines, a 58-year-old Democrat in Hamilton, Ohio, who supports Mr. Brown for Senate. Homes in her area now go for more than double that, she added: “I mean, it’s just not manageable for everyday people to be able to really even afford quality housing.”

Perhaps nowhere is Democrats’ advantage more remarkable than in Texas, where Mr. Talarico has been boosted by a growing share of voters — now 60 percent — who say that he has the right kind of moral values, up from 51 percent in June.

Many establishment Republicans, including Senator John Cornyn, whom Mr. Paxton defeated in a primary, warned this year that Mr. Paxton was a flawed candidate who could put what had been seen as a safe Senate seat at risk.

The poll suggests that may have proved true, with a majority of Texas voters saying Mr. Paxton does not have good character. And 45 percent say his past scandals, including his impeachment over corruption charges and a messy divorce from his wife, make them question supporting him — or mean they will not support him at all.

But Mr. Paxton will have a big financial advantage heading into November. Republican groups recently began spending large amounts of money to prop him up, reserving about $190 million in ads supporting him for the final two months of the race.

About half of voters across the five states — 49 percent — say they want a candidate who can provide a check on the president, according to the polls. Just 27 percent say they would prefer candidates who support Mr. Trump.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. Surveys

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 504 voters in Alaska conducted Sept. 24 to Oct. 1, 606 voters in Iowa conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1, 605 voters in Kansas conducted Sept. 22 to 30, 616 voters in Ohio conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1 and 615 voters in Texas conducted Sept. 21 to 30.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Nowhere is that more apparent than Iowa, where 53 percent of likely voters, including nearly 20 percent of Mr. Trump’s own supporters, say they want a candidate who can provide a check on the president.

Brayden Blocker, an 18-year-old Republican and college student in Iowa City, said Congress should be “less extreme.”

“With the new Congress coming in, I would say that I think it should just be more moderate members that aren’t necessarily, like, just what Trump wants to do,” he said. “It’s what their constituents want to do instead.”

The divide in voter concern about parties being too ideological is particularly stark in Kansas, where voters are more likely by a 10-point margin to say that the Republican is too far to the right than to say that Mr. Hamilton, the Democrat, is too far to the left.

Senator Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent, is an obstetrician-gynecologist who filed lawsuits against hundreds of patients over outstanding bills, leading to the arrest of at least 81 patients, a New York Times investigation found. That has become an issue in the campaign.

Half of voters also say they worry that he will support Mr. Trump too much.

“You couldn’t pay me enough money to back Donald Trump or anybody that backs him,” said Alexis Price, 42, a travel adviser in Kansas City who said she does not align with either party. “I think what the Republican Party and a lot of the Republican nominees are doing is disgraceful and disgusting. And I have to vote to my conscience over any sort of party affiliation.”

Across the five polled states, Democrats hold an advantage on nearly every issue, including on the cost of living, which is the single most important issue to voters, along with the economy. Even Republicans’ edge on immigration is slipping. Republicans held just a three-point advantage on the issue across the five states.

Among the strongest measures for Democrats is that voters say that they trust them more to do what’s best for ordinary voters. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola has a eight-point advantage on that question.

Ms. Peltola is viewed very favorably by a majority of Alaskans, including 15 percent of Republicans, and has managed to grow her lead in a state that nonetheless favors Republicans continuing to hold control of the Senate.

“I see her out in the community,” said Jessica Romer, a 38-year-old Democrat in Anchorage. “And I just really like that she’s interacting with people, like getting to know them and what their needs and wants are.”
